SMITHSONIAN INSTITUTION

Interview with
Herman Autrey
Part One
Interviewed by John S. Wilson

Washington, D. C.
April 23, 1975

PRO-TYPISTS, INC.
PROFESSIONAL TRANSCRIPTION SERVICE
AREA CODE 202 347-5395
P R O C E E D I N G S
Okay, this is John WILSON with Herman Aufrey in his apartment at 710 East --
-- 740 East 178th Street. Herman, how long have you lived here?
About three months now. Here in this apartment you mean?
Yeah.
Yeah, about three months. Uh-huh.
And how big an apartment is this?
Two and a half, I would say three rooms, you know. This is the living room. The bedroom's there, and the rest -- and the kitchen and bathroom and business. How do you like it, by the way?
It's a very nice apartment. You walk in and it has a marvelously warm, friendly feeling.
Thank you.
It looks lived in.
(Laughter)
Well, I hope to live in it peacefully anyway.
Who lives with you here?
My wife and I. Uh-huh.
Just the two of you.
Just the two of us, yeah.
And your brother's here with us now too as we're doing this. He just walked in the door.
Yeah, he just walked in. He lives on Long Island, by the way.
On Long Island?
Yeah, uh-huh. East Elmhurst. It's a very beautiful place. They have a nice flower garden and everything.
You're a city type rather than a country type?
Well, after 50 or 60 years, you tell me.
(Laughter)
I've lived in the city so doggoned many years, I -- well, I would say I'm the city type. I like the outdoors, though. I like, you know.
Let's just
(Recording interruption)
"SEE INSERT"
Okay, this is -- VON just remembered --
Yeah.
(Laughter)
your mother
-- how I met your father. How does it happen?
(I) came from a musical family. My father, a couple of brothers (unitelligible), played bass. And a brother who played baritone.
Baritone horn?
Horn yeah. Brass horn...brass band. And a little brother played trumpet. And cousins...different instruments. We did pretty good.
How far back can you remember your family? Did you know your grandparents?
Oh, yes very well.
Who were your grandparents?
On my mother's side there was Sam Travis, and her mother was Winnie Travis. And I remember visiting her when I was four or five years old.
Did they live in the same town?

No, they lived out in the country. He was a minister, a very successful minister, I would say. He had...I think he was the owner of a 300-acre farm, and he was a minister. Good following. We used to go visiting him once in a while. It was a good distance away from the little town where I was born. I remember him very will; we had lots of fun, because there was all kinds of fruits around there--peaches, apples, figs, plums.
Was this a business for him? Did he raise these?

Yes, I mean most farmers had those trees on their properties, and when they came...if they could use them, if anybody wanted them, 'go help yourself', you know. And they would can them one way or the other. Most people did that.
That was on your mother's side. How about on your father's side?
Yes, I remember very well my father's...uh, uh... I'm trying to think, I forgot the old man's name...
Anderson

Anderson Autrey, that's right. And Minerve. My grandmother, she was a very sweet woman. I don't know, I always loved her. Everytime she'd come visit us, she'd always bring me a nickle, she'd reach in her pocket...evidently, she didn't have but just one, because that was the black-est nickel I had ever seen. I said this can't be any good. I'd look at it and shine it up til I'd get to the candy store. It was alright (laugh).
It was? (laughs).
Yeah.
You mean, every nickel she brought you is just as black as that?

It seemed to me that way. I don't know what year she'd had them and all of that. She was...I knew the people whom she worked for. She was born in slavery and my father was born out. She worked for these people a heck of a long time, and I think she helped them to raise a couple of families, there, because I went to visit them on their plantation, and my grandmother was working there. She was housekeeper and cook and whatnot. And this man at the plantation, he was a banker, his sons and whatnot were (unitelligible) people, you know?
Was this the same family she had been in slavery to? That she worked for afterwards?
Yes.
Now, what did your father do?
My father was a brick layer. And he was very good too, because he taught...
No, not your father, I'm sorry, I mean your grandfather on your father's side.
Oh, he was a farmer. You know, one of those two or three-acre farmer. They starve to death from the day they start until the day they die. 'Cause ...never get anything out of it.
Not like mother's father, who had all the acreage and everything.
No, no.
Very different. Now, where abouts did Anderson Autrey live?

He lived in the little town, Evergreen, where I was born. He lived there, in and aroud. And as I say, my mother, she always wanted somebody out of the family to be a preacher and farmer. And I couldn't see anything in that business. (laughs)
Do you know how you mother and father met?
Let me think. No, I've heard them talk about such things, though, so many times. But really... Von, do you know how Mama and Papa met? Did you ever hear them say?
It was always a secret, I think. (laughter)
Von says "it was always a secret".
We talked about our lives, 'Cause my mother, understand, had been married before.
Oh, I see. She had been?
And when she met my father she had four children.
Oh, so you have four step-siblings.
Yeah, three boys and a girl.
Had your father been married before?
No.
Now, you were born in Evergreen, Alabama, when?
December 4, 1904.
(Recording interruption)

Yes, my father was introduced to my mother by a good friend of hers and a neighbor of ours who lived next door, and Von just reminded me that my father played baseball. He was a very good baseball player, and a good musician, which he and worked, played together in the same band, you know, in the beginning. And that's how they got married. And -- but since Mother was married before -- and I think Yvonne said Papa was kind of hard to get.
(Laughter)
He's kind of, you know, so --
He hadn't tried it himself.
No, no, no. So he was introduced to Mother, and after that I think she won him over. I'm quite sure she did. Quite sure she won.
Were you the first child?
Yes. And then Von.
And you were born in Evergreen. How many more came after you?
One.
Just one?
Von and me, yeah.
Von is his full name?
Well, it's a complicated thing. It's Le Von Autrey, but there's then some before that, you know.
(Laughter)
Yeah, a Greek lady named him.
Oh?
So you can imagine what --
Le Von Autrey.
(Laughter)
Why was he named by a Greek lady?

Well, she was a very good friend of my mother. They were, for years they were friends. She'd come to my house and sit on the step with my mother, and she would -- they would talk, and she'd bring a basket. Always I can see it was a little basket now on her arm, and she'd have some goodies in there. Each time she came -- some kind of cake, candies or something she had made and she wanted my mother to taste it, and every so often my mother would pick out a day she would go to her house and take me along, you know, and they would sit and talk for a couple of hours. I don't know what they were talking about.
(Laughter)
I would be looking for someplace to play, but they were very, very good friends.
Where did your name come from, Herman? Was that a family name or what?
No, no. This is a good story, because you see when I came, being the first, you see. Going to name him junior? My father said no, never, said, one Moses in the
family was enough. His name, we didn't get to that, his
MR. WILLISON: (Inaudible). name was Moses.
(Laughter)
He said that's enough, and I'm glad he stuck with it.
What was your mother's name?
M-a-r-i-n-a, Marina. Marina.
Marina? That's an unusual name.
It is.
Was that from a Greek lady too?

No, no. No, my mother's family were more or less Indians, the greater part, her mother and her father, the greater part Indians, you know, and -- I have a picture of her around there somewhere. You can see her looking like a squaw. I show it to you before you go.
(Laughter)
Herman, whereabouts in Alabama is Evergreen? What's it near?

Well, that's -- it's on the L & N line there below Montgomery. In fact it's 81 miles below Montgomery on the L & N line of the trains, you know, and this -- well, Brewton, Alabama, is 20 miles below. You're on the way to Mobile, in other words, that section between Montgomery and Mobile, you know.
When you were growing up in
Evergreen, what was going on there, what -- was there any kind of business?
(Simultaneous remarks)

Yes. Yes. Factory -- in fact I worked in there, at this factory. It was a basket factory where they made strawberry crates and all kinds of boxes and crates for this and for that, and I worked in there, my brother too, 75 cents a day.
75 cents a day? How old were you at that time?

Oh, must have been about ten or 12 maybe or something like that. And -- well, they would go out to cut down the pine logs. It was very -- it was quite interesting to see them prepare the logs for this. They put them in a big vat deep as this room, maybe deeper, so it was water and different chemicals, and they'd boil this thing. They'd let them really -- actually cook them, and then when they got to where they wanted to take them out and put them in a machine, and it was like you put an apple -- a pivot on each end of an apple and let it slowly turn over. As it turned, the knife would shave it to the size of boards that they wanted, and you can imagine a strawberry crate. You know how thin they are?
Yeah, I've seen them.
You can imagine how thin.
(Laughter)
And you get you a million of those things and you try to make -- I think I got three cents a crate for making them.
Gosh!
(Laughter)
Two and a half to three cents, and that was -- they thought that was big money. I tried that for a few days, but I couldn't make it. I really couldn't. I put it down.
(Laughter)
You were saying that your whole family was musical. When did you first start playing anything?

Well, about four or five years old. Naturally, My father had the tuba there, and he -- actually, the tuba was bigger than me, and he said -- he'd tell us, don't touch this. I'm going to work. Don't bother it because if it falls, it'll break, and I'll have to have it fixed. So he says, besides, you can't lift it. It's too heavy for you. So I figured out how I could play the doggoned thing and still be a good boy. I used to crawl on my belly over to the thing because he had it sitting on the bell, and I lay on my belly and take and blow into it and make a whoo -oo-oo, until I got so I could blow. So I'd have myself some fun, and I'd play the
doggone thing until I got tired, and he come home. It was sitting right here where he left it. He had no way of knowing that I had bothered it.
Were you actually getting any notes out or just --
Well, not at first, but shortly, yes, I did get notes out, and I could play it, I guess, so I could play it. Then my brother brought his instrument home, the pck horn, you know --
Are you talking about Von or one of your stepbrothers?
Stepbrother. No, later in the years Von played guitar.
I see.

And I could pick that thing up, so I picked it up. I didn't like it, but I got so I could blow it, and they put me in the band. n-too-n-too-n-too-too-too-too, you know, the alto horn or peck horn, what they called it, so playing marches, light overtures, things like that.
Were you able to read music at all?
Oh, yes.
How had you learned? Had your father taught you or --
Yeah, my father helped me quite a bit, but the same man who taught my father taught me.
Oh? Who was that?
Nick [Longmeier].
[Longmeier?]
Yes, I remember he used to -- well, we had about 50 kids in what we called cadet band, like the -- what is that name the kids have today? We called them cadets then.
Boy scouts?

Yeah, and all of us had instruments, and we used to take a piece of wood, and you had to -- and a knife and hew you out a gun, shape of a rifle, you know, and paint it, and then we had the bandanna, handkerchief around and the little uniforms, and the thing would be --
(Laughter)

Used to drill us, and we got the band started. I remember we used to go every night. It cost us ten cents a lesson then. He had this cue stick from a poolroom and a huge blackboard with the five lines or spaces, all that sort of written up there and the notes, and he would take and --
(Laughter)
And that's where we started the whole old solfeggio.
The old solfeggio, and how old were you at that point?
Oh, I must have been -- see, because, well, I was playing in the band, the alto, when I was about
ten or 12, so, you know --
Now which of your brothers was it who had the peck horn that you --
That was -- his name was Sammy. He was named after his grandfather, S. J. We -- because they had so many long names in between.
(Laughter)
We called him S. J., another one was called H. B. He's the only one that didn't bother with the music, and another brother, Theophilus, the same Greek lady named him.
(Laughter)
Was there a sister too?
Yes, Edith.
Edith. Well, that's a simple name. Now their last name wasn't Autrey, I suppose.
No, no, Harris.
Harris, I see. And so it was Sam Harris who actually got you started with the peck horn.
Yeah, uh-huh, and then Theophilus, he helped me quite a bit.
What did he play?

Well, he played the baritone and trumpet. In fact he was playing trumpet up until it got time to go into the Army in the First World War, and I was playing the peck horn, and I had to switch to the trumpet, and I
was able to and strong enough to play lead trumpet because they had no trumpet player in the band.
That was your first experience with the trumpet then?
Yeah. And afterwards I switched over and started playing -- I knew all the marches anyway, and --
You must have been what, about 14 at that time?

Yes, close to it, because when they went up to go to the Army, to go to war, I was playing in the -- of course, my mother didn't like that because all the men in the band, the old men with the handlebar mustache --
(Laughter)
And everytime she says, they're out there killing my poor child, blowing his brains out and what --
(Laughter)
-- because every time they'd have a kind of a convention, Sunday school convention or whatnot, whatever, they'd have the band come out, you know, and play and --
Were you the youngest one in the band then?
Yes, uh-huh.
Von and there was -- were there 20 year olds too in it?
Oh, well, they were much older. They
were like my father, you know, much older.
How was it? It went all the way up to much older people, but I suppose there were some in between.

Well, the leader's son, he and I was about the same -- were about the same age, and he played trumpet, but they had to take him out. He was too weak. He was physically weak, you know. I think the doctors told him no, but I kept on.
Well, at this point -- when you were playing trumpet, did you play anywhere except in this band, or was that the extent of your playing?

That was the extent of my playing, with the exception, I had -- I got a couple of nights work that really cut wherever they knocked me up. The first time I had ever played in the band -- in fact there lived next door to me a lady who was married to one of the finest trombone players ever.
What was his name?
I can't recall his name -- Martin -- Jerry Martin. He was with the Silas Green shows. Did you ever hear of that?
Silas Green shows.
Yeah, a minstrel show.
A minstrel show?
Yeah, uh-huh. Well, all the minstrels

used to come in, naturally, come into to town, and when we -- I used to -- four or five years I used to sit and watch. They couldn't get me away because that music -- I don't know. It meant so much to me. And my father would take me by the hand and go -- let me go and hear until it got too -- kind of late. And he'd bring me home, and he'd go back out.

Now Jerry Martin, he was friends with a lady lived next door. They were very good friends. And I used to hear him play, and I talked with him, and he encouraged me to keep studying, whatnot, and the parades, you know how they used to parade through the street with the red coats on and shiny instruments, and this, and this is the trombone. Oh, man, that was it! And that was about -- let's see -- Rabbit's Foot Minstrel, all of them.
Was Rabbit's Foot Ma Rainey's show?

No. Ma Rainey, that's different, but I knew Ma Rainey, played for her. Sure. Knew Ma Rainey. And the minstrel -- you asked me the first job, they gave a dance in Brewton, Alabama, that was about 20 miles from Evergreen. And they were short of a man. They needed somebody to be the trumpet player, and so they got ahold of me and asked me to come down and join them. And I'd never played a dance before in my life.
And, well, the argument was talk your mom into it.
(Laughter)

She said, well, I don't know, and maybe but -- I said, but Mother, that's a chance. She said, but in a dance hall, and she couldn't see it. Nothing about in the dance hall, but when you mention the dance hall, it was out, you know. I mean a preacher's daughter --
And was she a religious woman herself?

Oh! Very much so, yeah. And finally I talked her into letting me go, and I went down to play this dance hall, and in this dance hall with these lights and, you know, the guys in there tuning up their horns and a piano. I never played with a piano before. Had a banjo, clarinet, and the first time I'd ever seen a man play trap drums. That's what they called them then. And it was usually -- in a minstrel show it was one guy playing the snare and played it, you know, on the shoulder, and the guy with the bass drums and the cymbals, you know.

But this was all in one, and I was amazed, and he was doggone good too. And we started playing, and everything, to my mind, everything was going fine, and a big man, huge guy walked in the door and pulled out one of those big Texas pistols, I call it.
(Laughter)
About two feet long?
Yes. He says, don't a man make a move until I make this shot! And, well -- pss-s-s-s -- people
[ scattering ]
start straddling to make it.
(Laughter)

So the clarinet player -- I never forget this -- he jumped behind me and he said, 'now don't move. Don't move. Stand still now. Don't get excited. Don't move. Stand right there. This is how I lost my eye.' He was one eyed.
(Laughter)
Jesus, this is how I lost my eye. Somebody stuck him struck me in the eye in the dark. And I said, you're hiding behind me?
(Laughter)
Man, don't move. Stand right here and protect me, he's saying to himself. And he was an older man. And I was just -- a little boy. Well, nothing happened, but --
What was the instrumentation of the band?
Oh, it was -- let me see. I don't know whether I told -- piano, banjo, trumpet, bass fiddle, yes, bass fiddle, drums --
Clarinet, you mentioned.
Yeah, clarinet player.
Trombone?
No, I don't remember trombone, no.
Do you remember the music you played, what kinds of things they were?
Sort of. I couldn't right off tell
you what tunes, but a few of them I had heard before because in Evergreen we had, to my mind, had the best string band that -- in the world, I thought, because -- huh?
What kind of a string band?
Mandolin, guitar, bass fiddle, small violin and voices.
And playing what kind of material?
Well, they were playing --
(Simultaneous remarks)
Pop, or yeah, and a little ragtime and those schottische, what they called schottische.
Schottisches?

Yes, and voices, and those guys were beautiful, and I can remember about 6:00 o'clock, five or 6:00 o'clock in the morning. We were sleeping, you know. They'd be coming back from a party, and they worked for the rich people, of course. That's where they got their money. And you could hear them, mm-m-m-m, hear the music, and if you happened to awaken and hear it, you'd think you were -- this was it, the pearly gates, --
(Laughter)

-- because it was so pretty, you know? Beautiful! And I remember those guys, Coleman Simpson; a mandolin player, he was called Jackfish, tall, 6'3" or 4". He was that tall, and he was good, sharp all the time. And most of the time -- I can
see them now wearing those derby hats and shoes shined to perfection. I mean their suits pressed.
What kind of suits did they wear? What did they wear to play? Did they have a uniform?
No, no, they were box back, because that was the latest then.
Box back coats?
Yeah, and they were tailor made -- and money -- and you could see them, if you look at some of the material, the material spoke for itself. It was you paid for that, you know.
(Laughter)
But you were saying that you knew the tunes that the band you were with played because you heard the string band play them.
Yeah, I'm trying to think of the name of some of them. Way back -- that was so doggone far.
So far -- let me ask you something else. Were you reading from music or --
No, not then. No. I could read music, but they didn't have any music. I had to listen to them, use my ear to follow them to play what they were playing, you know.
Sit out for one chorus while you found out what it was kind of way?
Yeah, and you listen, they lead into it, and
you join them and you felt sure enough of yourself, you'd go ahead and play the melody, play something, whatever you felt like playing, you know?
Was it all ensemble playing, Herman, or did people take solos?

Well, they took solos after they knew what they were doing. Then the ensemble, for those guys had such fine ears harmonies and voices too. I mean you heard, you know, you heard that stuff. It was terrific.
Are you talking about the band you were with or the string band?
Well, both. I only worked that one night with this dance band. That was a -- that was enough of that, I think. My mother heard about the other part of the story, and no more, you know.
(Laughter)
Well, what became of your career with dance bands? Did it just stop there?

Well, then, as far as I can say, then I'd start -- I was playing in the church choir and then playing in the brass band because we'd go -- they took us here and there for different, say, conventions, you know, take the entire band, and, as I was saying to you, we had this blackboard -- had 50 young kids. We have 50 pieces in the band, but only one came out, and that was Herman. For some
reasons, the other guys quit. You know.
So you were the one graduate of that school, huh?
Yeah.
(Laughter)
And, well, when you say you were the only one who came out, how long was this, a year's training or what?
Well, no, I stayed in there until I went to school, you know,to boarding school and continued my musical education in school.
In school. Where did you go to boarding school?
Calhoun.
Where was that?

That was also in Alabama. That's the name of the little town, Calhoun. That's about -- that was not too far, well, 27 miles below Montgomery, and it was a subsidiary of Tuskegee. It was, you know, connected.
Was this the usual thing for a boy to do, like you to go away to boarding school like that? Or was it --
Yes, it was. You know, it was the usual thing in that, you know, the kids who could afford it, parents who could afford it sent them to Tuskegee.
I see.
But this was a school, Calhoun, they allowed you to work. You could go on the farms there and work and trade, you know, how they make --
Learn a trade? (Inaudible).
Yeah, where they build things. I worked in the blacksmith shop for quite a while there, and learned to make horseshoes and plows and fix plows and wheels and learned quite a bit.
Was it mostly a technical, vocational education that they gave you, or did they have -- English mathematics, did you get all that, too~ (simultaneous remarks)
Oh, yes.
-- in addition to the --
Uh-huh. Oh, yeah. Sure, uh-huh.
How much music did you get there?

Well, I got quite a bit because my cousin, she married the professor of Hampton Institute when he came there. He was quite a musician. He was -- had been in the First World War and playing clarinet, and he got his musical education from Hampden.
We're now past the First World War now, huh? We're into what, like 1920's?
Yeah, well, yeah. Yeah, because I entered -- what -- school in 1919? 1918? Yeah. And I came out in '23, something, yeah, '23. And by me playing trumpet

when I went there, it helped to encourage the group. In fact they didn't have a band. And I was so lonesome after I got there because the horn that I was playing in Evergreen wasn't mine, which means I had to leave it.
Oh, I see. Who did it belong to?
Well, it belonged to - - the man who owned the baseball team. He owned everything.
(Laughter)
[McDowell.]
And he had (inaudible).
Well, he owned all the instruments.
Oh, I see. He owned the whole --

Yeah, because the band that my brother and father in law played, they got the instruments for these guys, and they could use them here and there, you know, as they wished. And what a ball team they had. Oh, man, it was quite something. And I used to play drums, snare drum, marching around advertising the baseball game, and they give us free tickets, you know.
I see. So let me ask you, when you went off to boarding school, you had no trumpet, and there was no band.
Yes, so I looked around and I found a piece of trumpet. I think it had one valve in and one valve -- it needed a valve. Yeah, but it was jammed and somebody

had sat on it or something. And I got over to the thing, and I kept looking and asking, and finally I got a valve to get in there, and I got it in working condition, and what a happy man! That was me. And I used to play it, and I started playing taps, which they didn't have anybody to play taps there then, and they give me a whole big thick book that he brought back from the Army, you know.
Oh, I see.
And I learned all the calls, the things they used to play to make them --
You must have changed that school a little bit, didn't you?

I think I really did. So somebody said, well, let's have a band. It was different -- rich schools each year had given them so much. They would give instruments. They had trunks and -- I found out later they had trunks and trunks of instruments.
Really?
All kinds of instruments, oboes, flutes, anything you could mention.
In playable condition?

Yes. And this one, somebody picked this one up and and ruined it and sat on it and what-not, so they had the others under lock and key, so I found out later, and they had everybody come down and try out for
the band and see what they could do. So we had about 16 trumpets, 16 18, 18 clarinets. So they asked me -- the cousin of mine asked me to teach the trumpet --
I see.
-- because I was capable and able because I came there playing.
Now none of these kids could play an instrument when you started. They just passed out the instruments.
No, only Herman.
Just Herman and --
And the leader.
I see. Let's stop here just a minute, Herman. We're coming to the end of this tape.
(End of Tape One.)
We did have to pay something but not as much as you did on that.
Well, how did the Calhoun happen to be here, Herman, what caused it to come into existence? that existed?

Well, as I remember the story, and it's a very nice story, because our sister went there also before me or Von. And she used to tell us so much about Calhoun. It was founded by two girls, two women, Mrs. Thorn and Miss Dillingsworth, of England, and they were from Boston, and they set the boarding school up and, as my brother called it -- I

think it's a good word for it -- like a charity thing because they got money from different rich people, was handed down from different rich people, and trunks and trunks of clothes, yes, clothes, instruments, shoes. I can remember now all those things and the tweeds, the tweed suits and things they used to get. You remember those?
Oh, everything under the sun, even props for the stage for the plays we gave and we had and, oh, and barrels and barrels of candy, you know. Oh, I remember all --

Yes, it was really nice, and they -- these two women organized -- this thing going, and it was really something. And I used to -- I remember now, Dr. Dickenson, he was -- oh, what a man! He reminded me so much in voice later on that I got out of school of the Barrymores.
Oh, really.

Yeah, the way he -- the kind of the way his delivery, because I remembered one time there, one commencement, each -- they would pick out a student, encourage -- aiming at all of us, I guess, to participate and rendering some kind of -- well, I called it then a speech -- recitation.
(Laughter)
Yeah, and they would get somebody to tutor you to help you, and Dr. Dickenson had me, and he'd sit way away from me so --

'okay, all right, commence," and scared me to death, almost, and that stuff. He said no, no, don't sit that way, and he would come in, and just listening to him, oh he made it sound like music. It was beautiful. And I tried talking, mimicking him somewhat, trying to have round tones, and round, you know. And I did pretty good.
(Laughter.)
What was Dr. Dickenson? Was he the head of the school?
Well no, he was a minister there. He was (unintelligible.)
In Calhoun?
Yeah.
He wasn't necessarily attached to the school.
Well, yes.
He was, yes.
Yes, yes.
Yes, he was a one of the -- what do you call it? -- the trustees? One of the trustees.
Yeah, he was connected, yeah.
And a minister.
Cause he -- yeah, cause he was the brother-in-law of Mrs. -- of the one who founded the school.
I see.
Cause he was married to her sister.
Uh-huh.
Herman, you were talking before about learning all of the calls, the Army calls and everything.
Yes.
And you started doing them around the school. What became of all that?
Well, the calls?
Yeah, the ones I'm doing that (inaudible), What did it all lead to?
Well, I was playing in the band every day, you know, I was in -- I became assistant band leader.
Oh, by this time the band has been formed. We'd like before, when you were just going to start taeching the kids.
Yes.
Let's go back to that, then.
In six months, or less, I think we played a concert.
Really?
At the school there.
That's incredible.
Well, some marches, and light overtures.
By how -- could you teach them to play
all these different instruments, instruments that you didn't know how to play yourself?
Well brass, I know how to play all the brass, and the leader --
How about the woodwinds?
He was the -- claimed that he knew all the --
Oh.
-- woodwinds, and he taught them, so from the bass, trombone, anything in brass, I knew from a kid, and I taught them.
I see.
Yeah.
And in six months you gave a concert.
Yeah, we --
Of marches.

Marches. We marched out on the parade grounds there, and played a march, and later on, see, we went into the chapel and we did something, and then -- I never will forget, we went to Greenville, went to Greenville, Alabama. (Laughter.) And we marched, and I can hear those guys now, we had some big helicon tuba, and the great big tubas, and big basses, and we went to -- went on to what you call, the bridge, and guys got in there, Boom! Boom! Boom! I thought the bridge was going to take off.
(Laughter.)
How big was the band?
We must have had over fifty.
Oh, that big?
Oh sure.
Well no wonder the bridge --
Some of the guys weren't so bad there, you know, because you listen to the next guy to you, and that helps, and you had a little couple of salvos in --
You know if any of them, except you, became professionals?
Aw, I don't think so. I don't think so. No, not of the Calhoun band, no. No. There was a clarinetist there, Jack -- not Jack Butler. Hmmm.
His name was Butler.

Yeah, his name was Butler, but he kept playing. He played a doggone nice clarinet. In fact, the teacher came in one day, we were teaching the -- I was teaching to trumpet, and he was showing me the clarinet, and I was running the scales, and ohhhh, (the leader) man, he gave it to me. Put that thing down! Learn how to play the trumpet. That'll be enough. That day'll come when you'll be all right (unintelligible). So I put it -- I didn't bother any more. I stick with the trumpet.
Now this was your school for four
Hm, yeah, four or six. (Inaudible.)
You were there five years.
Five years, yeah.
And all five years you were involved with the band.
Yeah.
And in the course of the five years, did you extend the repertoire beyond the marching band pieces? Did you do other things?
Well, we had a little combo there that we used to get together downstairs in the boys' dormitory, and make a lot of noise. And no --
Just for your own pleasure, not dances or anything.
No, no dances, no. No. That wasn't allowed.
Oh (laughter). Then from the time that first dance you played, before you went to Calhoun, you didn't play dances at all anymore after that?
No, didn't play.
You didn't get out and do that.
No, I don't remember that. No, but
when I came -- when I came out of Calhoun, came -- left Calhoun, came to Pittsburgh.
Why Pittsburgh?
Well, I had a brother living there with his family.
Which brother was that?
Al -- Theophilus.
Yeah.

Uh-huh, and as soon as we could I got a hold of a trumpet, and one of those big Arbon books, Italian insurance man, he came in one day and saw me playing and he said, 'You play the trumpet?' I said, well, he said, 'Play something.' So I played. He said, 'I'm going to bring you something.' Next time he came to collect my brother's insurance he brought this big Arbon book, and I still have it, and that was 1924.
And what was in it?

Well, it's a music book. In other words, it's a (snaps fingers) exercises over everything. Everything. It's about that thick. He said, 'If you learn to play anything in this book,' he said, 'You don't have any more worries,' and he's right.
Herman, -- before you left Calhoun, what -- were you hearing any music? Was there anything for you to hear down there?
No, Only the minstrel shows.
Minstrel shows.
Minstrel shows and circuses, and things like this. Yeah.
So was that the -- that and marches, was the extent of your musical knowledge at that time?
At that point, uh-huh, uh-huh.
When you got to Pittsburgh, did you start hearing other things?

Oh, yes. Heard things like dance bands. Just a minute, before I leave Alabama I'd like to -- no, I heard him later. I'm sorry. Because I want to -- his son, from his son's a movie star. He played trombone. He played trombone himself, had his own band, white.
White? White?
Yeah --
Had his own band? Urble Herbie Green?
Oh no, no.
(Laughter.)
He wasn't even heard of then. I'll think of him.
Tell me this, Herman, why, even though you had a brother in Pittsburgh, what was the reason for leaving Alabama?
Well I came out of school in 1923, and
nothing there. I wanted to go where I could make a dollar. Yeah.
I see. Was Theophilus the only relative you had who wasn't in Alabama?
At that time?
Yeah.
No, they were scattered here and there. Because one of the brothers was living in Mississippi. He was down --
One of them.
Yeah, he was down in Mississippi, and he didn't bother music any more. He went into something else.
Did you go with Theophilus because of the music? Because he play.

Well, I had to -- well, not exactly. Yes, I could say yes and no. I had to have some place to live, and I never being east, or north, or I'd never been out of Evergreen, only just a couple little places around there, you know? So I felt I had something to offer, and I wanted to get out where I could play my horn, and that was my interest, and the chance to further my education, if I could, and that was a --
At that point had you decided what you wanted to do was play your horn? That was what --
Well I decided that when I was four

years old. I mean they tried to stop me. I said no, So my dad took me aside. He said, "You sure you want to play music, want to play this thing?" I said yes. He said, "Well I'm going to tell you, if this is what you want you've got to be good. You can't be pretty good. You got to be damned good." This is what he said. And he didn't swear.

My father, he -- you never heard -- don't hear him say any kind of a bad word, anything, you know? He said, "You really got to be good." I said, "Well, okay. I'm ready to try." He said, "In other words, you've got to get in there." He said, "You can't be pretty good." So I found out what he meant, because I had a chance to work with some of the best. I met somewhere everybody, I guess, and played with them some time or other. And I knew what he meant.
When you first got to Pittsburgh, where did you get a trumpet?

I think my brother picked me one up in the pawn shop. I'm sure it had to be. He couldn't -- it wasn't new, and -- but it was a pretty good horn. And I met some guys around, and we -- give you a kind of idea what kind of musicians I was playing with. Two guys worked at the factory there, two brothers. Both of them had saxophones. One had tenor, the other had alto, and I mean they were gold instruments. Oh, they were beautiful instruments.
And we got together, and we were going to play, play

for a little dance, or something. I said, "Come on, let's tune up." He said, "I'm tuned." I said, "Well, let's get the A with the piano, there." He said, oh no, this horn -- this is a brand new Conn Karnes, this is made in tune. I don't have to tune it."
(Laughter.)

And we argued that for a good -- I said everyone tunes their horn. Oh no, see flat, you don't touch that, you know, you don't supposed to pull that out and push this in over there. This is a brand new -- and it was. It was shining like brand new gold. And don't you know, he didn't -- first I thought he was making a joke. And naturally, when we did start playing, or blowing together, you can imagine what. (Laughter.)
Well when you did start playing, or blowing together, what were you playing? Had you heard jazz by then? Were you into that?
Oh, yeah, well sure, because at that time, 1924, and before then you had Earl HInes, you had -- heavens, I'd heard some --
You mean in Pittsburgh.
Yeah.
But I mean before you arrived in Pittsburgh, and got your trumpet, did you get a chance to hear any jazz?

Yes. I had records of Mamie Smith, 'Yellow Hound Dog,' and whatnot, and that stuff. You know. I usually didn't have the -- I had the records, and what, Bessie Smith, Mamie Smith, and I started running to all that, and I finally met them and knew them personally, and played for them, and that was a thrill. Yeah.
When -- did you hear any of Louie Armstrong's records at that point, with ---
Between '23 and '24? Yes. Yes, I'd be -- I heard, because he was at that time, he was in Chicago.
Yeah. Yeah.
And pretty soon there, you know, I had spread it how he got around, and listened to him, and other guys like him, and still there's never been but one Louie Armstrong. Never will be.
Well, how did you -- you first heard him on a record, I guess, didn't you?
Yeah, uh-huh.
You remember when it was? What your reaction was? What the record was?
I'm trying to think. Doo, doo, doo, doo, doo, doo, doo. It's been so doggone long. make these things come back.
It's hard to remember.
Yes it is. It is. Uh-huh.
Well we'll talk, and maybe it'll --
we'll sort of get into it. Let's sort of get back to the beginnings of you're being in Pittsburgh. Did you get a job? A non-music job?

Yes, I had a job working at Thompson's Restaurant, dishwashing. And that I'll never forget. I earned -- I was making, what, $16.00 a week. And I got paid, and -- this was a little later, not too much later, because some show came in town. It was there, and they needed a trumpet player, so I went to the theater and sat in the pit to rehearse the show. They wanted to try me out and see if I was capable of playing the music, you know, the show, and the dancing girls. I'd never seen girls in tights and things before.
(Laughter.)
So I said man, this is it. You know?
(Laughter.)

I always did like the girls, you know? Oh yes. So I had my money in a wallet. Somebody took my wallet out of my hip pocket there while I was rehearsing, you know. And I felt back there for my wallet. I'd just gotten paid, and my $16.00 bucks is in there. Man, I almost died. And every since then I never put five cents in my wallet since.
(Laughter.)
Never! I have a wallet now --
You carry an empty wallet around?
No, well I haven't -- my wallet is fat, cards, all kinds of addresses and cards, and stuff, but not one five cents.
Well I won't ask you where you keep your money, though.
(Laughter.)
How did you make out with the show? Aside from the wallet.

It was okay. It was -- because this guy, I found out later, he was world's best con artist, and he asked me if I would go with the show, could I go. I said I don't know, you have to talk to my brother. So he met me then. He outtalked my brother naturally, you know, and I wanted to go, and he said, 'Well I don't know. He's never been away from home. And I don't want him -- where you going?' 'Well, we're going to Chicago,' he told him. He said, 'That's not far.' And Indiana. 'We'll be in and around this section.' Phooey! We went out the first time we went out, man, Chicago, was at the Coppen Coburn Theater, and that was the worst. And just --
Why? Why? Why was it bad?
Well, it was just -- south of Chicago there, and the theater was falling down, and finally did altogether fall down, had such a bad name, and the shows had
been playing there, so we didn't -- didn't earn a dime. Didn't draw a dime, and naturally we couldn't get paid, so we went from there to Indiana, South Bend, Indiana, and got stranded. So we --
That's a good way to break in.

Yeah, we got there and couldn't get out, and they gave us -- they gave us cards, cause he -- you know, you go to the restaurant, and eat, and the man would punch your food card, you know. And naturally had to -- he said allright, don't eat too much. And the man who owned the restaurant didn't want you to eat too much, because he wanted to know where his money was coming from, see? So that ran out, that was gone. That didn't pan out.

So we came -- we got booked in -- we came back to Chicago, and got booked in (snaps fingers) -- that state, I haven't been in it since I don't know how -- I hate it. You leave Chicago going west, big cattle state.
Hm?
It's a big cattle state.
You mean Nebraska?
Nebraska, Omaha Nebraska. That's it Actually, that's the place --
You got booked in --
Whoooo , and from Chicago, the girls got some material, and they sat down and started

sewing, making costumes, because where they -- the last place they played they kept the costumes lack of money, they ate them up. The man wanted to have his money for his food, so he kept the costumes, and it made some more on the train, and we got to -- I don't know, they had all new -- (Laughs) had enough to go on stage, and do several numbers, and that's just what they did.
Now, from there we got on the train, we went --
How long did you stay in Omaha?
Hm, a week.
A week?
Yeah, because nobody could -- had to get out. Wasn't making the money there.
What was this show called?
That was Ben Bow's -- Ben Bow's 'Get Happy Company'.
Ben Bow's 'Get Happy' -- and the guy who led the band, was that Benbow?
Yeah, William Benbow.
William Benbow.
Yeah. And he had, you know, he had a big diamond horseshoe pin he used to when he keep the money, and he find some -- he called it finding some fools, to play poker? And they were waiting for him.
(Laughter.)

And he used to -- I had that hand. I was going to do this. And he come out broker than we were. You know. Every time. So I said well, I'll see we're not going to get no money, so we get on the train, and we started for Texas, you know, and had all that junk. Florida and all that stuff, and he would -- we had a coach, you know. If you had over 25 people, or 15 people, I think you could hire your own car, you know?

So he wouldn't be in there. He had to go as far as you can, and then you run into the baggage car, and the mail car. You know nobody walks through that. And he's way up front, and he's going in the diner, he and his wife, and his friends, they're having Scotch, plenty of whiskey to drink, and he can have it, and we're back there starving to death, because nobody had any money. Couldn't buy anything.

And nobody came through there selling sandwiches, and things, and how you going to get back there? You know, nobody had any money. And man, we were setting back there freezing to death, and starving to death. That I'll never forget long as I live.
Where did you wind up in Texas?

Ah, well we played Galveston, Houston, we played all over Texas, all over towns. Still didn't see any money. So when we got to Austin, that's where I grew up. I became a man. I -- he'd been calling us in and talking to

us. Well, you know it rained in the town, we didn't get any money, and so and so and such, the manager's going to wire me this, and now when we get to such-and-such a town, next week, every time I play there money falls off trees, we'll just rake up money. Isn't that right, so-and-so? Yes, that's right. You know, we'd always have one of those rounds.
(Laughter.)
And this sounds good, he said. I'm going to pay up everybody's back salaries, and everything will be all right. You don't have to worry about nothing. Uh-huh!

So I didn't go to this meeting. He called everybody in and his big ledger, you can open up the book and read, and said that, and said well we're hungry now. My mother wants some money. I'll give you -- next week we're going to get paid, and don't worry about it. Don't worry about it. So they came out, they came out crying.

I was outside, so when the last one came out I walked in, closed the door and locked it. Put the thumb latch on the door. He looked up and said, "Where were you? What do you want?" I said, "He'll find out." I said, "Man, give me my money now, quick, because I'm going to throw you out this window." (Laughs.) And he was a big man. Oh, he had a big gut on him, and I -- I hadn't been too long out of Calhoun, and I was a pretty good track man. Put the gloves on a couple of times with my cousin before I went to Calhoun, so

I mean I didn't care. I said, 'Well this is it.' He said, 'You'll have to kill me then.' I said, 'I'm going to throw you out this window if you don't do something.' He said, 'Well, a little boy like you fight a big man like me?'

I said, 'Well, I'm putting myself in a man's place.' So he said, 'Just a minute.' He said, 'I admire you. I admire your spunk.' He say -- he pull out a roll, and he said, 'Now don't tell anybody. I'll give you some money, but don't tell the rest of them.'

Now, I got money, and starving and hungry, so I come downstairs, [you, you,] waiting. 'What happened, Herman?' I said, 'Huh?' 'What happened?' I said, 'I don't know, we talked.' Now I'm telling lies, cause I can't tell you, you know, that I've got some money, because I know they didn't get anything. So I started to walk down the -- 'Where you going?' I said, 'Down to the corner.' Where? You don't know anybody down there. You know. See, I saw a restaurant around there before. With a lot of pies and things in the window.

I said I'm going to get me something to eat. They said you don't know anybody. We all came in town at the same time. They had -- they know -- they didn't know anybody around there. How in the heck did I know anybody?
Anyway, now that's a job, to try to sneak away from your friends, when you're to spend some of that money, which was burning holes in my pocket. So I somehow got a chance to

go and grab something. I got away from them. But I said now I can't stay here, because I'm going to get my money, but I couldn't look you in the face and know you -- you're starving to death. You didn't get anything. So I left the show and joined a carnival.
Did it happen to be in town the same
Yeah, in town. This was in That's the first time, in Florida. I was just in --
Oh, in Florida?
Yeah, uh-huh. Because I left Texas.
You just left Austin on your own?
(Inaudible.)
Yeah, no, this happened in Austin, but we got to -- went to Miami, Florida, and played a theater there, and that was during the centennial, yeah, when they start --
Yeah, '24, yeah, '24 and '25. Yeah. And they were building up the --
Sesquicentennial, something like that. Is that what you mean?

I did that in Texas, yes. That's right. I did that with Fats later, much later. But anyway, I'm trying to think what the heck was it. They were building railroad tracks, and trolley tracks through the town, and building
hotels. At that time they didn't have that -- what do they call it in Hollywood? You know, Hollywood, in Miami, all that?
Yeah, all that in Miami Beach.
Yeah, that wasn't there. That was just, you know, just a lot of land --
That's the big land boom in Florida.

And they were selling land, they were selling lots, as small as $10.00. They got guys in the street wearing big -- want to buy a lot? Want to buy a lot? They're building there, you know. Everywhere you look you see people working, and guys were laborers -- laborers had the jobs, they were getting 18, $20.00 a day, lots of them, you know.
Did you buy any lots?
No, I didn't -- I couldn't buy a lot of food.
(Laughter.)

But a lot of people were buying, and what happened, when they -- after they bought they went over and had it appraised, and the guy said tell me about this, and the man look it up, he say see that boulder way out there? See that waves dumping like that? He said that's where your lot starts.
(Laughter.)
God dog. Sold them water, you know,
and naturally the man who sold it to them is gone. You know. So -- and they sold thousands and thousands of dollars worth of that kind of land. People bought it up. So --
But you were with a carnival, by now. In Florida, right?
So I was in the carnival, and --
What was the name of the carnival?
It was Florida Tip Top Shows.
Florida Tip Top Shows.
Yeah, owned by Billy Wonder, and I worked with them -- I became band leader over there.
What kind of band was that, Herman? Was this again a marching band kind of --
Yes, it was -- yeah. Well, you had to double on and off. In other words, you go out and make bally-hoo to draw the people in.
Through the town.
Then you have to set down there and play the show, the singers, the dancers, the buck dancers, and whatnot, whoever they were. You know. And --
How big a band was that?
Well it varied. Sometimes seven, eight, eight, ten. Two trombones, maybe two trumpets. Bass. Baritone. And I never forget -- you know, a lot of jobs -- well

I'm -- I guess even now, a stranger comesin, he wants a job, he wants to sit in, or join the band. The guys try to make it -- some guys want to make it tough for them, you know. Say who is this guy? So well, we'll lay something on him and see what he knows, see what he can do. And they make it hard then they chase you out and they'll have a big laugh.

This big guy, a big young guy -- you see he was young. He had a big gut on him, and big heavy thing, and his socks, his heels were out, and he came in and he wanted -- he had -- I'll never forget. He had chops that looked like two doughnuts. Man, I never saw a kid with such big chops in all my life. And I say yes? He say I'm looking for a job. I say what do you play? He had a cornet -- wrapped up in a newspaper in a bag there. He said I play this. You play that? The guy looked at it and just started laughing as if to say this guy will never get those lips in a mouthpiece. No.

So they said, okay. So they finished doing what they were doing, (practicing,) and so they say -- took stick out some music. But they always -- on those carnivals and places they always had a trunk full of music, and most of those guys, they were classical players. I mean they were musicians. They didn't worry about playing jazz, and they called that hokum. Said you play that. You play that. That's not for us.
I see. You were the only hokum player there?

Yeah I was. That's what they were -- [preferred to do] (inaudible). You know? So this guy, they pulled out the music, and he say -- he say I don't need that. He brought his hand down and started to play, and then he zzzzz, rrr, rrr,rrr, played [fast] and took and looked over at another page another guy's playing. He stopped at that point. He played -- he found out he could play any of the instruments, and doggone well. He was a heck of a musician.
Who was he?
I was thinking about that the other day. I was trying to think of his name. By golly, I don't know, because --
Did anything ever become of him?
Not there. Not there. I don't know what became of him. He disappeared just like he did to me, and he was gone. And what a man.
How long did you stay with the carnival?

Oh, let me see, probably, well, we left Florida and came east. We came to Philadelphia. I'm trying to think did we come to New York. Yeah, we came up as far as Philadelphia and Pittsburgh too, I think. We played around the east and then went back to Florida and did Texas and whatnot, you know?
You were with the carnival for quite
a long time, then.
I would say a year or two years. I mean yeah, I don't know exactly. I was -- I stayed there, and --
Did you -- were you advancing on your trumpet while you were going with --

Yes. Yes, I was. Because I was the leader, became the leader of the group, and I think we had a pretty good band, and let me think. Who else was there? Oh, that's what I meant to mention. It was a trombone player on this -- Jones, he was on this job. We called him Trombone Jones, and he was a -- he had graduated Fisk University, and he was quite a man. And he -- I remember, and his shoes -- his feet were on the ground. He turned the feet, turned up, and they had ragged clothes on, and he needed a haircut, and he drank. He stayed drunk all the time, as often as he could -- whenever he could find -- get hold of something to drink.

Why I'm mentioning this is because I -- this is how I found out what a man he was, and he'd go lie down under the wagon and go to sleep. So this is -- different guys, you know, who did get a chance to go to school, and you sit down with them. They would pull out those sheepskins. You know.
(Laughter.)
They must let you know, I went to school too, you know, and my days of college and school and blah, blah, blah, blah, blah. So they're making some point

there, or something, and somebody came in one day and some explanation of something, and he said I know what I'm talking about, so-and-so-and-so-and-so, and this guy, you know, laying under the wagon, he said it was 18 so-and-so-and-so-and-so, and such-and-such, was the case, but so-and-so's theory is much better. Awnkk, went on back to sleep.
(Laughter.)
And they say who is he? Who's the -- and they stopped. They found out. He say I'm only a graduate of Fisk University.
(Laughter.)
But he was going down hill at that time.

Oh, yeah, but what a musician! He could play! He was then as good -- well, as the Dorseys now. I use that name because he was widely known. He could send a wire, send a wire to you, or so-and-so-and -- send me a ticket and a hundred dollars, I want to get on your show, and they'd be glad to do it, because they -- the news got around, they said, man, don't send that guy five cents. He'll drink it up. You won't see him. And that was -- you know.
Well was he a hokum player too, like you, or was he a legitimate --
No, he was legit. He was legit. He could play anything.
But not hokum.
Well, he didn't -- he didn't go to stay in that vein. He could play --
Well what were you doing? Were you going both ways?
I was going both directions. Whatever I could hear, what the other guys were doing, I did it.
Where'd you pick up the hokum?

Well, by listening to different guys play. You know. And what they call ragtime, at that time. Now at that time they had a lot of ragtime bands, some was pretty good, some of them were -- you know, so you pick out the best.

As you traveled around the country, you've been -- let's see, you started from Pittsburgh, you go to Nebraska, Texas, Florida, and then the east coast again. Did you have a chance to go hear other people, or --
Oh yes.
-- were you working all the time?
Yes, well that's it. Every time you get a chance, the other traveling bands and shows would come in town, go to see and hear them -- and meet them.
I see.
You go and meet them and listen, listen to them and see if they have anything to offer that you like.
If they didn't, you could put a deaf ear and forget it, you know, you say well, no, that's not what I'm --
Do you remember anyone from these other traveling shows that impressed you that you got something from?

Yes. I'm trying to think now. His name -- well, George [Gillam] was one. He was a trumpet player and he -- big old young boy. He'd take -- be playing a march, or anything. If you felt like it, he'd raise it an octave higher. And never miss a note. Psssss, psssss, pssssss, everybody'd be looking and listening, he'd blow. He was from Carolina. I'm trying to think now, Spartanburg?
Spartanburg? South Carolina.
Uh-huh. And trombone, I'm trying to -- I was trying to remember him a while ago.
Oh, this wasn't Jones that you were talking --
Not -- another company. This was another, yeah. Amos Gilliard.
Amos Gilliard.
Yeah, Amos Gilliard. Yeah. He could -- he was playing his trombone in a thing, concert, and a grain of sand got in there somehow, and bzzt, and it split the slide like it would have been a knife.
My gosh!
Sure, yeah, and -- I've got to think of this man's name. Had the band. He had a band like Paul Whiteman, that type of band, and he was in Florida, and --
A black band like Paul --
White.
A white band like Paul Whiteman.

Yeah, and he called this Negro man, this black man out to join them in a concert.. They were down in Florida, and later on I met his son, and we became very good friends. He's a movie start. I'll think of it.
So after maybe two years with the carnival, what after that?
Yeah, okay. Then I -- well --
That you got out, why did you get out?

Well, let's see, I think I came -- oh, I joined a road -- what they call a road show, and still in Florida, in Jacksonville, Florida, after having my own band I got the heck out of town, I joined the show, and I played the band, took the band over there, and I was with Pet then.
What's -- in this sense, what is a road show? Was that the same kind of show you were in with Benbow?
Yes.
That sort of thing?
Yeah, they had about 20 to -- 20 or 30 people, you know, show of chorus girls. Singles.
Was there one --
Comedians.
-- night stands?
No, theaters, the week.
A week in the theater.
Yeah, and three days a week, you know, like the old theater things, vaudeville thing. And --
What was this one called?
"Hello Lois, got the Pet Jensen's, "Hello Lois."
"Hello Lois."
Uh-huh, and by the way, she lived in Washington, and was her family lived in Washington, which I lived there later.

We came back east and we heared of what they called then at that time a Black and Tan show, which was forming, getting together in Boston, so we went, we came to Boston to meet and join these people, and anh, the show was pretty good. And --
Anybody of importance in it?
I'm trying to think. I'm trying to think.
C'tave in it? (Inaudible.)
No, no, Clara wasn't in that show, but we knew Clara then. Clara, Mamie Smith, all that came a little later. But --
Was this on TOBA?
Yeah, yes, just right, uh-huh. And --
It started in Boston, this particu- lar --
Yeah, called the Black and Tan, and we got together and starved to death, as usual, you know? (Laughter.)
And --
You had the band for the show? Were you the leader?

Yes. Yeah, well, and pianist, trumpet, drum, bass -- I think -- and I was going to say as you go to different towns each town had so many musicians, and you know, that -- in the theater, and we'd augment the group.
I see, you were just the --
Yeah.
-- traveling unit joined in with the local guys.
Uh-huh, and it -- sometimes they're pretty -- it's pretty good.
But you starved anyhow.
I starved. Ohhhh.
How long did you stay with this particular show?

Well, we stayed in, from there we came back -- we came back to Washington, D. C., but -- we came back to Washington, D. C. and I was working in a club there at 7th and S, and -- Andrew Thomas's place, 7th and S, that's what they called it. I used to work there upstairs and we had entertainers and the band and whatnot.
Was this at the same time that you were playing the show too, or had you left the show?
No, I mean -- oh the show? Yeah, we'd left the show, but I -- in a few -- couple of weeks after I worked there I joined -- I started working in the Howard Theater.
After you started working at Andrew Thomas's.
Yeah. I played at the Howard Theater, and the club.
I see.
See, and it was nice. They had quite a band there, and Howard Theater --
Who was in the band there?
Oh, let me see, the Miller Brothers, of course. They were in -- they were the best musicians around town, with their father, Professor Miller. He was

quite known. He had taught most of the musicians in and around Washington, you know? And I'm trying to think. Let me see, brother, well there was James Miller. I worked with all the brothers, at one time or another, the Miller Brothers. They say This is the Miller brothers, and everybody will know who you're talking about. I'm trying to think who else was in there.

Ah, Clay Robinson. I'll never forget him, God bless him. He was a very (big) something -- six foot seven. He had his bass tuba. Well, back in those days -- I don't know if you remember. Guys used to take a blue light, a red light, and put it in the bell of a bass horn?
Oh, yeah.

And he's a toot, toot, toot, would change the color, I mean change the light. One -- mash of his foot would make it red, green, blue, whichever you want. So we were kind of -- and this band was riding us. Okay, get in here, God bless you. Get in here on time, because you're holding up the show. You know? And say okay, so all right, let's hit it. One, we're late.

And Caroline (Thank you) had the band, because I'll come back to her. She -- bass would come in, he'd come in, because he's got to sit this rigging up there, you know, get this foot set, and plug in the lights (Laughs) this particular time he -- we started to hit the overture, and he say (whack) prrsst, the thing lit him up. There was a short in the wire
somewhere --
(Laughter.)
-- he said I don't know who did it. I don't know. I still believe Sandy Williams did that, the trombone player.
Sandy in the band too?
Sandy -- yeah, Sandy was in -- you know Sandy? Yeah.
Sure.
Sandy -- Sand was always up to something. Anything.
(Laughter.)
And thrrppp, he was trying to get this bass tuba from around his neck, and the sparks were flying, and Pffsst, say I told you to put that thing down. Now let that be a lesson to you. (Laughs.)
What about Caroline Thornton? You said you wanted to come --
Yeah, well Caroline -- Caroline was quite -- aw, what a musician.
She had the band?
Oh yes, and what a musician.
What did she play?
Piano.
Piano.

I've seen her play piano with one hand and write out a part with the other -- in the pit! And the show's going on. And when she hands it to you to play, it's right. Don't worry. It's right. That's how good she was. And oh, man, I was -- just the thought of working with her meant so much to me, and she was a -- well, that's the sad part about it. She was on the way to our house, my house, to visit me in Philadelphia, afterwards, and got in an automobile accident. And that was the end of that.
How did you happen to get the job at the Howard? That would be a pretty good job.
It was, a doggone good job. Come to be finally we had a 14-piece band there, and was playing heavy because see Caroline was conducting, and we -- I played (finger snapping) Ben Hur in that theater.
Really?

I really did, because they had 'Ben Hur,' then they had to -- we had to get the music, and screened it, and get it together, and we did the chariot race and all that stuff, and this was like silent pictures. Back in the silent days.
You played for the whole picture?
Yes.
All the way through?
Yes.
And then you played for the show too?
Yeah, well yes. Because that's -- they had chorus girls, and all that business, you know.
But you were getting into the band. Now this must have been a job that everybody wanted. How did you manage to get in?

Well, being able to read helped tremendously, because for a job like that you couldn't sit down and kid yourself -- you'd be kidding yourself. You don't kid them. You know you have to be able to play as they call -- then they were calling it jazz, play the regular music, you know, classics, whatever, because we played a lot of overtures and stuff, because Caroline set it up. She knew what she wanted, and sometimes she could just -- recall for one thing, she suggest something else instead, the same, you know.
How many shows a day were you doing?

Aw, man! Let's see. Four or five a day, and it all depends on what they have in there. They had a blues singer in there, you know, one of the Smiths, Bessie Smith, Mamie Smith, but mainly Bessie, and Clara. Clara wasn't bad. She was very good. Trixie Smith. I played for all of them.
Was it usually a blues singer who was the headliner?
Yes. Yes, back then, yes, because they would come in and bring their own show, you know, see,
and comedians, so many chorus girls, and whatnot.
When they brought their own show didn't they bring their own musicians too?
No. Well, maybe a pianist, because -- and he would sit down and tell you what we want, this is the way we do it, such-and-such-and-such. You know?
I see. Now while you were doing this at the Howard you were still playing at the club after the show at the Howard?
Yeah.
What time of the day did you start at Howard, and when did you get finished at the club?
We'd play 'til 3:00 and 4:00 o'clock in the morning.
And when did you start at the Howard, 1:00 o'clock?
Yeah. You have to get there an hour before that, because -- and be in there oh, 10:00, 11:00.
Yeah, because they start screening the news, and fill up getting ready for the matinee.
And then how about rehearsing your overtures and things for next week? You had to get that in too?
Yeah, we had to rehearse. See can I

remember the day when -- when was that, now? Was that Wednesday, or Monday? Monday, I think, we had to rehearse, new show and this, and then they started that -- well, what do you call it? The talking?
Vitaphone?
Yeah.
Vitaphone.
Yeah, they'd screen that, and you go in and see the show, and they'd get it together like that.
When you had to rehearse for the next week's show, how did you fit that into your day? when was there enough time to rehearse?
Well I -- I don't know. You just poured some more liquor in you and poured yourself on the job and --
(Laughter.)
-- and when I think about it now you ask yourself how, why, what, and you need some sleep, you'd better get some sleep, and you don't, and so you drink some more liquor.
I see. At the club, were there acts there, or were you just playing for the --
No, they had singers.
-- singers.
Entertainers.
And otherwise you were playing for
dancing there too? Dancing, people (unintelligible), and they'd stop and they'd bring a entertainer, girl, singer.
Were they any good?
Pretty good.
Pretty good?
Pretty good.
Who was in your band at that time?
I'm trying to think was there anybody that finally made good, or was pretty good. I remember one guy who worked in the Post Office. He played alto sax, he -- Toby. Toby.
Not Toby Hardwick.

Naw, no, no. He was fair. He's -- I don't know. He owned the horn, I would say, you know. (Laughs.) And Jeff -- what was Jeff's last name -- on piano. He smoked a big cigar like -- let's see, who died? The man? Willie Willard the Lion, yeah, but he was -- I'm trying to think who was the drummer.
How long did you go on playing both the club and the Howard?
Oh, I worked the Howard Theater about four years.
Four years?
Yeah, stayed about three -- three or
four years.
You worked at the club for four years too?

No, no. I finally put the club down, because there was too much -- talking about violence, man, oh shoot. It was too much happening, you know, in there, for one thing, and then there was too much work, you know. I'd rather go and play the theater, go and take care of the theater and let the other thing go.

Well now this was -- when you got to Washington this was the first time that you'd had a chance to really stay in one place for a while. And what was your personal life, your social life like? Were you married by then, or what?
(Laughs.)
(Inaudible.)
Huh?
Of course you were married then.
Yeah.
He'd been married many times in those days (unintelligible). Everybody knows you've been married lots of times.
Yeah, I was -- I was very much married then.
Very much married? When did you get married for the first time?
Let's see, which wife and what year?
Well, the first one.
(Laughter.)
Which wife and what year. I'd have to stop and think and look at them. You know, twenty what? Let's see, '27, '27, '28. Yeah, '27.
That was your first wife. Her parents, yeah.
Yeah.
Well this is the period we're talking about in Washington, isn't it? Is that where you got married?
Yeah, then when I -- let me see, when I came out of Florida too I was almost married, you know, when I left the carnival. And that --
Almost isn't quite the --
Almost, yeah. And that went on for -- she was a singer and dancer. In fact, it was her show. And things were --
Was this Lois?
Hm?
Was this Lois?
Uh-huh. Pet Gentry was her name.
Pet Gentry.
Pet Gentry. 'Hello Lois' company, very fine woman, very fine people. Personally, very fine.
And she was from Washington.
Uh-huh.
Originally.
Yeah, well, she wasn't born in Washington.
No, but I mean --
But she lived there.
Is that why you went to Washington after the Boston experience?
Yeah, uh-huh.
I see.
Uh-huh, uh-huh, because we needed a job, and she knew people and knew the theater, and whatnot, so said we'd go to Washington, and she said -- see, I was thin then, said I'm going to fatten you up.
(Laughter.)
Fatten you up for the kill, you know?
Did she?
Yeah, uh-huh.
She got you fattened up. And did this break up after a while, or what happened to that marriage?
No, now --
You weren't quite married, that's what you're saying.
Well no, we got married, we stayed to-
gether. We got married and stayed together, and lived in New York 'til '30 -- around '35, I guess it was, something like that. And she passed.
Oh. Well we'll pick up the rest as we get -- I mean the way you spoke before it sounded like you had about ten wives before you got to Washington.
Well, nine and a half.
Nine and a half.
(Laughter.)
Yeah, my brother laughing over there when you mention how many wives come through there, because he was in Washington the same time, you know.
This is a family joke?
(Laughter.)
Well, so you stayed at the Howard for about four years?
Yeah, three or four years. Uh-huh.
And after you left the club, were you doing any other work on the side, or was it principally at the Howard?

At the Howard, and when I left the Howard I came to Philadelphia and to the Standard Theater. And we worked in there for Gibson, worked in his theater there for about three years, maybe, or something like that, and that was a very good job. Sandy Williams and I, we were --
Both again?
Yeah, we were -- we came -- we left the Howard and we came to Philadelphia together.
Why did you go to Philadelphia?
Well, they needed a band there. They needed some musicians, and the pay was good, sounded good, so we (finger snap) picked up there.
Were you the leader of the band in Philadelphia?
No. The Nicholas father -- Nicholas brothers' father was the leader.
I'll be darned. What was his first name?
He used to be called Nick for short. I don't know his --
Well, that's sort of hard to figure. (Inaudible.)
(Inaudible.)
Yeah, what was his name?
They always do.
What's the Nicholas brothers' father? Fayette and what's-his-name were the two boys. I saw them grow from here, from there, and the wife played piano.
Oh, really?
Uh-huh, Mrs. Nicholas.
The whole family act there.
Uh-huh.
But Herman, was the pay in Philadelphia that much better than the pay in Washington? Or did you want to get out of Washington?

Well, yes. At that time it was better, but I found out later I moved too soon, because the owner of the theater in Washington, Mr. Litchman, offered me one of the best offers I think I've ever had. He wanted me to get my own group. He said I'll put your name in lights. I'll make you -- do this for you. And -- you know, when you're young, and I thought about all the heartaches and things you have going -- trying to have a band, and finding a good musician, which at that time it was too hard to find, I mean to get what you want, you know, get somebody that you could work with, that could help you along. And I said I'm tired, I don't want to teach anybody else, you know. And there's 14 15 too much work.
But all this time, at the point that you went to Philadelphia, you never had worked in any of the traveling bands at all, the -- you know, the name bands.
Yeah, well I joined one in Philadelphia. Doc Hyder. He had a very good band. You know.
How do you spell Hyder? Do you know?
H-y-d-e-r.
H-y-d-e-r.
Uh-huh, and he had a very fine band,

and -- well, Russell Smith was playing first trumpet for him. That -- he's the man who carried Fletcher Henderson's band for so many years on trumpet. And the greatest first trumpet player in the world, in the country, you know.
That's right.
And I went in then, and had a chance to play that book after him.
Oh, you followed him. Now were you in Doc Hyder's band while you were playing at the Standard Theater, or was that --

No, I didn't double that time because we were working down at 69th Street there, and it really took all your time, and then we came out and we came -- went on the road, and some one-nighters here, through New York State, and Pennsylvania, in -- you know, Maryland, one night, you know, one night, one of those things. And -- anh, it didn't pan out too good.
You see, I found out later in life that a lot of that stuff was dependent mainly on the leader, the man you worked for, yeah.
That's a money problem.

Oh, yeah. So when they -- we came to New York, and came over to some friends to visit, and some of them, '33, '32, and I came over before that, because this was: '27, '28. I was working in the Standard Theater in Philly.
And -- I almost lost my thought there.
Well I tell you what we're --
No, what was I going to say?
-- coming to the end of this reel, so --
Oh, okay.
-- we'll pick it up when you get to New York. Okay? I mean because is that where we're going now? From Philadelphia to New York?
Yes. I jumped back (unintelligible). Herman, come on Herman. (Laughs.) What was I saying, huh? Because I had a good thought there. I didn't want to lose it.
I'm afraid to talk because I'm afraid it will pick up on this.
It will. It will.
(Simultaneous remarks.)
You stop it? You stop it?
Yeah.
(End of Tape Two.)

Well Herman, at the end of the last reel we were just about -- you were just about to go from Philadelphia to New York. But before we do that I'd like to stop and go back a little bit and clear up a few things in the earlier part of your career. Now for example, how did your trumpet style develop? Who were the people that you
listened to, or had any -- had some influence on the way you play?

Very well. I would like to say Pittsburgh. From Pittsburgh, I joined the show, and we went from Pittsburgh to Chicago, playing the -- was it the Corcoran Theater, or Monogram? Well, I kind of get them confused, because you know, both were small theaters at that time, in each town. Well anyway, after Chicago we went to Detroit, I'm almost positive. Well there I met and saw a very fine trumpeter, trumpet lady, maybe I should say. She was playing trumpet for Ethel Waters. She was a backup for Ethel, because Ethel was singing all those beautiful things, and blues, and whatnot, and that time making movies, and I had never seen or heard her, and being with the show, being a youngster, and just starting out, I heard and saw her take a Harmon mute -- that's what they called the wow-wow mute that was used, I would say by Henry Bussey, but she was the first I ever heard go Wow-wow-wow-wow-wow. But she used it, and she took my hand, put the mute in my hand, and showed me how to go wow, how to make those sounds. With her mute. So --
What was her name?
Dyer Jones.
How do you spell that, D-y-e-r?
I think -- yeah. And she -- oh a very pretty girl. She was a cute little thing, and she had hair

hanging down to her waist, and she -- when she sat down in the theater her feet hardly touched the floor. And I -- tell you the truth, I fell in love with her just looking at her. I'd never seen anything as pretty as that before.

So while I was setting there in the pit playing this show -- show -- she came in and sat down, and the other trumpet player in the house band, they knew each other. Looked at him and said oh hi, Frank, Joe, whatever his name was, and said hi, how are you? I don't know. I didn't know who the heck -- who she was. I hadn't noticed her trumpet then. But she took the trumpet, put it down there and stuck it under the seat, which I still didn't matter. I said boy, she's a good looking gal.

AND the show went, and I was playing, playing, playing, so while he was sitting there he said Dyer, I'm going to run across the street and get a drink, or a sandwich, or a soda, or something. Sit in for me, will you? She said Okay, go ahead. She reached under the seat, pulled out this trumpet case, and took the trumpet out, and sat beside me, with one hand, her little legs just swinging, you know, the seat, started hitting F's and G's and everything, and I had never seen a woman play trumpet in my life before. Never mind the high notes. I'd never seen them. I didn't know a woman could play a trumpet.
Anyway, and so the -- everything was so perfect.

Everything was so nice. And I'm sitting there trying to learn -- this is my well, second or third day in show business, maybe the second week, and I'm trying to learn, hoping to be good someday, and this woman sat there, and she was out of this world. So finally she turned to me, and she said, "What's your name?" And I told her. And I said, "What's yours?" And she told me. "How long have you been playing?" I said, "Oh, I started -- " (Laughs.) "I've been playing since I was about eight, nine years old." "You have? Nice." You know, which I knew, [redacted]. She knew that, but I didn't.
(Laughter.)

And I say, "How do you do that?" And she picked up the mute, and she says, "Well I'll show you." So while the show was going on she took my hand and placed it around the mute to make this -- how to make this sound, and you to do this, and how to do the other. I said, "Well what is this? What's the name of this?" And she told me that's a Harmon Mute.

This is called a So-and-so mute. This is a -- then picked up a rubber thing. I said, "What's that?" She said, "That's a plunger." Plunger? She explained all that to me there. So -- but I tried to buy everything I saw her with. And I went in the hotel, and drove everybody nuts because I was sitting up in my room making all these noises.
But to me she was the greatest trumpet player I had

ever heard, because I never heard nobody play like that. And well she had made a lot of recordings with Ethel Waters at that time, and made movies, and such a very nice person, which later -- much later -- I met her daughter. Her daughter also played trumpet. Louie Armstrong helped her, she told me. Louie helped her quite a bit.
The daughter, or Dyer?
The daughter.
The daughter.

And Dyer and Louie were friends. They knew each other. They -- I guess he must have helped her some time too, in the -- you know, happenings there.
