But the daughter was very nice, real sweet, and -- but she had -- at that time she told me she was inspired by a lot of trumpet players, and one in particular who had inspired me. He was with -- had been with Don Redman, different bands. Hmmm -- he's working now for the airplane company. He's working out in Jamaica -- Long Island there. Oh, what the heck is his name? You know. Oh boy, what a trumpet player.

Anyway, he had taught her, showed her a lot of things, and helped her, and she was more a modern, I would say, modern gig, because she was playing more changes, running the changes, what we -- you know what we mean by changes, the kind -- the -- uh!
The chord?
Harmony -- yeah, the chords. Harmony, running the changes renditions. And she could do very, very well and sounded doggone good.
What was the duaghter's name? Do you remember?
Dolly.
Doll --
Dyer and Dolly.
Dolly Jones?
Yes. Dolly Jones.
I've heard of Dolly Jones.
You have?
Sure.
Well, she's the lady. But I haven't seen Dolly in so many years. I hope she's well and doing fine, but --
What became of Dyer? Do you know?

I think Dyer passed some time -- I'm almost positive that she passed some time ago, but what a trumpeter, you know, what a trumpet player she was. And she and I were pals there for quite some time. So I used to kid her, after I met her that time I came back years later. I said "Remember? Remember me?" She said, "Yes, I remember." I said, "I dare you to take your horn out of your case. I'll blow you out of here." She laughed, you know. "Where have
you been?" I told her, and said Well, I went all down in Texas, Alabama, Florida, and everything, and Louisiana and everything. I said, "I'm ready for you now." So she said okay.
How long did it take you, when you first got the mutes and everything, and she was showing you how to do it, how long did it take you to learn how to do it? Hard?

Well, it was -- I would say a week or less, because I was -- man, I was driving everybody -- I know I was driving everybody nuts. They wanted -- who -- who is that guy, or whatever it is, next door, if they heard me. But I didn't care, because I kept trying, I kept -- because I wanted to make the sounds, the things that I'd heard her do. You know. Because I liked it.

And when I started recording with Fats Waller I was the guy, I think. I got a lot of the credit, because I was one of the first to put it on tape -- on -- not tape, record with Fats for Victor, and we were the first small band on Victor, so I think I got a lot of the credit, because I was doing it. They'd never heard nobody play behind a singer like me, and behind Fats, and I heard it from her. So I want to be honest. I --
Well now you got -- you got your wah-wah effects from Dyer. How about the buzz mute effects?

Buzz? Ah, that's another story. A good friend of mine, Frankie Newton, in New York, I was working at Charlie Johnson's band down at Small's Paradise, and that's where I first met him. Frankie Newton, one of the greatest trumpet players in the world, I still say, and he has a lot of fans who think and see it the same way, because he's passed.
But we worked together, and we were good buddies. But Frankie has his -- I never saw the buzz thing. It looked like a coffee strainer, or -- that's what I used to call it.
(Laughter.)

-- piece of . And he would take this thing, and buzz, buzz, and drive everybody nuts. Not to -- annoyance. I mean there were -- they were happy, they enjoyed it. They enjoyed listening to him, you know what I mean, and so did I. And he showed me how to use it, and I watched him, and we were sitting side by side. So after the time that we'd worked together he gave it to me.
First he sold it to Johnny Buggs, and finally got around back to Herman, you know. Johnny Buggs, John Hamilton, the trumpet player. Another --
Yeah, yeah.
Oooh, what a trumpet player he was!
Anyway, that's the way the thing went.
Did Frankie invent this, this (buzz) mute, where'd he get it from, or (inaudible).

Naw. No, that I don't know. I tell you why, because I think it was Frankie's idea. I'm almost positive it was. But later on, at that time I can tell you because we had a lot of musicians, a lot of everybody used to come in Small's, come to Harlem to see and dig the musicians, and then what are you doing? Why did you do that? What is that? And then we'd sit down with a pencil and paper and draw it, so some guy made this thing into -- went over to his factory and built it, and made it. That's how the plunger and the wah-wah came to be, because they saw us with the rubber toilet plunger -- that's what it actually is, is the -- you know.

And you pick out the size that you want, and could handle and use, and you made a mute out of it, and from that they made other mutes. Not the Wah-wah. There was Harmon. And [crossed out], I'm trying to think of the name of the mutes now, but that means you send -- they use that for guide, for --
Pocket mutes, and things like that?
The bucket mute, very well. You know where the bucket mutes came from?
Where?
Bucket mutes came from -- (Laughs) --
bean cans. Sauerkraut cans. Any kind of can that we saw that was useable, that we could handle, garbage -- you know, we'd take them up, and then fix it like it was and (unintelligible.)

When you walk in an average bar, well, I mean club, one that had a band, you'd look at them and you'd think you were looking in the garbage dump, because they had all kind of cans using, and you'd say what happened? Didn't they empty the garbage? And those guys are using them for mutes. And the smart -- some smart guy walked in there and saw these things and watched them use them, and he took a pencil and paper and drew them and made them and sold them back to us, five, six, eight, ten dollars. And we bought them.
But they were fancy ones.

And the bucket, the bomp, bomp, bomp, bomp, the derbies, those were gallon buckets. Yeah, those were gallon pails, those buckets that they sold lard, syrup, anything that came in a gallon bucket we took it and used it, and they sold them back to us.
How about the felt hats?

The felt hat, the derby hat, that all ties in, because we used a derby, people throw derbies away, you know, they take them away until they turn. They buy a black derby and wear it until it turns green. You know.
(Laughter.)

Seventy years, you know, and then they'd finally throw it away, and it would be -- some of them gray, you know, the different colors, and the guys -- we'd use it, and then instead of the derby hat, they made tin hats.
Yeah, wasn't the effect different than when you made them out of metal, then when it was out of cloth (inaudible.)

Yes. Yes, much different. Because for years, even I recorded with Fats, I had a tin hat, but I put a felt hat, because I would take one of my felt hats and cut the crown, you had to cut it out, and stick it in there to make it mellow, make it softer. And play in that, instead of playing -- it made it too brassy, you know, the tine, just the tin.
When it was just the tin.
Uh-huh.
Now how about felt hats that had holes cut in them to try (inaudible).

Well we did that. I cut hats, and one -- when you see them cut in there it's cut in there on purpose to suit the artist, the person who was using it, because if it's all closed in there's a tendency to muffle the sound, so by cutting small holes through the sides in there it lets the sound come out as much as you want. You don't want it wide open, you want it -- trying to shade it to make it a sound that you want. And sometimes it's good, and sometimes it
depends on your hearing, you know?
Well, does that mean that everybody's felt hat mute was a personally cut --
Personally cut.
I mean you wouldn't go out and buy that.

No, no. No, no. You never -- they don't sell them. In other words, you get an old hat, you find an old hat, or take one of your old hats, and cut them up, particularly like you want it to be, and the more you handle it, in --
Squeezing it together with your hand.

Squeezing it together, and using it, and when you finish playing you take it out and roll it up and put it away. The softer it gets, the mellower it gets, and that's when you lose them. So you've got to go find --
(Laughter.)

You've got to get to packing up, you leave without the stand, or somebody steals it, and you've got to go and get you another one, so that's just what happened. That has happened to me so many times, and boy, do you get mad at yourself. What happened? Where's my hat? Then you go see -- you start looking. You don't know what happened. You left it.
When you do that and it's an emergency,
Yes, I've done that plenty of times, so you pick out one of your oldest hats that you don't wear too much --
(Laughter.)

-- and cut the crown out, and you start mashing it, and handling it, and mashing it, which is going to have to run into weeks, months, and years, for it to get where the other one was, you know. You know, you get oh, seasoned.
Well what else have you used for mutes besides, did you use water glasses?

Water glasses, cuspidors, everything (laughs). Anything that you find you pick it up and you use it and you get the sound, get a different -- because usually everyone was looking for sounds, a different sound. The guy who sounded different on trumpet, or trombone, or saxaphone, yeah, but he has a different sound. He has the sound that we're looking for. Maybe it's natural. He was playing from his -- from his lips, his own way of thinking, or he used some kind of mechanism to make it sound different, and the public liked it or bought it, you know.
So that's what happened. And I'm just saying, well Louis Armstrong, who sound likes Louie? No one.
Well, now this reminds me. We were starting to talk about influences on you, and a lot of people
have written that you have a lot of Louie in you. Do you feel that you've got a lot of Louie in you?

I think so. I think it's impossible for any human being, any trumpet player who came along, with Louie or after, you have to have some of Louie, because he was the daddy, the greatest, I mean it had to rub off on some guys, you know, some of the people had to. You couldn't duck him. I mean you know.
Well how old were you, Herman, before you were aware of Louie? You have to hear him first before you can be influenced in any way by him.

Yes, but I'm trying to see. That's going to be a kind of hard one. Well, I was on -- as I told you, I was out of school. I came out -- it must of had to be '23, '22 or '23 that I heard -- maybe heard a record. I never heard Louie in person then, but I heard some of his recordings, and maybe there -- maybe -- and being from the same part of the country -- I claim that helps, because -- may I state this right here? -- because when I was a little kid I told you remember from four years up, I do, believe me, because in back of my house there was a huge cotton field, well, huge to me. I don't know how many acres, being five or six acres, could have been more.
And I'd pick cotton out there a few days, and you know, when I grew up, not at four, but a little later, and I

could see the people, I saw the people every morning with their wagons, their oxen, or whatever they had, however their transportation -- or walking, coming there to work in this field to pick this cotton. When I saw them hoe the cotton after it was planted, and help it grow, and I saw them pick it. So when cotton picking time came I got a job out there as water boy. I was taking pails of water out to the people, you know, because that sun was -- oh, my God, if there's ever such a thing such as I would say 150 degrees, which is Washington, but --
What it felt like.
(Laughter.)

Yeah, and I don't know, got, I don't know, 25 cents. I got a few cents for doing it. We didn't think too much of it. And at time we had to be careful of rattlesnakes, (unintelligible). Now, the field was full of people, I would say about 25 or 30 people, in this field, down the road picking cotton.
Working.

Working, yeah. And for some reason, at different intervals, when they were asked, was -- somebody would start the song, and they would all chime in, and you never heard such things in your life, such sounds, such harmonies, and they just -- they were congenial workers. They didn't stop working, they just stood up and looked at each
other, watch out, you get a little flat, you get a little sharp, and they kept on going.
(Laughter.)

And I enjoyed -- I liked that, and I listened, and those people -- and they would tell a story. For instance, sometimes I -- that's how they told the news, what happened last week, or what happened to such-and-such wife was fighting, and this on and on and on, blah, blah, blah, and they were singing a song and tell the story, just like news, like reading the paper. Then we'd go into a religious theme, and then -- you know, and they would sing. Oh, it was so nice.
Was anybody the leader of the singing, in particular, or did they just come up that way?
Yes. Yes, yes. That's -- I'm glad you asked me. For instance, you, Herman, Joe, Jim, they had their particular song that they did, that couldn't nobody else duplicate.
Oh, I see.

In other words, to our minds, or their minds, well you sing this nice, we wouldn't want to hurt your feelings, but you don't sound like Louie Armstrong doing it. You see what I'm saying? Such-and-such a person sang this, but 'tisn't our regular so-and-so who does this, to -- when we are together. That was how they identified each other, and
one another, see, and that's -- to my mind, that's how Louie became the greatest, and there's still nobody sounds like him.

They used to get together and sing, as I told you they sing, and when I got -- and the main -- another thing I got out of this was you go to church and you hear people say be good to this one, and be good to the helpless person, blah, blah, [and round and round we go.] I saw that happen. I asked questions. I said well how is Mr. So-and-so, that'd be coming in, or Miss So-and-so, not so good. No? What happened? They would discuss it. The whole church -- well, so many people, they would take a day off, cooks, men who could drive -- put down posts, fences, fix wagons, do this, do that, they would go to thatperson's house and take over while they were laying there sick, and so -- and plow. Take and have their horses and plow. They would plow his -- if he was the right person.

But he had to be the right guy. I mean you know, and they were laying -- and so I learned from that by watching-- he said well, he's very nice. These are very nice people, and we have to help them. We want to, and [every never sit there]

Now, with -- I imagine two or three guys on the fences, posts, and this and that, and plowing, and in five hours or less everything is taken care of, and women in there cooking, cleaning, darning, sewing, whatever's needed to be done, somebody's in theredoing it. Now they get the little kids, four or five years old, like me, you know and other kids

that were there then, and they would give them buckets, pails, and send them out in the woods -- we didn't have to go too doggone far -- pick berries, bring the berries in, and those ladies in there cooking would make pies, and you would have so many of whatever was cooking, whatever the meat was, chicken, goat, lamb, pig, whatever it was, they would -- they were preparing it, and when they -- when they say okay, come on, let's eat, they would start singing. You never heard such -- oh, and naturally I was playing the trumpet, so I was sitting in there with them.

I was playing the trumpet in church, you know? So when I knew most of those hymns, and religious things, so I would just sit there and play with them, so I really got my kicks, sitting there with them, and hearing them play, sing, and be jolly, and all that food, and you sit down and eat, and finally, when the time came that they said well, good night, well, good night, and they'd go home, and the sick people are well. Their houses are clean. Their fences that had broken down, the postses -- posts were rotten. The cow and everything is fed, cows milked, everything is in order.

So everybody went home happy, because they had helped a friend. Now, should something happen to anyone else, you would find that couple, or those people -- if they didn't, no more, good-bye, good-bye. They'd drop them like a hot potato. We won't talk to them any more, and we wouldn't -- you
know.
Everybody helps everybody else.
Everybody helps everybody. If you were the right guy. You didn't have to ask. You didn't have to sit down and beg. They would get together and come to you and take care of you. And why --

Another reason I'm glad you asked me that. Let me mention this. To my mind -- I've had a lot of people come up, I've heard them ask others, how was jazz started? Who started jazz? Who was the first to do this? To my mind that was it, because back -- the same thing, back in the time of the same thing up there, it happened to all the people together, singing, shaking hands, praying, with all those gospel songs, other religious songs, that's how it came about, I think. Now, that's the way I think.

Because it gave it the feeling that you can't study, you can't pay a teacher a million dollars to teach you that feeling. Give me that feeling. How the -- I was looking at a program last night. I won't call the name, but they were doing the best that they could, and now the thing was swinging. But this particular person, who's been in the business for 50 years, she did the best she could do. She was -- she was clapping her hand on the beat, Hah (clap), hah (clap), hah (clap) Hah (clap) hah (clap), you know. But I mean that's not the way. And when you're doing jazz, but what are you
going to do about it? That's the way she felt it, and that's the way I've known -- that's thousands, and maybe millions of people feel that beat, but that's not it.
It's the (snap) instead of the (snap) (snap) (snap), you know.
You can tell the difference.
Yeah, I mean that's the way they feel, and they -- they don't know. Let's get hot! Jah, jah, jah, hah, hah, hah, you know.
Now, is part of what you're saying, like you talked about coming from -- you and Louie coming from the same part of the country. Is this a part of what you're saying about Louie's background?
That's right. Louie came through that same thing, because I heard him tell a story about him being an orphan. He was an orphan, see, and it's the same -- it's the same.
But he lived in a big city, whereas you were talking about a small community out in the country.

Same thing, though. New Orleans -- I mean the part where he was color'd -- had to live, over there in Algiers, and all that business, it was the same thing. The same thing, because -- because he came up the same way. The same way as I did. You know? And hearing those songs, knowing those songs. We learned them, we heard them when we were
babies. We grew up with them. They had to be -- that was us. That was us. That's all we knew.

And those old people, they didn't know too much, and they beat down our heads, be good, you know, they had (unintelligible), be nice, and grow up and do what you're told, and so and so and so and so. You know. I mean that's -- that was it. Was nothing else to do.
And those who had -- well, who had a chance to go to school, and learn, had the break in life, I would say, you know?
But basically this is where you're kind of -- the way you play trumpet got influenced by what you heard --
By what I heard --
-- all the time.

Yes, and that's -- to me that's it, because to hear those people's voices, and the songs they were singing, and the sound, the feeling that they put in there, would move anybody, even now when you hear those old gospel tunes, and certain tunes, you -- you -- I don't care how old you are, you still feel it.

Well tell me this, Herman, when you are playing some current pop tune with Fats, for example, in the back of your mind do you still feel or hear something of that going on, or is it just sort of subconsciously function-
ing on you then? Yes, yes I -- do you mean do I hear the name of the tune? Or --
Well, the feeling, the way --
I associate myself with the tune, or what's happening, the title of the tune, I would say, and how it's constructed. That has a lot to do with it. Yes it does have a lot to do with it.
You remember this old thing, (Sings) Wade in the water, wade in the water children, wade in the water, God's going to trouble the water.

Now, I don't care who you are, you'd have to -- oh it'd be done better than I sang it, of course, but I mean, with that -- surrounded with those things happening, it makes you think and hear that type of voice, it have to mean something to a person. I don't care where they're from. They could be European, they could be -- well, what's happening? What's that? You just say well (snap) that sounds (snap) -- that sounds right (Snap) (Hums), bah wo dee (snap) dee (snap, bee (snap) bah-m-dee(snap) dee (snap) dee (snap). Bee (snap), bah wa dee -- it has to be. You've got to feel it.
Right. You -- before, you mentioned one other trumpet player who you feel had an influence on you. Tommy Ladnier.
Ahhh, Tommy.
What was --

He was a beautiful cat. He was recording with Bessie Smith, and he had such a beautiful trumpet sound. He was a good musician, and a couple of things he did that I will never forget. I forget the name of the recording, (sings) Dah, doo, doo deh, deh, doo, deh. Beh, deh, deh, deh, doo doo deh doo. Just the introduction for Bessie. Lah doo doo deh, doo deh, Deh-eh doo deh-eh-eh -- and that used to knock me out. And I've never forgotten it.
Right now, if You offered me $50.00 to tell you the name of the tune, I couldn't. But I knew him. I knew him and I remember the introduction of the tune, you know? And --
Did you -- from that did you try to copy some of Tommy's way of playing, or --

Well the feeling -- yeah, yes, yes I did. I felt it. I mean as I started to say, it's in here. I mean you're -- you say I like that feel. That's what I want. And it's the way I feel. That's the way I want to feel. I feel what he felt. You know, instead of aw, the heck with that guy. I don't want --
(Laughter.)
But it's sort of kind of like you're walking down the street and you see somebody and you recognize yourself coming at you? In a way?
Yes, I would say.
That's just exactly --
I would say he's in -- that's it.
That's it.
That's what I said, as the guys say.
(laughs.)
Mentioning Bessie Smith, earlier, when we were talking, and you said that you had known Ma Rainey.
Yes.
Where did you know Ma Rainey?

I met Ma, I think the first was down in Texas. It was Houston, Texas, I think, and I was with this show that I was telling you about. And Ma was there with her show, and we came -- how we came in contact with each other right now I don't remember, but I can see a picture of her face, a big round fat face, with all these $20.00 gold pieces on her chain. She had a necklace with -- turned around her neck, $20.00 gold pieces reached all the way down to her waist, and I had to -- I got a chance to play for Ma after that. I'm trying to think of was it then.
I played for her, but Bessie, Mamie, Clara --
Smith?
-- Trixie, all them, I had played for them too many times, you know?
Well before we leave Ma, tell me
She was very nice. She was a very sweet person, and she liked all the young boys. I mean!
(Laughter.)
Why not? You know.
Why not?

Yeah, and I understand Ma was quite generous. I mean if she saw -- if you were nice, I mean we'd take each other to dinner, and have fun, you know. And she'd say well take this and buy you a suit, you know.
(Laughter.)
It wasn't bad.
Well you said she had a round, fat face. Was she short? Was she --
No, no. She was kind of a plump woman. She was --
But tall?
Hmm, not too very tall, but at least I would say a good medium-sized woman. She must have been five, two, three, maybe. Maybe a little more. But she was getting hefty.
Kind of round, like.
Yeah, kind of hefty, and a light brown skin, and a very pleasant person, I would say, you know? And I enjoyed talking with her, meeting her, and she seemed to be

Do the records that we have of her give any indication of the effect she has as a performer? Because they're -- most of the records are kind of -- a little bit dim. They're old, pre-electric recordings. Was she a really -- an electrifying kind of performer when she got on, or not?
No. To answer you -- wait just a minute -- to answer you, because when you say electrifying a person will -- bang! -- when those people really start out. Clara Smith, Bessie Smith --
Bessie, right, yeah.
-- and those people. No.
No.
No, she did her thing, but -- I mean you know, like when Bessie open her mouth, I mean you could hear Bessie all -- from here to Florida, man. You know.
(Laughter.)
Well what was it that Ma had that made her so --
Well, she was --
-- have such a following? Why was she so great?
I would say -- I think Ma, being one of the first, before Bessie and those people, I mean in the

South, anyway, I would say, who was famous, and I -- she wasn't more famous than Bessie, and after Smith. She was not! But I think Ma got on record, maybe. Maybe, now, now I'm speculating, before Bessie, Clara, and those people, maybe. But Ma did her thing, but she wasn't -- she wasn't into the Smith's, I mean when it came to banging it out and punch, you know, and being dynamic, because they says well all right, take in on loud, here come Ma with one of those A notes. She was -- and she had the only show. She had several shows that she took out with her. You know, several girls, comedians, the same type of thing that most people had in those days, with the show business.
Chorus girls, comedians, and dancers, and all of them got stranded, and owed everybody.
(Laughter.)
Well, I've always understood that Ma certainly had an effect on Bessie Smith, whether she taught Bessie or not. Do you know anything about that?
Well I -- no, I do not. I would be afraid to -- you know, comment on it. Well, could be, I would say, but see, I knew Bessie. I knew Bessie -- oh, I knew Bessie's whole family.
Oh, you did?
Oh heck yeah. Bessie and I -- maybe I shouldn't put this on tape.
Why not?
(Unintelligible.)

We were working on -- (laughs) -- we were working in Philadelphia, at the Standard Theater. I was there, I told you I was in the pit band there. Well Bessie was there, and she was a star, naturally, and the place was packed, and Bessie liked a little taste. She liked to drink just like Herman.
(Laughter.)

Well out in back of the Standard Theater was Catur -- not Decatur, Catur Street, and you could walk out there and buy all the corn liquor you wanted, you know, and most of it was stirred up in a pot or bathtub.
(Laughter.)
Right.

And you could die, and a lot of people did die, and it -- I was a runner. She'd come up and say 'hey Buddy.' I'd say okay. I'd go out and get a pint, and a half pint, and we'd take -- give one to her, and throw the bottle and drink, and she'd pass it to me, and she would take the bottle and throw it against the brick wall -- sprrrnng -- nng -- nng. You know.
(Laughter.)
One afternoon, between -- before matinee, we drank 22 half pints of corn liquor, of that stuff --
Just you and Bessie?
Bessie and I.
(Laughter.)
That stuff's kind of -- and you could taste the alum in it. It was the worst -- you know how many years that's been? That's 1928.
'28, uh-huh. You just told me you never had a hangover in your life.
Never had a -- naw, no hangover, and man, drinking that kind of stuff, I thank God I'm not dead.
(Laughter.)
And I still eat anything I want now. I still drink, and I still don't have -- oh God.
Well was that your biggest day? Those 22 half pints with Bessie?
Well that was one -- that particular time we were together so many times after that, and at that time she was married to a detective, who was a very --
Jack Gee?
Jack Gee! You know Jack Gee, huh?
Yeah.
Oh, you know him, or know about him?
I know of him.
You know of him.
Yeah.
Well he was a tough man, you know. And
one particular time (laughs) Jack told me, Jack told me this story. Then Bessie used to lay there in bed with a butcher knife telling him, saying when you go to sleep I'm going to kill you.
(Laughter.)

And Jack would be laying there with his .45, see, and I'm going to blow your brains out if you (Laughs.) Jack has his pistol in his hand. He says you start over here I'm going to blow your brains out. She's saying you go to sleep and start snoring I'm going to kill you, I'm going to stick you with the knife, man.
(Laughter.)
I said man, well Jack how can you sleep? He says ah, she ain't going to do it. But nothing happened, but man, the nerve. You know, but him being such a bad man -- (Laughter.)
She had a pretty bad temper, didn't she?
Oh, she -- oh, what a temper, and what a woman, you know. She was a big -- did you ever see Bessie?
No, before my time.
Well Bessie was darn near six foot, and big, and strong, had great big arms, you know, with a -- she looked like she could pick Jack Gee up by the collar and
lift him with one hand. She probably could have. You know. And Jack Gee wasn't a little man, you know. He was a man-sized man himself.

But oh, Bessie, and what a nice person. And she and I were good pals, and we worked together almost (inaudible). Later on in years when I was working with Fats -- now this is in the pit band way before Fats. I was working in the theater there, pitman, because I didn't even know Fats then. I'm in New York when I'm working with Fats, so one day Fats came by. I wasn't there. Fats came by my house, my room, outside was a taxi. "Come on, you big sausage," he called me. "I'm here, where you are?" Right?

You know, I tried to duck him, man. I didn't know where he was going. He wouldn't take it. "Come on!" He's sitting ouside in the taxi. "Come on, get in." I said -- he's scared to ask me. I didn't ask him where he was going, because if I had I would have brought my trumpet.
(Laughter.)

You know. "Come on (unintelligible)." I said okay. You don't know how to dress, I mean you're going with him. He says a couple -- a few times -- many times he's taken me out of town. I would have changed, I would have -- you know.
So he -- I'm going to continue to work with him, I don't want to make him unhappy, and so I go get in the car
with him, get in the taxi. He say, "52nd Street!" To myself I say now what's down there? Well, we get to 52nd street, and we go into the -- uh (snaps fingers) -- club, club -- Deuces, Three Deuces.
Three Deuces.

This is on a Sunday, and it wasn't open. The door opened, and we went in, there was nobody in there then, but shortly two or three people started coming in, a few people. You know, I look up and Bunny Berigan walked in, and I saw a couple of pieces of horns laying around there, they're Bunny's horns. Bunny was working there. Fats sat at the piano and started bling bling bling linga, playing and playing. Bunny came in and sat there, so Bessie Smith walked in soon, and people started coming in.

Before you knew what was happening -- he never explained nothing, what is happening. The session was on. So he said, "Come on!" I said, "I ain't got no horn." Bunny say, "Here, use one of mine." So I took the horn, while we were playing Bunny Berigan, Herman Autrey, Bessie Smith. So Fats would take four or five. Bunny would take four or five. Herman would take four or five. That's the way until the place was packed, they was standing on top of each other.
I never saw so many people in all my life. It was the darndest session I ever done in my life. I only wish I had a tape of that. And Bessie was -- oh my God, every time

she opened her mouth it was -- oh, in fact, it was backing up, and Bunny and I -- and oh, it was beautiful! And people was screaming and enjoying, and everything, and we were -- and every time I was looking up a waiter was coming over with a tray of liquor.
(Laughter.)
We got hungry, and finally I saw some spaghetti and something kind of -- I decided to eat, and that's what kept me alive, kept me from dying, you know.
Spaghetti.
Oh, man, 'cause I drink, I must eat. So that was the greatest thing I -- to my mind -- that I had ever done, is playing with Fats Waller, Bessie Smith, and Bunny Berrigan.
Just the four of you.
That's all.
How long did the session go on?
Oh, all afternoon!
All afternoon?
All -- my God, that means -- and the place was packed! (Laughs.) It was --
Did you ever find out how the whole thing had come together?
No. I don't know why or how, whether Fats was invited down, because I didn't get paid. Nobody gave
me any money. I hadn't asked for any money, you know.
It was worth it anyhow.
Sure it was worth it. I don't know what happened, and to me, it looked like Bunny just happened because it was Bunny's job, they were Bunny's horns.
Yeah, yeah.

Hanging -- laying around there, you know, two or three old piece of horn, and there was -- they had lived. I mean the horns had been around for 50 years by the look of them, you know. And pretty soon I had -- well, a good trumpet player, and I wouldn't say I was good, but experienced, and one that had been around. You keep your mouthpiece with you. You don't know where you're going, what you're going to run into. I happened to have my mouthpiece in my pocket, see?
So that was -- it gave me something to work with, and he gave me -- he provided the horn. So that I'm very proud of. I will never forget it. Never regret it.
Did you ever run into Bessie's temper?

No, not between she and I no, but I saw her -- I knew her sister. Her sister lived in Catur Street, down at the beginning of Catur Street. She had several children, and we used to go in there and buy our liquor. This was during prohibition, you know, days, and she

sold corn on the side there, you know. In fact, you stick your head out in the alley, you see a guy standing there by a garbage barrel, and you put one finger up or two fingers, that's what he brought you, one pint or two pints. He reached down in the garbage barrel and bring it to you.
(Laughter.)
specially mixed by Bessie's sister?
No, no, no. No, no, Bessie -- no, this was the big boys.
Oh, I see.

Had somebody selling it for them, you know, but Bessie's sister had some in her house too, and in fact, she used to tell me -- they were from Kentucky, and -- not Louisville, or -- oh, she had a riverboat.
