That was a gig in here, a couple of gigs there, and I ran into this man from Washington whom I had been working under. He was --
You want to take a break a minute, Herman?
No, no. I want to get the Kleenex,
but I can't get over there. I'm going to turn it off just a minute. We'll pick it right back up.
(Recording interruption.)
Well you were -- you went out with Fletcher after the rehearsal at Fletcher's house?
Uh-huh, uh-huh.
And you said you wanted to stay with Fletcher.

Yeah. Yeah, after doing this thing we had a -- I think it was a New Year's Eve thing. We did it with Fletcher, and the band went pretty good, and where I was lucky and happy afterwards for doing this recording, and I didn't have the music, and I memorized it, and everything went well.

Well after that we had a couple of days, or one day, in the Savoy. Well for years, before -- even before I met Fletcher, or joined him, he and Chick Webb (laughs) had been battling, you know, and music, you know, who's the best, who's greatest, and when the people would pack the place to see it. So while I was with him he's saying we had a -- oh, strenuous rehearsal. He said well I'm going to play against that little guy again. He said this time I must -- I gotta get -- I gotta get him.
I said who? He said Chick Webb. I said all right,

nice, you know. I was for it. I had never played against Chick, and I knew Chick. I knew him, naturally, as much as I knew about him. I knew about Chick and both, because I'd been hearing about them for years. So we get to the Savoy. The place is packed. Ohhh, you never saw so many people. And Fletcher's playing -- you know, Fletcher had something with that beat, dunh dee, dee, pa-daddle doo dee duh duh dum, bah bee, dah dah jussle, and look out and he'd see the people. You'd see the heads bouncing.
(Laughter.)

You see hundreds of hundreds of people on the floor, and they were bouncing in the beat, and it made you feel good. And -- well, Fletcher had always had this problem, when everything he played against Chick before, his brother Horace, who would steal his arrangements, and sell them to Chick.
(Laughter.)
As his absense, of course, so when you get on the job, instead of him playing something that Chick hadn't heard, Chick would beat him to it and play it before he heard it.
(Laughter.)
And most times, played better. That's how good Chick's band -- oh, Chick had a heck of a band! Oh man! And the band would play it, and Fletcher would say How
did they get that? That'sounds like one of my things!
(Laughter.)

You know? And Chick would be -- all -- well, when you buy it, and Horace would sell it and make him some money. Horace could play very nice piano himself, but he was still a stinker. He was -- steals his brothers things and sell it, you know. (Laughs.) Wow!

So we would sit there and play, and I had never played any of the arrangements like Fletcher's in my life, you know, I was so elated I was just knocked out, because he would -- he would bring his hands down, and the band would start the rhythm, uh-one, two, three, four, one, two, three, four, and you stayed there, and you didn't have to move, and it was no -- you were comfortable, just play. And then those were there, I mean you didn't have to look -- to me, you didn't have to worry about reading, because everything was there, and it was-- the way he wrote, that was the way he wrote music.
And --
You mean he was logical?
Oh, logical, oh man, it was so pleasing, them things were so nice.

So at the end, Fletcher jumped and screamed and said at last! At last I've got him! Because for years they had been doing that, and Chick had been winning out, you know? At last I got him! I got him! I got -- you know. And -- but
I mean everybody was happy, and people enjoyed the music, and we got paid, and Fletcher was happy. But Chick had been winning for so many years it didn't matter.
Herman?
Yes?
From what you say, and from what I've heard, Fletcher seems to have been a rather odd person, in a way, in that --
He was.
-- for example you tell about Leora could come in and make a comment like that about the trumpet player that Fletcher thought was so great, and letting his brother steal his arrangements.
Well --
Was he easy -- very easy-going?

He was. He was. He was very easy, you know, he was one of those types -- I did, I felt sorry for him because he was -- well all right. Yes. Okay, you know. He's always -- always so willing to -- I'm with you, whatever you say. If that's the way you want it. Okay. Everything's all right with me. You know. And to me people took advantage of him. I think.
How had he been able to get such great bands together and keep them together, if that was the way he was (inaudible).

Well being such a musician he was, and now, meeting the guys, and getting the guys, somebody sent me. He didn't ask me. Somebody said well Fletcher needs a trumpet player. And he said go over there and tell him I sent you. Or just go there. One of those things. I happened to walk in. I was glad, and Fletcher was glad. Now whether -- he had people like Bobby Stark Stocks. Oh, no greater trumpet player ever lived than Bobby.
And that's a man who has very little been mentioned, one of the most underrated trumpet players I think in the country. Bobby Stark Stocks (sic) was a heck of a trumpet player.
Why was he so underrated?
I don't know. I don't know. Nobody mentioned him. He was with Chick, and he was -- and he could play, and did play, and a heck of a nice guy, a gentleman.
Was he too nice a guy? Was that his problem?

I -- well maybe. Buy then I mean you know, maybe had he been one of those guys who was a knock-down drag-out like me, Sandy, and a whole other cats, maybe he would have been better off, maybe. But -- I dare anybody now to bring out a recording that he's on and they can tell me they do not like him. Because he was just that good, and he's a college graduate. I think he went to Fisk. No, not Fisk, he went to the other place in Ohio, the other college in Ohio.
: Wilberforce?
Wilberforce. Yeah. And he's a doggone good man. You know?
: Was -- while you were with Fletcher -- you were with Fletcher several times, weren't you? A couple of times?
No.
: Just that one time?

No, that was it. I went in and I played first trumpet after what's-his-name, and I was proud of it, and I stick my chest up because I was able to go in there and play that book without a rehearsal, and he was happy, I was happy, so that makes me feel doggone good. Okay?
: What sort of a relationship did you have with Fletcher?

With Fletcher? Well, I mean playing his music, everything was fine. And (Laughs) til he got to the other part, where I came in, I told you I was with carnivals, and road shows, and I knew I was with the greatest con men in the world, you know? So when he said well folks, we're going to Philadelphia, the scales and so-and-so, I can't play with so, I said Good-bye! And that was it, you know.
(Laughter.)
But I would -- I said -- and I thanked him very much, and I split, because I knew the end of the
story, and I went through that when I first came into show business, you know.
So you know when to get off --
Oh man, I know -- I mean I knew when to run out, you know. (Laughs.)
So when you ran out, what happened this time? Where did you go from there?

Well, from there I went to -- I'm still staying in New York, and I went down to -- I hadn't met Charlie Johnson's band in Philadelphia before I came to New York, and bass man, who's gone now, the greatest bass player in the world --
(Laughter.)
Pops Foster.
Oh, Pops Foster.
(Laughter.)

Well Pops always did think a lot of me. He want -- he said Boy, come on in the band, but he's with Louie Russell then, so he wanted me in the band, and he said you should be here, you should be there, you should been -- so when I -- aw, I missing, when I did come to New York, I -- and got this room, I needed a job, I was hungry. They have no room, and I didn't have money to pay room rent, or anything, so somebody called me and gave me this job, I think it was four or five dollars, in the Village, and when I got there

they didn't -- well I had a tuxedo, but no one told me tuxedo, so I grabbed my trumpet and a dark suit and I ran on down there. So I got ready to get on the stand and the manager who ran the place, somebody, said Who are you?

I said I'm the trumpet player. Well where's your tux? I said well nobody told me to. He said well you can't get up on -- you can't get up there, you know. Well, I figure speak for four or five dollars (unintelligible) you know. Until you get the tux you can't get on that stand. Maybe he was waiter. I don't know who the heck he was. Pops walks in there, and I sat back there alone. What's the matter, boy? What's the matter, fellow? Huh? this man says I can't get up, I says (unintelligible). Why can't -- why -- what? Okay, if he doesn't get up, I don't get up. And that was it. And Pops sat packing up his bass. He said wait, Pop, wait, wait. I said well nobody told me to wear a tuxedo, so, and so, and see, so he says if this man goes home, I go home, and I'll pull the whole band out of here. So man, was I having a ride. I loved him after that, because my wife and I needed the money. We couldn't eat. I had no rent money, nothing to eat with, or anything. So that five bucks was really -- and Pops came in there with a tuxedo, stiff shirt, tie, oh man, he looked like he's going -- just walked out of the movies, or going to walk into the movies. You know.
Because he was with the big band there making money,
but he didn't know [Mike] and anyhow -- I guess he knew, but anyway, but he stood up for me, and I loved him until this day for that. You know?
Right, yeah. I know.

Because he just said well, sorry sonny, you don't have a tux, goodbye, you know? later, you know. And I had to get -- I don't -- I doubt whethr I had over a nickel to get back there, the subway was a nickel then. I guess I had a nickel to get back uptown, maybe I did. I don't know if I had, but I got to done more -- you know. So that was it.
And I've never forgotten him for it, and --
We were going to -- you were starting to talk about Charlie Johnson.

Charlie Johnson, yeah. So little things like that, picked up a couple of dollars, kept me eating. So I went down to Charlie Johnson's, and I had met Ham Davis, who's a trumpet player. I had met Charlie. Oh, drummer, uh, I'll recall his name in a minute. One of the greatest guys -- uh, I -- oh, what, what, what,what? Trying to think. Oh, Roane-- Kenneth Roane was the trumpet player in the band. He was a very fine man. When he -- I still say he's one of the greatest trumpet players that ever came to New York, ever around New York, and arrangers, and all that, because I played a lot of his music. You ever see any of Ken-
neth's work?
On records --
Beautiful!
-- I think, that's all --
Beautiful! It looks like a picture.

I mean when he sits down and writes it's -- he's a perfectionist, playing, and writing, and when he's -- back when I first with him, years ago, I mean playing, I mean anyway, he's -- I still love him. He's a great guy.
My man playing drums, I can't remember.
He may come.
I -- anyway, I went down to see him, Kenneth told me, come in, sit down. And he heard me play. Kenneth say play this for me, or play that for me. I played. He told Charlie I was all right.
(Laughter.)
So, Charlie said okay fellow, you in the band. And meantime, Mr. Smalls, [crossed out], called this guy up, and said pick him up, [crossed out] Jimmy, take him down to 802 and give him a card.
Oh, you didn't have your card then.

No, I wasn't -- no. They took me down to 802 and got me a card and put me in the union, and back that time -- so it was easy. I was a union man. I was in the union, I had an 802 card in my pocket, and a job.

So everything was fine, and Charlie had a doggone good band, you know. He had Benny Waters on Tenor sax. He had Johnson -- Bobbie Johnson on guitar. He had -- uh, uh -- I'm trying to -- he had Bobbie Johnson's brother on sax -- let's see, what's his name? Gooseneck, we used to call him.
Gooseneck?
Yeah, he plays piano, and -- in the -- and saxaphone there. Bobbie Johnson and -- Howard Johnson.
Oh yeah, Howard Johnson,
Yeah.
Yeah. Lonnie -- what's his name? He's a tenor saxaphone player too. He was in there. Lonnie Johnson -- Lonnie -- Lonnie Simmons.
Lonnie Simmons.
Yeah. Oh, Billy Taylor on bass. Old man Billy Taylor, and what a bass man, you know.
Who were the trombones, do you remember?

Yes. Hmm, yeah. Story, Story from Kentucky, Ralph Story? What was his name? Paducah? Used to call him -- his nickname was Paducah, Paducah, Kentucky, that's where he's -- that was his home. And he played trombone. What was Paducah's name? Doggone it, that's why I can't think of his name that way, because of Paducah. That's where he was from, that's the name -- was Paducah, Kentucky.
Ah, Ralph Storey, that could be. Yeah.
Sounds right.
Yeah, Ralph Storey. It had to be, yeah.
Sounds right.
Yeah, Ralph Storey. But what a band! Yeah, what a band it was. And I was working there with them, and of course I'll tell you about the trumpet player. I -- uh -- with the buzz mute.
Oh, Frankie Newton.
Frankie Newton.
Frankie Newton.
Yeah, and Babe -- Babe from Baltimore. Babe -- uh, it's a heck of a -- another heck of a trumpet player. I forgot Babe's name, but that was a band.
Were you playing first trumpet with the band?
No, second.
Second.
'Cause Kenneth Roane was playing first.
Kenneth Roane was playing.
I was playing second, and they brought Babe in, and Babe was playing in there, and we used to swap the -- you know, concerts. I mean the solos and stuff. And --
Well tell me a little bit about Charlie
Johnson, Herman. He's a guy who really never has gotten as much publicity as he deserved.

He -- right. Right, right, because he wrote a lot of tunes before I met him. I heard him talking about them. 'Fat and Greasy is one thing he did. Naturally that was for the -- you know, the gutter, for these -- but he did a lot of nice things, did, and I never heard about -- he didn't hear about either, because I don't know, at that time -- hm, let's face it, a colored guy couldn't get out. And you had to right some hokum, some junk, something like 'Fat and Greasy' before they considered it, maybe, and it stinks, and I mean -- 'Fat and Greasy'. Who wants it? Who needs it? You know.
And he was a good musician, good piano player, and I'm trying to think of --

For example, Herman, we take three guys who are contemporary then. Let's take Fletcher Henderson, Duke Ellington, and Charlie Johnson, all of whom had good bands, and yet Charlie Johnson is the least known of the three.
Yes.
What -- why would that be?
Well, I would think that Charlie stayed in Small's so many years, because he's -- he -- I don't know how they met, when, but Charlie stayed there so many years.

I mean it's one of those things. Stay here, this is home. (unintelligible). You don't have to worry, have to run out on the road like those other guys, out, not [ ], not going to pay you, you don't say that. I ain't going to pay you nothing, but stay here, you know what I mean, you know. Forty years and you'll always have a job, and I'll be a millionaire, you know. Because you know, just like down some places, still going downtown, 54th Street, Ryan's, you know.
You stay here and work, and you can go out and work when you get ready, but come on back and we'll be here, and I hope you can make it back, you know?
But still, Charlie had a hell of a band.
Well he did have a hell of a band. Red Allen, Louie Armstrong, he's had some of the best people you can name, at one time.
Was Louie with him?
Oh sure. Louie worked in there --
How about that.
Heck yeah.
Well, was there a -- did you -- was there a wire, radio wire in Smalls?
Well, a couple or few small times there they had this connection with the radio station, where --
But not --
-- they would broadcast, but it wasn't --
Well it wasn't like the Cotton Club, or Duke was on the air every night, or something like that.
No, no, no. No, no.
Or Fletcher with Roseland Ballroom.
No, no. No.
Well was this what made the difference, do you think, the difference in --

No, well that -- and the money, the it might have an interest. There wasn't nobody gived a damn. Let's face it, you know. The more you're in front of the public, naturally the more the public hears you. But nobody gave a damn, and they spend their money, and that was it.
Even though it was a hell of a band.
Oh, yes, sure, hell of a band. And he came out, and went in the Apollo Theater, and died like a dog. I was with him.
Really? He did?
Oh sure. I was in the band. We went -- not the Apollo, Lafayette. That's before the Apollo. I was in the band. And --
But even within the community of Harlem he wasn't that well known.
Well it wasn't that he wasn't well-known, maybe, it's what's happening. I mean if you can't get

the money, you can't draw the people out, I don't know, what you going to do? Now they came to Philadelphia. That's where I first met him. He was playing a dance date there, and I met him and the band, and they had a hell of a band. And they were blowing the walls down.

You know -- let me see. I mentioned Ham Davis. I'm trying to think who was the other trumpet player. I think -- I think it was -- I think it was Rex Stewart was it? It was the God damndest brass -- excuse me, oh, sorry.
That's all right.

Best brass I ever heard in my life, the loudest, strongest, and the band was blowing. They were playing, you know. And, who was in the band? But man, what a heck of a band! And Rex -- I'm pretty sure Rex was in there, Ham Davis, Rex Stewart, and who else? Because I mean when you -- you've got to stick your finger) your -- the main -- you could hear them ten blocks?
I mean that's the way the bands were playing and sounding in those days, you know.
This was loud, but good too.

Loud but good. Sure, that's before I came to New York, and I went down there to join them. Well those guys was with them, Ham Davis wasn't there. Kenneth Roan was there. Me, and -- Babe somebody from Baltimore. And it still was a good group, but not loud and -- well, but
and good arrangements, and --
Who did the arranging? Charlie?

Well, tenor sax man, uh, he's in Germany now. Benny Waters was doing some, and who else? In the band, was doing arrangements. There were two or three other guys doing the arrangements, banjo player who used to be with Charlie. He was -- I didn't care for them. I didn't care for his arrangements, but he did some of them.
And then Charlie would buy some, and here and there, and different guys, different people would bring in arrangements, you know.
Did you do any writing at all at this point, Herman?
Not arrangements, no. I wrote a few things, you know. I mean composed a few things, like the 'Yacht Club Swing.'
Well this -- this was later, with Fats.
Yeah.
Yeah. I was thinking of this particular time. How long did you stay with Charlie at Smalls?
I can't think how --
A year or so?
-- many months.
Oh, not even a year.
Maybe a year. Maybe.
I've got a note here says it was around 1933, 1934 you were with him.
Uh-huh. Yeah. Yeah, yeah. Uh-huh.
And this was all at Smalls Paradise? Did you go out of town with Charlie at all, or was it just -- you stayed at Smalls?
I don't remember doing any dates out of New York with Charlie. I don't remember. Maybe so. I don't --
Why did you leave -- Charlie?
To go with Fats.
Oh, to go with --
Fats -- yeah, Fats Waller came in to Smalls and saw me, happened to be in there in a little party, and saw me playing, and -- uh, I like this story too. I like this right here.
Okay.

When Fats came in, I wasn't aware of it, because I didn't know him, I hadn't ever met Fats. I'm sitting on the stand, all the fellows -- most of the fellows had gotten up and gone here, gone there, gone over to the john, parties, wherever, whatnot. I sat on the stage by myself, and I dunno, I was just like -- if I'm playing a part, okay. I'm in this band, I'm playing first. This particular tune, well I knew what could happen, see, because
I played it. Now I would like to see the second part. (Laughter.) : I see.

You know? So I was sitting, so I reach over and get a look and see what the second part looks like. After I see that, now let me see the third part, you know. And I was sitting there, and I'm looking, and a man comes by, you know, just and the harmonies, and because while I'm playing (laughs) that I know, I'm sitting playing. I hear you playing. I know when you make a mistake what I see, that's not what's there. I know what's there. Because I saw it, you know. I can hear it, and I know what's supposed to be there.

And -- but I don't jump on you, because I -- you know. It did me good to know, for some reason, why -- I don't know. If you ask me now why did you have to know? I couldn't answer you. You know? But I like to know, and he was right, or he was wrong.
: It's part of the whole picture.
Yeah, yeah. I guess. I don't know.
So that was the thing, sitting there with Fletcher -- I mean with Charlie, and --
: Fats was in the club?
Fats is in the club one night, and he saw me doing this. So he asked somebody, who is that guy?
After he heard me play. Say his name is Herman Autrey. Herman Autrey? Yeah. But -- Bud Scrippy, Arnold Bolding, did you ever hear of him?
: No.
Arnold Bolling.
: Arnold Bolling?
Bolling. He's from Florida.
: B-o-l-l-i-n-g?

Very fine drummer. He was with -- Arnold played some with everybody. Wait a minute, some of the big bands, a lot of the big bands. Wait a minute. Dog-gone it, I don't know where I am. (Snaps fingers.) Some of the bigger -- Don Redman Bradman. He played with -- what the heck, Arnold played with some of the best bands around town.

Anyway, I'm -- see I'm -- I mean said where does he live? So I said I live down the street, 123rd -- 129th Street, at the end of Seventh Avenue. So he told -- I asked him if he'd like to do some records with me. Fats. I'm laying up in bed asleep with my wife, Herman! I said what? Herman! He says, hey, he says, 'how you doing? My name is Arnold, this is Bud Scripp, you know me.' I say yes, Scripp, you with Arnold Bolling.
He says Fats Waller sent me down and ask you if -- would you like to do some records with him. I say man, (Pants), like I was speechless. I said certainly, sure. He

says okay. That's it. He went back and told him. So he says well go to this address, and he says (unintelligible). I say my name is Herman Autrey. He says well I'm Fats, hello, come on in, and he made (unintelligible). We met each other. What did you think? I said man, I'd be tickled to death, you know. You know the rest of the story from there.
No, I want to hear the rest of the story from there.

Well I mean -- would you like to make some? I say yes sir! I'd be very happy, tickled to death. And I never made a record in my life, and never been near a studio, and I'm -- you know, so I'm all everything, elated, and everything.
So he said okay. Meet me down at Victor's studios tomorrow morning at 8:00 o'clock, at 24th Street, and --
Third Avenue?
I -- yeah. I guess. It's been so long. I would be there. So man! You should have seen me getting down, and standing in front of the doorway, for this place to open, and --
(Laughter.)
You were there early, then.
Oh sure. I saw him come, I saw the guys come up. We went inside. I didn't know what to do, and they pulled off their jackets and coats and thing, and

take out their horns, and sat there and I saw other men come in, and engineers and stuff, and set up this, and putting up the mikes. He was sitting at the piano, trying to find out which was the best A. You know. I didn't know what was happening.
Your first time in a recording studio.

First time in a recording studio. And we got started, and started playing. Oh man, he would play something, he would play this. He said all right, Herman, you come in and you do this, you play down the first sixteen, the second sixteen, second eight, and do -- you do this, you come in, this and that, we'll try that. We tried it, and ah, pretty good. It was okay, we'll try it again, and the engineer said that's pretty good. Give us another one, you know.
He kept saying that, otherwise, 'all right, nice, record.' Fats Said (Unintelligible) 'well, play it back.' And we played it back and I heard Herman I says 'Is that me?'
(Laughter.)
Is that me? Oh man, I don't know what -- I don't know, you know. Hearing myself for the first time.
What was the piece, do you remember?
Well, I have a thing there, bomp, bom dah bom, dee, dah dah dah. That's one of the tunes. 'Chamber
"Porter's Love Song?"
"Porter's Love Song, to a instead of Chamber Maid." And "Arms Full of Sweetness." I think that was it.
: Uh-huh, "Arms Full of Sweetness."

Dum, duh dah dum, dum ba, dum ba dah. Yeah. "Arm Full of Sweetness," and, and I think the "Chamber Maid" is one. I think that's the first set. And it knocked me out. Hearing myself play. And now I'm my worst enemy.
: Why?

Well, I didn't like what I heard. Me. I figured it could have been better. Why didn't I do this? Or why didn't I pinch a little more? Or why did I pinch too much? You know. That's the thing, then you start giving yourself the devil. Why? Why? Why? You know. Why don't you rehearse more? Why don't you practice more? Why do you do -- And why? Why?
And I don't know. I went -- when I came home I was very upset.
: Well, it's probably a good way to be.
Maybe. Maybe. But I mean I wasn't happy with what I had done.
: Well what did Fats say?
Oh, he was -- "bye, see you fellows. Good night." You know.
That's it. You know, these things that you played, these were pop tunes. Did you know the tunes before you went in the studio?
No. No.
Did you have music, or did you --
No, you didn't know what you were going to do. You're standing there, and they come up, and they hand them out to Fats. Fats turn and put them on the piano, open them up.
First time he's seen them.

Firsttime, and then he says, well, you know, now okay fellows, and he pass out a lead sheet to each one, to me, to Gene Sedric, guitar, you know, chords, maybe, or maybe a lead sheet, guitar, and to the bass. And when we hit (unintelligible) it had been -- uh, uh, some published -- you know what I'm trying to say, it was open --
Stock arrangement?

Stock arrangement. First you see Fats hit the ceiling. 'No! Why did they do that? Bring me that bass part.' He would take it and change it. 'That's lousy,' you know. 'Who's doing this?' You know. That's the wrong bass, the wrong notes, because naturally the man would start playing what he sees, and a man like Billy Taylor, you know, he wasn't making a mistake.
(Laughter.)

'Oh After all, my, my, they'll never learn. Fats says bring me the part, and Fats would take it, and then he'd say play these notes, you know. And we'd make the record, and it would be beautiful, because they had the right notes, the right chords, and he knew. Believe me when I say he knew, he wasn't guessing. He knew.
Who -- on this first session you did, Herman, who was in the group at that time? Gene? Gene Sedric?
No.
No?
No. No. I'm glad you asked me that. Nobody ever mentions his name. He's gone now. Is -- ahhhh -- alto saxophone player. Ben Whittig.
I remember the name. Ben Whitted.
Ben Whitted. You remember the name now?
I remember the name, right.

And nobody mentions him, and nobody ever asks me about him, but -- but he was a darned good musician. Oh, he was quite a musician! He was with -- uh, uh -- down at Charlie Johnson's. In that band. Yeah.
In Charlie Johnson's band.
Yeah, playing first clarinet and sax.
This is where Fats is picking people up.
Yeah, and what a man he was. Ben -- oh Ben was just there, and he had -- he looked like Cyclops sitting in there, with his eyes. (Laughs.)
Really?
Oh, he did. He had very bad eyes, and they had --
Was this the first time he played with Fats too? Just like you?
Yeah, the first (unintelligible) and and the last time he came out and played, because Fats asked for him. Had to.
Billy Taylor was on bass? Or who?
Billy Taylor on bass.
And who was on drums?
Ben -- uh, da, da, da, da, da, da -- Apple Jaws Jones.
Apple Jaws Jones.
Yeah, I named him Apple Jaws Jones.
(Laughter.)
Very good drummer. I haven't seen him or played with him since then.
He was just on this one date then?
He made two or three records. For some reason, Victor didn't like him. They (unintelligible).
(Whistles.)
Well, we can check that out.
Okay, I check that out later. He --
How about guitar? Who was on guitar?
Al Casey.
Al Casey.
Al Casey, yes, because Al Casey was a kid then, in school. And he took Al Casey out of school and put him in the union. Afterwards.
Oh, I see.
Uh-huh. Yeah.
But this was now -- when you started with Fats he'd already been making records for Victor, with the group, before that.
No, no, no, no.
Was this the first one?
No, was the first -- I was in the first group. This was it --
This was the first --
-- because Victor had never heard of such animal, and didn't want it. Al -- so Mr. Kirk and a -- not Kirkaby --
(End of Tape Four.)
Well Herman, this recording session you did with Fats was the first one, you say, of a series that Fats did with this small group at Victor. How did this happen? Who was after who? Fats? Or Victor?

Well, here's what happened. A very good friend of ours, a man that was handling Fats then, Phil Ponce, and well, to me he was a great guy. To Fats he was a great guy. You see, in the meantime, Fats was in Cincinnati, working there by himself, and he start --
Was that when he was at WLW?

Yeah, WLW. Well Phil Ponce was there with him, in -- holding his arm up, you know. In other words, his ego, and trying to help him out, and telling him he should do this and do the other, and Phil was a good man for him, so if -- they came through that thing out there, and from there Phil brought him to New York.
Now, when they got to New York Victor -- he talked Victor into letting Fats have a small band, six-piece band, and they screamed Murder, never! You know, never heard --
Why? What was their objection?

Well, they'd never had a small group, a small band like that before, and they didn't think it would be advisable. They didn't think it would pay, and would be nice, and so and so and so and so. So they finally agreed, under some reason why I do not know, but I'm glad they did, because when we started recording, well, it was fair. (Laughs.) As our first date came to -- they paid us $13.00 for the first day.
Twenty-six for Fats?

(Laughs) I don't know what Fats got. But I know that's what I got, because the thing didn't do so well. Okay. So we took the thirteen bucks, and the next time we recorded we got a raise, $3.00, I think it was.
(Laughs.) Well how long did it take before they wanted Fats back to do another one?

No, that's what I'm saying now. The next date was Three bucks, and it -- the thing began to turn. It was a standstill. I mean nothing happened. Now, on the second date it -- the wheel began to turn a little bit. They said aw, well, there's a possibility. And from there we went into it and worked it up until we got into money, and after that -- after -- well, the world knows, he was the greatest recording artist ever.
And Victor still thinks he's the greatest. I know he was the greatest. But I -- that's the way it went, you know. But we were the first six-piece group that ever was, I mean --
And from -- I gather from what you tell me, Herman, that the six-piece group was put together awfully casually, just what, a day or two before the date? Got you --
Well, yes.
: He got you, and he got --
Yeah.
: -- what did --
Well, he got me, guitar player --
: Al Casey.
-- Al Casey.
: Had he worked with Al before?

Well, no. Well Al, Al used to come around to his house a lot, and play with his children, his kids, you know. And Al was a kid himself at that time. You know, a little boy. And Al would come around there and play his guitar, and Fats would throw him a few crumbs, you know, show him no, do this, hit this chord, hit that chord. So then the thing come up for Fats to do some recording, Fats said well, I'll use you. Do this, do this, and do what I tell you, and Fats used him on the dates. You know.
: So he used Al, who he had known, and he used you, I mean just --
Well he met -- met for the first
: -- (inaudible) time.
Yeah, 'cause he saw and heard me down at Smalls Paradise. I was working down there.
: He heard Whitted too?
Who?
: He heard Whitted at that time too?
Well Whitted -- he was working there in the band before I was, before I came to join Ed Small he had been in the band. I don't know how many years, but he'd been there.
Did Fats work with him before?

I doubt it. I don't think so. I think he just heard him, because at that time most all of the celebrities from New York -- New York, I mean Broadway -- would come up to Harlem on Saturday nights and let it run into Sunday morning, 7:00, 8:00, 9:00, 10:00 o'clock in the morning, to jam sessions, supper clubs, what you want to call it, breakfast dances, and they had all kind of names for it.

And that's what happened, and that's how they happened to hear the bands. The guys were working there. That's why they worked so late, and that's how I happened to -- Fats happened to hear us. That's how we happened to -- met so many movie stars, so many this, and so many that, who came up to hear us, and that's the way the thing went. You know?
But at that point Fats had no group of his own. He had to put something together for this recording session.

No, he had no group. No, he had no group of his own, he had no -- coming down in a party. I don't know who was in the party. It just was happened, but he evidently had the idea, or knowledge that he was going to be
offered, or had been offered this date, and then they needed a band, because he heard me play, and sent word to me asking me if I wanted to join him, and I was very happy about the whole thing.
After the first date, then you went back and you were still in Charlie Johnson's band, this was just --
Yes. Yes.
Just this one recording date.
Yes, uh-huh.
Then how long 'til the second one?

Well, I mean be start -- let me sound, let me try to think. And I don't know, maybe a month, or a couple of months, you know how those things work out, and then you hang -- you move, or whatever's happening, and you get another one, and I said well, it looks like something's going to come -- become of this, or something's going to turn out good, so you know, beware, keep cool, be straight, be ready to bounce, you know?
Did the group change from date to date?
No, we stuck there. Let me see, we had the same group, Herman Autrey on trumpet; the guitar, same; bass player, same; Eugene Sedric, the same;
You've got Sedric now, because before
you had -- you said you had Whitted in the first band.

Oh, Whitted. Oh that's -- after the first date -- now just a second. There was no Whitted. Eugene Sedric came in, because I did know the reason why, because Sedric came out and had something to do with a date, another date that we had, and they brought in Eugene Sedric. Truthfully, right now I can't think, but there is a particular reason, and it wasn't -- uh -- nothing inferior, I would say, I mean about --
About Whitted.

-- about Whitted, no. Whitted is a heck of a nice guy, and we loved him. Fats enjoyed his work, and all that. I'm trying to think now how Sedric got in there, and I do know, and I'm trying to think of it. But from there, that Sedric got in, that was it, you know? Uh-huh.
Had Sedric worked with Fats before?
No.
I see. He didn't know -- what had he been doing at that time?
Ah, well Sedric -- Eugene Sedric had been to Europe with -- uh -- I'm trying to think of the big band. He'd been to -- he'd been to Europe.
With a big band.
Yeah, with a big band. A big -- a very -- big name, too. Very nice guy, a very fine man. But

I didn't know Sedric then, while he was with this band. I don't think Fats did either. But I found out later, he had been to Europe with this group, you know. And -- a year, and had been back, you know. And no, oh man, I can't think.
That's okay. Now how long did the -- did you play on all of Fats's dates?
Yes.
At the beginning? I mean there were some later on that you weren't on.

I did -- the only ones I did not do was when I was sick with a cold, or something. John Hamilton, "Buggs" Johnny Burks, took my place, and another time I didn't show up, Bill Coleman did a date for me. A very fine trumpet player, both these guys, terrific. Bill Coleman and Johnny "Buggs", or John Hamilton, whichever is the preferred, you know?
Now how did the group develop from just a recording unit, to becoming a regular performing group? When did that happen? What brought it about?

Uh, you mean the large group? Well, after we did those -- did our dates, and the people liked them, and they'd be -- they were buying them, then had some people to write in about dance dates, you know, if we would do some, you know. Some one nights here, and then, you know. So the managers, they set them up.
Was this still Phil [Ponse]?
Well, yes, for a while, Philip Ponse. Later on he got very ill there, and he passed. Then went on to other agents.
That's when Ed Kirkaby came in?
(Laughs.) You know Ed Kirkaby?
(Laughs.)
Ho, yeah, well Ed came in then.
(Laughs.) Well, Herman, tell us about Ed Kirkaby.
Well, he's a very nice man. I mean, oh my, should I? Do I?
Why not?
Must I?
You don't have to.
Oh, well. I mean, Ed's a nice guy.
But he was a problem?
He still is. I mean --
(Laughter.)
Oh, God! Well no, no. Ed's all right. (Laughs.) You dropped me that time. You laid one on me, baby.
(Laughs.) Well, we'll get around to that one in a little while.
Well now Fats had Ed to take care of his business, some business for him, for him, and Ed moved in
there to -- smooth operator. He was working for Victor. Victor had to let him go. He almost owned Victor.
(Laughter.)
And a couple of other places he worked he almost owned them. Ed's Ed, I mean, you know.
Well why?
He's a great -- he's a good business man.
He's a capable guy.
You damn right. He's a capable --
A good guy to have on your side.
On your side, yeah.
On your side. Was he -- well, you could feel he wasn't always on your side.
I don't think so.
(Laughter.)
He wasn't on mine, anyway.
On your personal side.
No, no. No.

Okay. Well let's go back to how the group developed as an actual performing group, rather than just as a recording group. When -- where did you start? Do you remember when, or at least where the first -- you first played together in public, rather than in a recording studio?
Other than at a recording studio, huh?
Well, I'm trying to think now --
(Telephone interruption.)
Okay, the phone just rang, and now we're off the phone. We were talking about when the Fats Waller group first started playing before the public.
Well, I think -- well I know we did a few things up in Connecticut, and all that. I heard --
Those were one-nighters.

Yeah, well I have a -- I've got to tell this. We went up to -- uh, not to far up into Connecticut. By golly, what's the name of the damn town? Anyway, we went up there, so when the bus -- we had a bus. It took the small group, the six guys -- (laughs) -- we stopped right in front of the joint. A lot of guys run out to see, oh here's the band.

And now -- I've got to name these guys. Charlie Turner is bass player. He weighed 290 pounds, at least, you know. And that's a pretty good sized man. At that time Fats was weighing 285, 90, maybe three, you know. At that time Herman Autrey was weighing about 245 or 50. Emmett Matthews was weighing about the same. And we had a drummer with us who is now -- he's working in the parks. He works for the Park Service. The thing here in New York? Uh -- uh, uh, uh, he's six foot three or four. He was weighing 200 and something, and who else was on -- who else was there? He's the
drummer.
[You had the]
: (Inaudible) drummer?
Yeah, piano I'm trying to think.
That's about everybody, isn't it?
That's about six of them?
I think so.
And when we stepped out of the bus, man, the guy said, Jesus what a band! Got football players, or what.
(Laughter.)
All of the big guys, and there was some -- naturally we were some pretty grown up men.

Now after we did the date up there, we sounded pretty good, but after that we went to Virginia, we started working down in Norfolk, Richmond, Virginia, a few things around there, I'm trying to think -- now I'm trying to think, we -- did we go into the Carolinas then? I don't think -- I'm not positive.

And back in New York, we did go to the Carolinas, and on down, we went down, on further down, we hit Georgia, and Alabama, and all that stuff, much later, you know. Doing one-nighters. But that's the way it -- that's the way it started, you know?
By that -- obviously by then you'd left Charlie Johnson.

Oh heck yeah. Oh, before that we started one -- weeks, theaters, Washington, D. C., Philadelphia, the Howard Theater in Washington, D. C. Philadelphia, Lincoln Theater, the one on Market Street where I got married that time.
Was this just your second wife, or how many?
Well, I -- I'm trying to think if this was when I got married, on Broad Street. I --
Got married in the theater?
Yeah, in the theater, on --
On the stage?
-- the stage.
Doing the show?
Uh-huh.
And who did you marry?
The mother of my daughter, now. Elizabeth, I married Elizabeth Radcliff.
Radcliff.
Uh-huh.
And your daughter's name is what?
Autrey, naturally. She became Elizabeth Autrey, and my daughter's name is Patricia --
Patricia.
-- Autrey. Uh-huh.
How old is Patricia now?
Patricia, Patricia is what? Thirty -- 31 or 32. Somewhere along there.
Married?

Oh yes, she's -- she's married to -- has two children, Tony and Angela, around ten, ten or eleven, and her husband's a colonel in the Army. He's in over -- in Saiwon, Saigon, or somewhere over there. He's -- he left here as a major and now he's a colonel.
Oh, great. What's his name?
Harrison.
Harrison.
Yeah, Harrison. He's (clap) I'm trying to think toofast, about Tony -- Anthony, his son's -- I'm thinking so much about his little son, who's a trumpet player. My grandson's a trumpet player.
This Tony?
yeah, Tony. Yeah. He's named after his father.
How old is Tony now?
Tony must be about eleven.
Oh, so he's just getting started.
Oh yeah, uh-huh. Uh-huh.
You've got hopes for him?
Oh sure, yeah!
Sounds good? Good.
Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Uh-huh.
Well anyhow, so you got married in Philadelphia during the show. How did you happen to get married during the show?
Well, we were working there. We were there during an engagement, you know. We got two weeks, and I had promised her, and she caught me.
(Laughter, clap, clap, clap.)
You know how those things -- you know how those things --
Did you promise her it would be on the stage of the theater during the show?
No, I didn't -- no, no.
How did that come up?
Well Fats, God bless him --
(Laughter.)
-- my pal, he say, I've got an idea. I said -- I'm always afraid of his ideas.
(Laughter.)

Let's do it in the theater, and it'll be very good, I say publicize it? No. I will give you this, and I will do that. No, I say, I let him out-talk me, so that was that. We got married in the theater.
Were you the hit of the show?
Uh-huh.
You were? (Laughs.) Did Fats do things like this to you, very often? You said you were --
Yeah, he would come get me, and wake me up out of bed --
What kind of --

-- and 'Come on, you sausage, get up out of that bed! Come on wake up.' I'd say sh! 'Naw, come on. What are you doing? What are you laying there? Come on with me?' I'd say where are we going? 'Never mind.' You know. (Smack) that was it.
And you would go with him wherever he suggested?
Yeah, well, because he was such a heck of a nice guy, and I -- in a way I couldn't lose. I wasn't married then.
Oh, this is before --
I wanted -- I wanted -- man, I wanted to sleep. I wanted to stay there and sleep all day. But going with him, making him happy, you know.
Was Fats a happy person? Do you know?
Very, very, very, at all times. Very. Immensely.
This was not just a front then.
Naw, heck no. No.
Because I've heard so much of the idea that underneath it all he was rather disappointed that his music -- he wasn't playing Bach, and --

Nah, nah, he was happy. I mean -- and he would preach that. That was his -- be happy. Do what makes you happy. I mean that was his check on own life. He would tell people, you know. "Use it." (Raspberry) don't do it. Forget it. Do what you want to do. Make yourself happy." You know. He said life is short. Life is short. Be happy." You know?

That was -- he -- looked like he was -- to me, he was in a rush, keeping things moving, going forward, just move forward, be happy, enjoy life. Be gay, enjoy this, and be nice, to and this person, and enjoy, and you know. To me that's the way he impressed me.
Musically, Herman, what did you get from Fats?

Oh, many things. Many things. Much. Because I mean a lot of times you'd be playing things, you might say -- he'd say well, how about this? How about that? Uh, stop and think, or he would play it on piano. Listen to this. And you'd have to, and you'd think of what he meant, or what he was saying, and you'd go from there. You know?
Don't be -- in other words, you don't pay any more -- he didn't want to see -- he didn't want -- he never was a grouch.
He didn't want you to be a grouch. Be a nice guy. Be lovable. Love people. Love life. Love things. You know?
He -- that's -- that's the way he impressed the world, as far as I'm concerned.
Well certainly that's the way he impressed the world. This was what you saw of Fats on stage, but I was wondering, off stage --
No.
-- he was the same person?
The same --
He didn't have --
No.
He must have had low moments, didn't he? When he felt unhappy?
Well --
Or did you never see them?

I never saw them, because if he did I didn't know what they were about. You know. I -- it would have had to have been his secret, or it was personal, maybe, or maybe, I don't know anythings that happened to him, like that. I don't know.
Did -- in the years that you knew Fats, did he change at all? Or was he always the same?
Always the same.
No difference.
No. No. No.
Were you closer to him than the other guys in the band?

I think so. I've been accused of that. I've been accused of being his right-hand man. We hung out together. We drank together. We went on parties together. And we did -- I don't know. I don't know. I don't know if -- oh, I remember his wife saying a couple of times, I wish I knew my husband as well as you do.
(Laughter.)
Did you have an answer to that?
No, I don't have -- I say well, you know, what am I going to say?
Well, of course you were on the road with him all the time. Did she get to see him very much? Did he get home at all?

Yeah, when we -- well, we -- we'd stay out long as the thing lasted, the one-nighters, the tour, whatever it was, lasted, and we'd come home. You know. And somebody said something one day about money. She said give my husband $2.00. He'll find a woman.
(Laughter.)
Why Lord, and I don't know how good that was after, maybe it was nice of her. That's the way she felt then. But he was such a heck of a great guy. The
greatest.
What did you -- what do you remember most about Fats, the things that impressed you the most about him?

Let me think of that, let me think. Well, I've seen -- well I thought -- I think it was in Pittsburgh, one thing -- I think the thing I often think about, we'd get into town, and he would need a shave and a haircut. I don't know for what reason, or who called and told him about this man. He called this man. The man came to the hotel, gave him a haircut, a shave, so it lasted for -- I don't know how many years. Each time we would go in and out of Pittsburgh it lasted, several times.

So I happened to be there with him on this particular instance, and at Christmas time, and he needed this man's services, haircut and shave both. At this time he bought this man's wife a winter coat, his son, little boy, must have looked like -- to me -- about 12, 13, and the husband, a suit, and coat. Said Merry Christmas.

To me that's one of the greatest things I had ever seen. The man cried. The man did not expect it. He was a poor man. He had a -- it was a poor family. Now things like that, I think, are worthwhile. Maybe I'm wrong.
Fats was very generous that way, wasn't he?
Very generous, very generous. And I liked that. To me it -- I don't know. Well, maybe I'm an old -- what do you call them? (Laughs.)
Sentimentalist?
Yeah, but I liked it. I felt that was kind of nice.
(Inaudible.)
I think so.
Did he do things like this quite often?
Quite often.
In various ways?

Quite often. Quite often. I'm trying to think of some more, but I've seen him do a lot of things that were so doggoned nice, and to other people, and -- I thought it was nice. Oh! In Washington, D. C., after we stopped doing sat down one night here, and started doing theaters, well he had three children then, and it was all, you know. I remember, we were in Philadelphia. This -- I really enjoy telling.

As he would come out, stage, backstage, out in the alley, well, out in the streets, trying to get some air, naturally he had to see people, hello professor. So a kid one day -- a kid walked up, and he spoke to him, because he loved kids. Can I see the show? Fats said, just a minute, what's your name, he told him. Uh-huh. Where do you live? He told him.

You have any boyfriends? Girlfriends? He said yeah. He says okay. Fats say, for instance, come back here Thursday, or whatever day it was, tell all the friends in your block that I say you bring them and come see the show.

Now, that one -- he told one kid, now when this kid goes back to the other kids and they come back to see if it was true, then another kid might come up and say well I want to go in and see the show. And Fats would tell him the same thing. He did that. When this particular day came, God dog! You never saw so many kids in all your life standing there.
Now the manager, the manager didn't know a damn thing about this arrangement, of the theater.
Fats hadn't said anything.

And this was Washington, D. C. The Howard Theater. So the people there -- so Fats told his valet, chauffeur, go out, go to the five and ten, go there and buy me 50 pounds, a hundred pounds of candy, bags, and put it all in bags, you know. And he did, and had it all, you know, had little bags of candy, and I don't know how many he had. He had them -- (laughs.)

And as the kids -- and the kids came up, somebody said where you going? said Fats told me to come up. Somebody came around in back and said Fats, come, they need you cut front, says, man, there's a thousand kids out there waiting (laughs). So the manager says, 'What's going on here?'
(Don't worry about it)
What are you doing? Fats says (unintelligible). Fats told him, said get the candy in bags and stand right by the door.

And the manager, 'What's going on here,' he say. The kids are coming, but who told me -- didn't know, he -- this can't happen. Fats said, 'Naw? He said I'll pull the band out. I'll walk out.' 'Wait! No! Wait! Wait!' The man started hollering and was going crazy.
(Laughter.)

So Fats said, Follow me! Fats walked in leading the kids, and as they walked down the aisle the guy was-- handed each one of them a bag of candy. You never saw so damn many kids in all your life. (Laughs.)

They went -- all went down to the front, you know, and fill all the seats. When that was filled they started going upstairs filling all the seats, and the rest of the people couldn't get in, nothing but kids, and kids and candy, and when the curtain went up, you know, you can imagine what happened.
Ra-a-a-y-y-y, Fats!
Fats play a good show?

Good show, and played to the kids, and sang to them, and all their requests, and asked them what they wanted, and played for them. And the kids were happy, and went out, and the manager was out there, and they were giving him salts, smelling salts, headache powders, aw!
(Laughter.)

The next day, and the rest of the week, in fact, they held him over. As far as you could look, parents, grandparents, everything, was standing in line. 'I never heard of this man. I must see the man who gave my son, grandson, a free ticket to the show. I've got to see him. He's got to be a good man.' 'I've heard of him, but I've got to see him.' And they were -- they were standing in line for miles, look like, around the corner, down the corner, trying to get in the theater, had to hold him over.
That's terrific. Did Pats do things with kids like this very often, or --
He, aw, everywhere, everywhere he could, and naturally, you know -- the manager was happy, oh, he was happy! You know. But I mean before that the manager was about to go out of his mind.
Right, well he didn't --
He let all those people in there, and nothing going in the cash register.
The greatest public relations in the world.
And he's paying Fats all that money.
Right.
He says how am I going to pay him?! You know. (Laughs.)
He found out.
Yeah. Yeah. And I thought that was beautiful. I thought that was one -- you know. The most wonderful gesture, thing, I'd ever seen in my life.
I think that's great, because Fats is usually presented as a very hard drinking sort of guy who is jolly, and everything, but you don't hear this side of him too much.

Well, I know. I know. I know. Fats drank, yes. Fats paid for it. He drank, but he paid for what he drank, and I think Fats ate well, doggone well. Fats ate the best of steaks, the best of this. He'd always -- get me a steak, and diced tomatoes, and this and that and the other, and he would eat damn well. Don't let nobody kid you. And whomever was eating with him ate well.
And did you guys in the band eat with him very often?
Oh yeah.
You were quite well fed.

Oh yeah, he would say come over and sit down. Come sit down over here, and he'd say 'Hymie,' and I'd say yeah, 'What do you want?' I'd say give me this, give me that. He -- Arrcch! -- I would get one. Fats would say well give me two of those.
(Laughter.)
Like for instance --
Two of everything.

Yeah. I'd say well give me half a -- you know, half a chicken, and (unintelligible) and Pats would say well give me a whole one. Dice and me two pounds tomatoes, cucumbers, and this and that and the other, and blah blah, and when he got up, it was (unintelligible). I mean Money meant nothing to him.
Was he -- did he treat the band as if it was a kind of a family thing? Was everybody --

Family, always. Always! That's the way he treated us. And we'd go and record, or go on the stand to play, he'd buy his whiskey, and he'd say well -- okay tell the guy, his valet, bring a bottle for the boys, whatever they're drinking, bring them whatever he's drinking. And should you walk backstage to see him, Hello Fats, how are you? He had a memory like an elephant. Oh, he could remember. Oh, he -- don't think he wouldn't remember you. If you had ever met him and known him. If it was bad or good, he still remembered. (Laughter.)

And he say well have a drink. He'll say well I'm very sorry, Fats, very sorry. I only drink Scotch. I don't drink Bourbon. Well, whatever you drink. Well, I like a little Duff-Gordon, a little this -- okay -- a
" Bobby! Come here. Go get me three or four bottles of so and so. Okay! A case. Sit down."
(Laughter.)

You sit, and that's yours. I mean he's got -- I got mine, now you're here to enjoy yourself. And you don't get up and run out on that, because you're going to drink that, or a heck of a lot of it, because that's what you like.
If you order a case, or two bottles, or two quarts, or what, that's yours. (Laughs.)
It is true that he carried a suitcase with him that was -- had a complete bar, that could just open up?

Well yes, because a lot of places we went to, I think in West Virginia places, dry states, you know, a lot of -- they didn't sell anything. So if he didn't carry it, you didn't have anything to drink.
I see.

You know. So he sits on the stand, and once in a while you see somebody go over to this case and pick it up and walk off in the dark behind the curtain, and then they (unintelligible) come and sit it down, you know. So naturally that created a -- what's in that bag that Fats carries? You know.
(Laughter.)
And if he didn't have it, then of course you couldn't buy it. That's the law. You know. And where you could buy it it was no trouble.
When -- when you were working out a piece, or the various things that you played, were they all just head -- head arrangements, ad lib, or did you work things out?

No, well we had -- all you need's a lead sheet, on anything. I mean what's happening, what's going down, and a good musician, even today, I mean on anything, give him a lead -- unless it's a lot of things happening, changing from here to there, a zzz, zzz, zzz together, eight or ten or fifteen instruments, doing it together, then you've got to have it on paper. Okay.

But if it's a matter that -- a matter of melody, or something, you don't need, and then you've got to have an arrangement so you can end up where those guys end up. You know. That's the arrangement. And --
Well once -- let's say once you've made a record of something, then did you sort of try and stick to the record, or --

Yes, yes. You had to. I'll tell you why, because I remember, we were in West Virginia one night, and we were playing, and some woman had a -- she had a house. She closed her girls up and brought them all with her and --

to hear us play, and she was a fine looking woman, and had some fine looking gals, and she had plenty of money, and she walked in there and sat down, and she asked for a certain tune. So I said, 'I'm very sorry.' "What do you mean you're sorry?" I don't have that. She said, "well, you recorded it." You say well no, I don't think so. You've got me" -- she said don't tell me. I have it in my joint on the jukebox. Oh God!
(Laughter.)

Fats say, you do? (Laughs.) Fats starts thinking. She say I have my own business back in such and such a town. I closed up tonight and brought my girls with me because I wanted to hear you play. He says, what's the name of the song? La, nm, nm, nm, nm, and so he -- so he called us out. He say hey fellows, did we record the splk-ll-blkk? The guys say I think. We don't remember. She said don't tell me! I have it on my jukebox. So he sent his valet out. He says go out and look for this. He wrote it on paper, on a piece, and the guy came back with the record.
You'd all forgotten it?

Fats took it, we had -- took it in the back room, in the dressing room, and put it on his machine, played it. We started listening. (Laughs.) He says well I'll be damned! I think that sounds like me. And that sounds like
me. And that sounds like me. He said well we did make it, didn't we? You know. (Laughs.) Find out it was a record.

Now, we had to stay back there and learn it all over again and go out and play it for this woman. This woman come all these miles to hear the -- you know, she didn't want no stuff. You know, we had to play the damn --
She knew what she wanted.
Yeah. And so Fats apologized. We came out and played it for her. That's it! That's what I want! Don't tell me.
(Laughter.)

And we played it. And one night I think we were in -- Indiana, or someplace, some simple old man came out, and I hated myself for this, some man came up, and we don't say nothing -- well, we always had some laughs going, some jokes going, and this guy came up and walked up to Fats and said (mimics speech impediment) (unintelligible). Fats said what did you want? And (mimics speech impediment) (unintelligible).

Fats say I don't know. Says -- he say Hermie, I say what? Do we have that? I said I never heard of it in my life. And Fats fell off the stool laughing. I'm sorry I did it. I shouldn't have. I never could -- I mimicked the man. That's the way he talked. I shouldn't have done that. But the poor man walked away. He went away. But I mean, but you don't stop to think, you know. You know. I wouldn't have
done it. Well.
These are things you regret after.
Yeah, yeah, (mimics) and I never heard his head in my life. And Fats started laughing, and grabbed my hand, and he started, and he fell over.
Well, that happened. I couldn't call him back. I mean you don't take those things back, you know.
Over the years, were you with Fats's group right to the end of the thing?
Well, yes and no. I'll tell you why I said that, because I had stopped -- I had left Fats to go with well, maybe Stuff Smith. I was with Stuff for a while.
Why did you leave Fats?
Well, he was only -- on the outs. He was beginning to close, and things were happening, and he didn't look like he was going -- he just made this movie, uh, uh, the last movie he made.
'Stormy Weather?'

Yeah, 'Stormy Weather', and I had to leave him while he did that, and while he was doing Stormy Weather I was -- had to be working, of course, and things didn't look up and like it was going -- he had a few dates in Boston around, so I then picked up some other guys, side sight guys, you know, let them, picked them up and do it, and they will soon do the thing, and meantime I could see the writing on the --

handwriting on the wall, and I got my own group, and I had a chance to go to Philadelphia, the Midway Musical Bar, so I took a group into there. It's between Market and -- Market Street and what's the name of the street? I don't know. Tch, tch, tch, tch. It's between 15th and 16th Street, and Market and -- Sansom. Sansom Street.

So I was in there with my own group, and it was during the war, and people were happy, and sailors and everybody, and I was making a dollar, and the money was nice. I said aw the heck with it. So he came over the air. He'd gone. I was -- I came home on Monday, you know, my family. And then that's where I heard it.
Well how did you hear it?
On the radio.
Just on the radio?

On the radio, yeah, you know. Fats, oh my goodness. So I was on my way back to catch the train to go back to Philly, you know, and naturally I was a pall bearer, and whatnot, afterwards, and you know. Everything stopped, everybody was -- everywhere you looked people were crying, you know, and that was it.
Did the latter -- well, how long had it been since you'd seen him, before he died?
Hrrrrrrrrrrrr, it was when he went to do 'Stormy Weather. Let me think, where was I? He had come back
from Europe, and I was so and so --
Had you gone to Europe with him?
No. I didn't, no.
So it had been a long time you hadn't been with him.

Yeah, it's been quite a while there. Because before that, before -- after I left, I went with Stuffy Smith and played Chicago, and after Chicago I went with Stuff Smith to Hollywood, and played the Treuville Club, and at that time Fats was moving. John Hamilton, Bugs was with Fats. They played the hotel in Chicago -- (Snap).
Congress Hotel?
Huh?
Congress?
No. No. No. They were recording -- I mean they were broadcasting, I can't -- and --
Sherman.
Sherman.
Sherman, that's the one.
Yeah.
Panther Room. Anthony.

Yeah, that's right. And I followed -- I was with Stuffy, and I went on -- I was with Stuff and the Kirkaby -- that was Kirkaby's doings. Yeah, Kirkaby was glad to get me out of the band. So he had to keep me out of there.
Oh, that was Kirkaby getting you out.
I see.

Yeah, you see, so -- and Johnny Buggs was there. They going to have -- he was scared to look me in the face, because of a lot of reasons, because I knew him backwards, and anyway, well, we won't go into that.

And so I went out to Hollywood, in the Trouville Club. Bergs Trouville Club, with Stuff Smith, and Buddy Rich, and all of us, did a jam session out there on, you know, how the heck was -- I've got a picture of Buddy Rich, and all that sort of thing. And Stuff Smith playing, and his violin, and oh, it was really nice. You know.
Then, came back and -- no, it was after Chicago. I came back and then I got my own group, and I went to Philadelphia and Fats was out there doing this picture, and then he passed.
Did you -- the last times that you saw Fats, did you have any idea that he was this sick? That it could happen to him?
No. No.
He didn't seem any different to you at all?
No, no, no. No, he wasn't ailing, no. It was just one of those things.
Just one of those things that happen.
Uh-huh.
Well let's go back to the earlier part with Fats, Herman. Did the -- did the personnel of the group stay pretty much the same over the years? Didn't it? It was you, and --
Sedric.
-- Sedric, and Al Casey.
Vic -- I don't mean Vic, I mean Al Casey, Slick Jones --
Slick Jones on drums.
-- on drums. Uh-huh.
And who on bass? They did change quite a bit, didn't they?
Who?
The bass players changed a bit, didn't they?

Oh, they did. After -- first, what I told you was Billy Taylor (Unintelligible) he was a great man. Well, he was with Duke, and this and that and the other happened, and from there we -- I'm trying to think what other bass. I know -- I know two or three. I'm trying -- I'm trying to put them in con- cession. Charlie Turner, then before that we had Cedric Wallace, bass player.
Oh yeah, uh-huh.
He was with Fats. He did quite a lot
of things with Fats. Then came Charlie Turner, fat man. He did quite a lot of them, yeah. And I can't think.

Now the one person -- the two people who seemed to be as consistent as you, through the -- not quite as consistent, but all through, are Gene Sedric and Al Casey. What -- tell me something about Gene Sedric? What sort of a person was Gene?
Aw, a lovable little guy. I'm the guy who named him Honeybear.
Why?

Well -- (Laughs) -- that's a good story. We were on our way out somewhere, New York state, and we stopped at a diner for coffee and whatnot, and when we came out, we were sitting on the bus waiting for him. He had on one of those -- (laughs) -- one of those coats, a camel-hair, remember those brown --
Oh, camelhair, brown. Tan.
Brown camelhair. And he was -- he was about that tall, and about that big around.
How tall would you say that is?
(Laughs.)
Five foot?
Five foot, couple. (Laughs.) And he came out of the place. We were waiting for him, and he loved pie. He came out, and ppppp! (Laughs). Eating. His jaws

were all -- he was chewing and coming toward us, and I said look, he look like a little honey bear. I said just look at him. He looks like a -- so they started -- started saying, Honey Baby Bear! You know.
(Laughter.)

Baby Bear, Honey Bear, baby. And that you know, how things, you say something and it gets around, gets around. So it stuck with him. Baby Bear. Honeybear. You -- Gene say Honeybear, Baby Bear. You know? I'm the guy who named him.
: As a musician how was he, Herman? What did you feel about --

Aw, he was a heck of a musician, damned good, and congenial cat, and he could play, and loved to play. Oh (laughs) Sedric told me -- tell about that man -- well, some years ago. He said when he first came to New York -- (laughs) -- well at that time, if you were in New York, I don't care what instrument you played, and you went into the Rhythm Club on certain days, when they had a -- any time a guy came in he thought it was good, he'd say okay (slam), I'm here.

There were (unintelligible) session. Now, this will be 50 drummers, 50 piano players, 50 clarinets, 50 trumpets, 50 anything, than the Rhythm Club, 132nd Street (unintelligible). That's what they did. Now, if you were good, if you

thought you were good, they would listen. That's up to you. And you'd better be doggone good, because them -- man, those cats'll blow you out. So the cats were playing. I don't care what the tune was, just ask you what'd you like? What tune do you want? Then they would play it, and you know.

"I Got Rhythm, Saint Louis Blues, Bugle Call Rag," whatever you name. I mean the standard tunes that they played, you know. All right. Turn the [PAUSE], be in there playing jam session, all and what not.
All at the Rhythm Club.

Yeah. Rhythm Club. I don't care how good you are, the guys would listen, and if you had something to offer they would applaud, and they would give it to you, and shake your hand, and whatnot. But if you couldn't play they'd -- Prffft -- they would boo you out of there. Right?
So that's what was happening. Now, who were we talking about?
Gene Sedric.

Gene Sedric. Sedric came up and while he was sitting there playing he was -- Willie the Lion was sitting there, ding-da-dingle ling, dingle linga linga, playing, you know, and Sedric say he'd sit there a while, and he looks, listens (laughs) so he take his bag out from under his arm, and lay it down, and Willie the Lion -- look -- Willie the Lion looks at him sitting there. If you can't play that
thing, don't take it out. You know, and kept on --
(Laughter.)
Ding-a-ling-a-ling-a-ling, (Laughter.)
: Willie the Lion, right?

Yeah, so the Lion -- so he's saying, he got mad. He said who the hell is this guy? Who is he to tell me that? Said he was very mad. Willie kept playing, said the guys were blowing. If you can't play it, don't take it out here, you know. That's the way they was, Willie the Lion was.
So he started crying, saying Ah, so he took this horn out, put it back in the bag and went on home.
(Laughter.)
: Really crying?

Yeah, that's what he told me. See, because he was -- he had hurt his feelings. So he went home (laughs) saying, and he said that so-and-so. Said he called him all kind of names, you know, and after he got home. So he practiced at home, got himself together, so he came back the next time. So when he came back the next time he felt ready and right. He didn't care who was out there, he took his horn out and started playing.
Well that's the way they did you. If you couldn't play, and you pulled your horn out, I mean you'll only make an ass of yourself, and you had to stay in there and get back
groove in the group, and get yourself together, and until you were ready.
What happened to you the first time you went to the Rhythm Club?

Well, when I -- (laughs) God damn! Thank God I was blowing. I was playing, but I never hung up on this thing like Sedric. I never had that, because well that happened downtown where I told you Pops Foster went in for me, stood up for me, and I went and played and everybody liked me, and I was a good guy. When I came uptown, and I went on -- another thing I was blowing, but I never really had to stretch until I went with Fletcher Henderson job in his house and took over the job as playing first trumpet, and he gave me all the first parts and moved me over in the first space.
That's why -- that was it, you know. That was my, you know, one of those things. I happened to have what was needed, and I kept going, and kept moving, you know.
Well we were talking about Gene Sedric. And you're saying he's a very nice guy.
Aw, he was a heck of a -- he was a sweetheart, sweetheart of a guy.
How did he fit into the group as a whole? Does each guy have a sort of a place in the group, contribute a certain thing?

Yeah, now I told you Ben Whitted was our first clarinetist we had, and saxophone player. But Ben didn't have it. We couldn't have sold that group, we couldn't have. Victor or nobody else would have bought it, because we weren't offering anything, you know. It wasn't bad. The -- the thing, what they call it, sales power, that what made things move, I don't care what you name it, what you call it, anyway, that wasn't it.

But when Eugene Sedric came in, with us, boom! We had something. And the people saw it, they heard it, and they liked what they heard. And from the first to second, as we kept going, kept going, they liked what they heard, and it was great, and we moved up where we got into the money. And naturally now everybody was good.
Do you know what brought Sedric into the group?
I'm trying to --
I remember, I think we talked about this a little bit before. You weren't quite sure.

Yes, yes. Yes, I think so. I think it's the time there when we were in the theater, the Apollo Theater, and Eugene Sedric and Slick Jones was in the band, with Charlie Turner, or some group, is how we got -- I think this -- I think that's how it happened.
All three of them came in, then, at
the same time.

No, Slick Jones, and him. I was in the group. I think that's the way it happened. Anyway, when Fats heard him, because Sedric applied, I mean Sedric, as I told you, had been to Europe with -- uh, uh --
(Inaudible) okay?
Uh -- that's slipped my mind, because I think --
Well, we can find out.--
Yeah, they got a great band, though, great band, yeah.
-- who he went to Europe with.
I understand he's getting the band to group -- group again --
Oh, is he?
-- in Philadelphia, yeah, uh-huh.
Tell me about Al Casey. Now you say he was just a kid in high school when he joined the band.
Yeah.
How did -- how did he develop? Was he shy at first when he came in, or --

Yes, he was shy, and Fats grabbed him and Fats taught him a lot of chords. Don't do this. Do that. Put this here. Put this there. Do so and so. Hit it, now. Buy this. You know? And his -- he was -- he's beginning to
spread, you know?
(Phone rings.)
[PAUSE]
Uh-huh, okay. Fats taught him chords.

Yeah, he taught him the chords, and taught him this, the right way to do this, don't put this there, put this here, spread your chord, bring this back, do that, you know? So he learned a heck of a lot about music that he couldn't have, or didn't -- had not learned from his teacher. When he was studying, you know?
And once I saw that happen to a great pianist, a man who studied in Boston, in fact in the Boston Conservatory. Uh-uh-uh Johnson, I was -- hm --
This was somebody that Fats --
Yeah, he used --
-- brought out?
-- he played second piano under Fats.
I didn't know Fats had a second piano.
Yeah, when we had the band.
Oh.
Hey, Mary?
Yeah?
What was Fats --
[Or] your brother.
Listen a minute. What was Fats' second
piano player's name, with us.
Don Donaldson.
Don Donaldson.
Don Donaldson.

Don Donaldson. He graduated -- he went to school in Boston Conservatory, and all that, but I sat and saw him straighten Don on a lots of things when it came to harmony. He asked Fats, well why do you do this? How do you do this? How do you arrive at this? And Fats told him, and showed him. And I have a lot of respect for Don. Don's a very fine musician. He's still going.
But he will tell you, and he knows he was not a first Fats Waller, and he went to his conservatory -- Boston Conservatory.
I'm glad you mentioned the big band, Herman. How did the big band happen to come into existence? Why was the big band, since you'd been doing so well with the small group?

Well, here's what happened. The bookings, because we were playing here, and playing there, and the bookings came up and then people asking, we would like to have Fats Waller and his band play a dance here and a dance there. Well, you can't send six men out to play a hall where you'd been having fifteen, twenty men playing. You know, and make everybody happy. So, they told them, say okay, I'll

augment the band, get some pieces, get some other guys. So Fats had Don, other guys, to hire five, six saxophone players, two, three trombones, two three trumpets, you know. Pick the band, and get some arrangements, and rehearses, and they make it, you know, and take it on the job. That's what we did.
How long did that last?
Oh, aw, we did one nighters, oh, two, three, three or four years.
Why did it stop?
Maybe more. Why?
Yeah, why?
Well, it's like he stopped, and the bookings stopped, and he stopped, and he didn't want to do them anymore, maybe. You know.
Was the big band as successful as the small group, from an audience response?
Yeah. I think so.
He could have gone on.
I think so. Oh, heck yeah. He could have gone on, but he's a small, big, he could -- but evidently he didn't want -- he -- you know.
Did you enjoy playing the big band, or did you prefer the small group?
Well, I -- I preferred the small group, because you know, let's face it, you don't have all those big
arrangements.
Right.
(Laughter.)
There's more opportunity for you in a small group, right?

Yeah, I mean you know. You play, open up, open up three or four, five sheets of paper, and you've got to read it all, hit all those high notes, you know, and all that mess up, for what? You know. And most times our arrangements stunk.
(Laughter.)
You know. I mean they were lousy.
Who wrote them? Do you know?
Yes, I did. I did know that, and I want to be fair to this guy, but man, some of our arrangements were lousy.
Who wrote the better ones?
(Laughs) well, it's usually a guy who's close by who did not get paid. Would you believe that? Who wrote the better ones.
Who?

Well now, I'm going to tell you a little story. When I went in the group I was -- I'll tell you about Rudy Powell. Rudy Powell played clarinet, played clarinet and alto saxophone (or) a lot of Fats' things. And I think

a lot of people looked on that knows is that him, you know, when they shouldn't have, because Rudy -- he's a great cat. Did some fine things, you know? When he came in the band, even Sedric was there, and he's sitting there playing, you know. Rudy made some arrangements --
(End of proceedings as recorded.)
(End of Tape Number Five.)

Interview with
Herman Autrey
Part Three

Washington, D. C.
May 1, 1975

PROCEEDINGS

This is tape number six, with Herman Autrey. We were talking at the end of the last tape about Fats Waller's big band, and the people who wrote the arrangements for it. As I remember, now, that I think of it, Herman, you didn't really think much of most of the arrangements for that band. What was wrong with them?

Well, as I think back, most bands -- I would say most bands, well, the bands that I have been lucky enough to work with, and play with, most of their arrangements were mediocre. I mean lousy, to be frank, brutally frank.
(Laughter.)
And -- but you had to play them anyway. I mean if you want to work, well you play what the man has. You play what's there, you know?
Yeah.
(Laughs.) I can drop a little joke in here right here. Speaking of arrangements, and music, uh, uh, Benny -- not Benny --
Piano ?
Yeah, piano, yeah. Jelly Roll Morton.
Jelly Roll Morton.
Yeah, Gosh, you know he had a nice book of -- well arrangements, stocks, everything that come out. Years ago you could walk downtown, any music stores, and

just ask for some music, and they would give you a bundle. You couldn't get uptown with it. You'd have to tie a string around it to get uptown, and you'd pick out what you wanted, and the rest of it, you threw it away, or give it away, you know.

So he was doing a dance somewhere, in Harlem, or Jersey, or somewhere, Brooklyn, and he always had himself a ten or twelve piece band, you know. They wasn't making any money anyway, but you know, and he'd get his baton, looked like a long broomstick, and he would direct his group.
Oh, he stood up and conducted?
Most times. You know.
Did he sit down and play piano too?
He'd sit down and play piano, yeah.

And anyway, but what I'm trying to get to, as you call out some tune, they played it, and the set went down, the dance, so the guys sat there waiting. So okay, Jelly Johnny, what's next? He say, what you mean, what's next? Well, I mean we just finished playing. What other tunes do you want?
He said well, what did we do? The guys say one, two, three. He says okay, four, five, six.
(Laughter.)

You know. What the heck, he has them all numbered down, but you know how they numbered music, these days, the waltzes was this and that and the other. You coudn't go -- well anyway, you got -- wait and see what he's going to

call. Well that happens in too many bands.
