The guys want to be kept interesting, you know, say well let's do something interesting to each other, and be nice when you did call out an arrangement that was good. A guy felt like doing it, you say I did it last week, or last month, and I enjoyed playing it, but every night, and when you finish, you say whew! When am I going to leave this band and join a good band, you know? (laughs.)

Well Herman, so far as playing the same thing every night, that's part of what you're talking about. When you're with a successful band, or when you get a band that's got a real hot hit, you've got to play it all the time. what happens?

Well that's bad enough, but it's as you say, a hit, and it's got to be good to be a hit, so that you don't mind, but I mean you sit there night after night, and you play those things, and you wonder why they guy bought them, you know, and you -- so -- I don't know. You're not happy. You're not -- and in those days, that's what counted. You were trying to establish the mood. You wanted to go forward. You was hoping someday, well, if I get with this guy, and he'll enable me to get with another guy bigger and better, maybe one day I'll hit tops. I mean that's what's always in back of your mind. That's what you're hoping for.
And to do that you had to be playing something. So -- and --
You mean something good?

Something good, yeah, because I mean you couldn't use your own ideas all the time, and I mean to advance. You'd be lucky maybe to get in a nice hot chorus, hot lick, as they call it, or something good, and somebody would say anh, pretty good. But I mean to get it on record, on paper, I mean you had to be responsible, you had to be an arranger yourself.

Now getting back to Rudy, this time we was with Fats. We had -- he had some arrangements, and they were absolutely no good. And he'd paid for them, too, dearly. Too dear. And when Rudy came into the band, Rudy had a few little arrangements, a few things he'd done, you know, and this tune and that tune, and we put them in the band. We rehearsed them, and we started playing them. And each time we played them we were happy, people were happy, they -- we got hands. There's your answer, you know.
And say what happened, said the deal went down. We were playing more of Rudy Powell's arrangements than anybody else's. And which he did not get one five cent for.
Why not?
Well, he didn't ask. They didn't offer. You're in the band, so you belong to us, and everything you've
got belongs to us. That feeling. They didn't say that, but it means -- I didn't like that idea. Still don't.
Were there some of these arrangements, were they original pieces by Rudy too?
Not original tunes -- I doubt it. I doubt that. I don't remember.
One thing I was wondering was if Fats also followed the custom of putting his name on --

No, no. Fats wouldn't do that anyway, in person. He wouldn't -- that's -- you've got -- I think you've got to have a dirty mind, or a low thinking type person to want to do that anyway. You know, to sneak in on somebody else's thing. Okay, if they ask you, well come on in and help me push it forward. I mean okay, and he just deserves to have his name on it. Anybody, I think. But no.
Did Fats write any of the arrangements for the big band?
Yes. "Beefsteak Serenade -- Serenade", "Come and Get It," I cant think right off now, but the big band, that's the --
But he did write quite a few-- (inaudible).
-- big -- what do you call it, 12-inch, I think it was, we did. Yeah, uh-huh. More or less. Yeah. Okay, when we recorded with the big band, 12-inch. And he
did most of them, and of course we had another -- (laughs). Another country was -- Mr. Kirkeby eased in there, you know. (Laughter.)
That dog.
Well, how do you mean he eased in there? Was he --
Well, at that time he was managing things for Fats. He wasn't managing Fats. Fats hired him to take care of his business for him. That's the way that -- (laughs). And he took care! (Laughter.)
Of whose business?
His.
(Laughter.)
Well, now, you're saying things that sort of reflect a little bit on Kirkeby. Really -- actually, what did he do? Was it just a personality problem? Or --

Well, I really -- maybe I shouldn't say the things I have said, because I don't have the proof. I was -- it was hearsay by some very important people. For instance, Bergaman? You remember him? Mr. Bergaman? Jack Bergaman? He's a publisher, vocal --
Oh, Bregman. Bregman.
Bregman. Yeah.
Bregman Voces and on Kahn, yeah.

Well he's the one who published my tune, 'Yacht Club Swing?' And I have a copy here somewhere. Anyway, Fats -- I did it while Fats was in Europe, and he too -- Fats came back, he put his name on there to help --
Fats did.

Yeah. To help -- so to help -- in 1938, help the sale of it. And it went like hotcakes. They were using it like a theme from New York to the coast and back, and all that. I got a few dollars out of it, but not what I should have.
Anyway, that's another story. Which we should put -- I should put in my book.
(Laughter.)
MR. WILSON: We'll get to that in a minute.

And -- well, that's one of those things, that's the way those things were done. So I spoke about it to Fats, and not so much Fats, was the guys around the band who helped -- who helped to run Fats, because that Kirkaby and all the rest, where you could hear it. I'd say why buy up all this junk from publishers that's no good, and rehearse our brains out, trying, and when you hear it it's not going to get any better. You have a man right here in the band we're using his stuff, has given us the best we have to play.
I said you don't offer -- won't even buy him any

manuscript and ink to write with.' Say 'haven't offered him a dime.' 'Well, he's one of -- I say no, no. So we had quite a discussion there, and I got kind of mad, and I said if any of you don't like it come outside one by one. I'll fight all of you. I mean --
(Laughter.)
I don't know how much I could have done, but at that time I was weighing about 240 pounds, and I thought I could protect myself, maybe I could have and maybe not.
How tall were you then?
Oh, five nine and a half, something like that.
Pretty husky five nine.

Pretty good, yeah, and I was -- I had, you know, I had a pretty good punch. (Laughs.) Years ago. I don't know about it. I had a lot of fights here and there, you know. Could talk loud anyway, you know.
(Laughter.)

And so I mean Rudy heard me and said that, and ever since then we've been like brothers. I mean he seems to have thought to me -- I don't know. I've always been for the underdog. I don't like to see anybody -- I don't care who they are, what color they are, if somebody's thumbs down, and walking on them, and something, I don't like that. I don't like to see it. I don't want -- I don't want to see

that.

So if I'm around, and I have a chance, I got to speak up. I've got to say something. You know.
Herman, what was Fats's attitude about what was happening to Rudy, about Rudy not getting any --
Well Fats says well, I've got to -- whatever's right to be done, do it. I -- that's the end. He would take off.
He said this to Kirkaby?

Everybody, yeah, to Kirkaby, yeah, take care of this, like the first time he went to Europe. We were supposed to have gone with him, the band, the six pieces, and he talked -- Kirkaby talked Fats out of it. And we were standing at the boat, at that time we go on the -- what? -- Queen Mary, one of those big boats. And we were standing down there like little fools, to the last minute. Well we -- he said Kirkaby's here. He'll be here. He'll tell you what to do.
We were packed and waiting, and hoping, and the last minute -- we didn't see Kirkaby. Fats said well, fellows, bye, I'll see you when I come back. You know.
You mean nobody told you in advance that you'd be --
Naw, right to the last minute Kirkaby told Fats that -- ah, it was too expensive, and he could save

money by not taking the band, and he could hire some musicians after he got over there, and do this, and save, and he did the same thing when they made "Stormy Weather". We were supposed to have gone out there to do that with him. Kirkoby talked him into hiring some standbys, and so and so and so and so on, so I can put the other money in my pocket, and that's just what he did.
Is that why, on the records in Europe, there was different -- a whole different band?
Yeah.
And the records in California was a whole different band?
That's right, a whole different thing. That's right.
I had always gotten -- you mentioned before that on the arrangements for the big band Fats had bought this -- bought these arrangements, and they weren't much good, and he paid too much for them.
Yeah.
I'd always heard that Fats was a very, very generous man --
Very. Very.
-- passed money out everywhere.
That's right.
Now, obviously a guy like that gets

taken a great deal, people take advantage of them. Now here we have an almost opposite situation of Rudy Powell being in the band, writing arrangements, and getting nothing. That doesn't sound like Fats.
Well, because he was not dealing directly with Fats. This went through the bass player, who was -- de, de, de, de, in the band.
Cedric Wallace?
No, no. Charlie Turner.
Charlie Turner.
status staff.
I'm trying to think of his -- legal
Oh.
Uh, in all bands they have the guy who takes care of the union business, and this and that, and the other.
The business manager?
No, that's not the way this was. And the arrangements, and general -- getting it -- telling them, getting them tickets for to take this to the guys.
The road manager?
No, that's not --
I see.
It's unionwise, I think. Anyway, anyway, Fats wasn't -- Fats had he been dealing directly with

Fats, things would really have been much different, I'm sure. And because Rudy was just glad that the -- glad they're playing my tunes, my arrangements. But he would have been much happier, had they been -- say okay, Rudy, make an arrangement on this. Make an arrangement on that. And so on and so on, and the band then, and how much do you want? I'll pay you what you charge, or you know, some kind of business arrangement.

And he wouldn't have asked for the world, because he was tickled to death to be in the band, and he was playing damned good, and the only thing ruined him then, hurt him, I would put it, he was wrapped up in -- uh -- Benny Goodman playing.
Oh, you mean interested in --
Interested, yeah. All --
Trying to play like Benny Goodman.

Yes. Yes. And Rudy always did study. He's had some very, very fine teachers, and he knows the instrument, the alto, and he's very good on the clarinet, but he's terrific on the alto. That's always been the way -- you know.

And so I think I heard them -- I've heard it discussed by different clarinet players, the growl -- growling or growl, or whatever you want to call it, that Benny Goodman has done on the clarinet then. A few guys seem to -- to think it was great.
Sounds like a kind of dirty tone.

Yeah, so Rudy was messing with that, so he ruined his embouchure. He -- while playing it, he, whew! -- dah, dah, dah, whew! You know? He had that whistle sound would come out, and that happened on too many Victor wax.
But that --
They spoke about it a few times, and after a while they said well -- (slap) -- you know, I'm sorry, but get somebody else. Then they brought in Eugene Sedric.
I see. I see.
See, that's -- because Rudy was there before Eugene Sedric, see?
So it was because of Rudy's problem with his embouchure that --
Yeah, it was that whew, ssss, ssss, whew! You know. They said we can't have that, have to start again, and start again, and start again, and --

Was this -- you remember the way -- well, for example, the way Ben Webster used to play? Had a sort of breathy sound to it, because he got very close to the mike? Now is this what Rudy was doing? Or was it more of a whistle?
That was a whistle, because you could hear it while he was playing, you know. Everything would be

nice for four, five, eight, or ten notes, dah, dah, dah, wssst! De, dah, dah dah, dah, wsst! You know. I mean a definite -- you know. And you could hear it in there. It ruined -- well, it ruined things.
And that's one of the things that hurt him, you know?
You were talking before about Yacht Club Swing piece, your piece, had you been writing very much along down through the years?

Hmmm, well yes and no. I've had -- oh, I at one time, one time when I had so many things, and after Yacht Club, and band, before I got disgusted and said to hell with them, threw them away and forgot about it, because at that time, how good they were, I do not know, and fifteen or twenty minutes I could write a tune. I mean, and idea would come to me (snaps fingers) and I could hear it, and maybe put it on paper, and play it.
How -- did you write, or did you compose on the piano, on the trumpet, or on paper?
On paper, and trumpet.
On paper and trumpet.

Yeah, and mainly in my head, because I learned, I think I learned that when I was quite young, because as I told you, I used to listen to the minstrel bands, and hear them play, and I hadn't never heard the tune before, so
I was standing there listening to them play, remember it, whistle it until I got home, and play it.
I see.

And in a way I can still do that, you know? That's how good -- keen my ear was, I guess. And that's very important. In music -- I wouldn't say jazz only -- in music, is being able to play what you hear, being able to hear. A lot of people, they say they can't carry a tune in a basket. That's why. You know. You can't -- if you can't hear the thing, I mean you -- well forget it.
After you got home and played it, then did you write it down? Or did you just depend on --
No, no. Once I played it, and seemed to create a -- the thing that I'd already had then, and I would never forget it.
Oh, it just stayed.
Yeah. Now for instance, I can play -- I am pretty sure -- I haven't done it in a long time, but about a dozen standard marches I memorized back in my school days.
Really?

Yeah, Sousa's marches, and what not, and things back there I did. I played -- there's a couple here I hear almost every morning, Under the Double Eagle, and so and so. My dad and I played together, so I got my wife saying it
now, she says remember that? Remember that? Remember that?
(Laughter.)

And the things -- the Zamper, and the overtures old -- you know, Poet and Peasant, and those light things, I mean we did. By the way, I had to play that going into 802 to get my card, Poet and Peasant.
Oh, really?
(Laughs) yeah.
And you did it from memory?

No, no, from the music, and that's what burnt me. I played it for this guy. He said Hot Damn! I bet you could jazz hell out of that. And I wanted to call him, well I did, but he didn't hear them. You know. I said you know, I felt that was a hell of a thing for him to say. Bet I could jazz that -- and looking at him, he couldn't play it. He couldn't play anything. He was an executive now. He's sitting there talking my $54.00 then, which I understand is a hell of a lot more now, you know.
Man, 'cause my card number then was A667.
Really?
It sure as --
What year did you get it in?
'33? That's 42 years ago, ought to (unintelligible) be a few more in since then.
Yeah, I see.
Herman, of all these tunes that you wrote, why was 'Yacht Club Swing the one that got more attention than any of the rest?
Well, as I told you, Fats was in Europe when it happened, and we was out in Staten Island, three or four of us, a gig for that night. I will never forget it. Steve Wright had the band.
He had taken over Fats's band?
No, no, no. No, that was his gig.
Oh, that was -- it wasn't just using Fats's band.
No, I had nothing about Fats, you know. It has nothing -- there's nothing -- this has nothing to do with Fats.
Oh, I see.

He had booked a little job out there, and we were getting -- paying three or four dollars a night, and transportation, and go out there and play for a dance. So during intermission everybody got off but me, and I sat there, messing around with my horn, oiling it, or something, and for no reason I hear Bah dum, da, ladle, ladle, ladie, de dump dah doo, da, lidle leedy. De dum, da -- and while I was playing it, people started clapping their hands, and a couple of other guys came in and sat with me, sat down, they

joined in. And when we came back on the stand the joint was jumping (snaps fingers) because we were playing dah, de-de-de, deedle, deedle, dee dee. De dah deedle, deedle deedle dee, so we kept on 'til we made a tune out of it, during that same intermission.
And I came back the next day, that night, I put it on paper, and then I kept playing it until Fats came back and said What's that? I said a little thing I did while you were gone. Let me hear it.
(Laughter.)

He say yeah, yes, that's all right. Let's use it. So Fats got in and put in his two cents, and changed -- he maybe changed a few chords here and there, and maybe, you know, and we started using it for a theme song, and people started coming in, and saying hey Fats, what is that? He'd say aw, that's some little new thing we did there. And they'd say it is? And one publisher said give it to me! Give it to me! Back -- Bregman.
Bregman?
Yeah.
Jack Bregman.

Yeah, and the other guys came in there because at that time they were having a fight about tunes. You know, different guys -- you know, the big three, Robbins, so and so and so and so and so, you remember? The publishers?
And --
What was the fight about? I mean what --

Well, I mean who can -- you had a tune you wanted to get plugged, another guy would -- you know, they would say, you know. And we were broadcasting what, twice a week, three times a week, coast to coast from the -- from 52nd Street at the Yacht Club.
At the Yacht Club.
Uh-huh.
Explains the title.
Yep. Yeah, see, so they came in, and one particular story -- this knocked me out, man, because I don't know, I like people being people.

So this particular man -- I forget his name, I've forgotten his name -- who's a publisher, but he had been very good to Fats down through the years. Well I know you've heard the story about Fats. Fats could write a tune on toilet paper and sell it. And most times he did, because he wanted some money to buy some whiskey while he was downtown, he'd walk in any place and say Give me $50.00. And say Give it to me. Give it to me. You know. And he'd go right downstairs in the bar somewhere with the gang, and they would drink up.
You know, and sometimes they'd have a song title written on the paper, I mean, you know, whatever it was. So

the guys came in, and they would -- Hey Fats, (unintelligible) you're on the air do this for me. You broadcast, (unintelligible). Pats say, different guys, he'd say, yes, I remember you, I remember you, and wait a minute, you want this on the air? Yeah, well yes, Fats, he say how bad do you want it on the -- let me see your checkbook?
(Laughter.)
Oh, so they'd start reaching in their pocket, writing checks, you know. (Laughs.)

Okay, Fats, Okay. So a lot of them came to me, just two or three of them came, Hey Herman, could you help? Get Fats to do it. I'd say well, I don't know, well they're asking me a favor. I say I'll see what I can do! (Laughs.) Which I never mentioned to him, because he and I was supposed to be good friends by this --
(Laughter.)

And that's -- see, I learned that from looking and listening. So Fats accepted money from several. He pointed to his one man, and he say you, you don't need a dime. He say you haven't got enough money to pay me. He say you've been good to me for many years, he say, anything you bring in here I'll do it and it won't cost you a nickle. The man started crying.
He said Fats, thanks. He say no, you have done -- you -- a lot of nice things for me. Say oh, what you heard me
telling them, don't go for over you. Anything you want played, bring it in and I'll play it for you, and don't worry about any money.
Do you know if any of this man's tunes every became hits because Fats played them?

Yes. Yes, because -- I'm trying to think of the publisher, because he was a little publisher himself, but the big guys had snowed him under, you know. He would say -- get to where he couldn't move. He couldn't -- you know. Because Fats told me the story about some man had a tune, and sold it to a show, Broadway show, and somebody in Robbins, Robbins himself, wanted the doggone tune, and he couldn't get it.
So the show went to Paris, went to Europe, and it was doing fine, so Robbins went over there and bought the whole doggone show to get this tune, and he still made a quarter of a million.
You know what the tune was?
Hmm, Fats told me, because he was telling us in the club. And by golly, I forgot what the hell was that. he bought the show to get this tune, and still made a quarter of a million dollars. (Laughs.)
Well it must have been some tune!
Yeah. See, so I mean those -- I said boy, this is really something. And --

Herman, when Fats was playing these games with the publishers, with the checkbook, and everything, did -- was -- were you making up a lot of tunes right on the stand there? Did he just sort of start playing something, and people -- the rest of you'd get in on it?

No, not to -- no. No, not then. Not then. But I mean that did happen throughout the night. I mean after. Because when you're recording, or broadcasting, you want to be -- sound together. Want to be together, thinkingwise, playing. You know. Because you can't take too many shots in -- you don't know when you might miss, and that's bad. Yeah, you know.
Right, but in other words, you didn't do it for recording or on the air, but in the club you --

In the club you sit there, and you start -- guys who -- what's this? And Fats say well B flat, or C sharp, or -- he'd hit the chords, and so and so and so and so. And he would take one. He would say I've got it! I've got the first one by myself, and he would play, and you would listen, see the progressions, how the progressions go, chords and whatnot. And when you got ready you'd fall in. If not you, me, another guy. And you still listened. And you'd say gee, I'd like to have some of that. I had some ideas. I'd like to try.
So you come in with your ideas, and they might be

terrific. And it move from you, to the other guy, one guy will do something, will make that wow! You say man, listen to that! And it might be some other musicians in there, or publishers, something like -- what the hell is that? What was that? Do it again. Oh man, and then you'd get -- I'd put it on paper, and getting ready to sell it to him, because he's going to sell it right back to you at the end of the week, because he -- (laughs). They'll raise it, and it'll come out in the stock form. See?

He worked with Arthur Godfrey for a while. You know who I'm talking about? (Snaps fingers.) The publisher? Wrote more tunes, what was that? Hmmm, hmmm, hmmmmm, made millions, guy with tunes, and he's arranger here. He -- Martin Block. Not Martin Block.
I remember Archie Bleyer, if that's the guy you're talking -- Archie Bleyer?
Just the man.
Archie Bleyer, okay.

Archie used to come in the club. He -- I can name you so many sitting there writing on the cuffs of their shirt. Him, me, and some other guy makes something, and you see them sitting there with pen and pencil doing this, and --
Taking down the --
Sure. And they'd go back, back to his
office, and when you go down there to buy a tune, you buy -- you say man! That looks familiar. Isn't it nice? And that stuff's some of the same stuff they're selling back to us.
(Laughter.)
That you played last week, and it's your own thing.
I'll be darned.

And I would -- if you don't see that stuff in print, uh, you don't recognize it. You don't -- you've got to be mighty smart a man to recognize just what's happening, you know, and that's what they did.
How fast did Fats get these things that you did on the stand, in print out? Did he write them down right away? Or did anybody write them down?
No, no.
Aside from people writing on their cuffs?
No, no, no, they didn't. He didn't.
Did it wait 'til it was recorded, or something like that?

When -- that, or when he needed some money. (Laughs.) And after he got started with the band it was very seldom he needed money. This was more or less when he was alone by himself, with -- when he needed -- when he needed that extra buck.

I remember those stories back in the twenties, usually, when he turned out about -- what? -- one of those about every -- he wrote nine tunes for nine hamburgs, or something like that, one night. (Laughs.)
I doubt it was for -- it was for whiskey. He didn't write no tune for food.
(Laughter.)
Shoot!
Well when you -- when you got around to broadcasting, or in the recording studio, was everything pretty well routine then? Did -- or did you change things as you went along?

Change things as you went along. We didn't know what tune we were going to record until after we got there, and it was handed to Fats, and Fats reached up, because they was all piled up, five or six tunes, or more, lined up, and he had to pick -- had them stacked, and you take what was next, you know. That's the way they were brought to you, because -- just between the studio and the publishers, they had signed, and they would pass it on to you, because people would come up and buy, well I would like to have Herman Autrey do this tune.
Oh, well I don't know. He's pretty well -- say well, I still want Herman. Well, we'll -- anyway, and they'd write a check. (Laughs). If they wanted to, and pay for it,

and they'd move somebody else over, maybe, if they had to. You know, if they decided to do business. And they'd bring it to the studio, and I had to record it. Whether I liked it or not, which I -- that happened to us so damned many times!
Well this -- of course one of the incredible things, I think, about the Fats Waller recordings, all through that period, is that he had so many awful tunes in there, terrible.

That we did, and he threatened, he's hit the piano, I won't do it! I won't do it! So the manager would come out. Now, Tom. Now, Tom. Especially Kirkpeby. Now Tom. And Thomas, now after all, but -- now, I -- for me. I think you should, and they would go through this business, you know. And he would say well, maybe so, all right, but he was --
Now for instance, I remember one tune, 'Annie Don't Live Here No More.'
Yeah, I remember that.

Oh, God! Now we had to record things like that. And the meantime, what made it so hard, Dorseys -- one band, I want to check the other, they had arrangers. He had a guy who could sit down and write. He'd get a ridiculous tune. If the arranger should put this down on paper, it's no trouble. You play what you see. Yeah, you don't have to beat your brains out trying to think of ideas, or something, to

sell it. You play what you see and forget about it. You play whats on the paper (laughs). That's all you're required to do. Now if there's any squawk, give the arranger hell. Don't give me hell. (Laughs.) You know.
But when you get these dog tunes, and you don't have an arranger, what happens?
Well --
You've got more freedom, haven't you?

You've got -- you've got more freedom, but I mean you can't think of what you're going to do with it. I mean, a genius, you've got to be a genius to think something, and bring it out, and make it something. You know. You know, you -- in the first place, the whole idea is gone, is no good. You want to know who thought it up, why, and for what? And they want to -- no wonder they want to pay you to do it, because you've got to make -- you know, do what they didn't do.
Why do you -- why did you particularly remember 'Annie Doesn't Live here Anymore?' Is that -- something about that?

Seventeen -- 17 or 24 bar chorus, I mean it was irregular, and was nothing to it, I mean, so -- see, you're going to have a -- you must -- should have a 32 bar chorus. I mean to work with, to be sensible, or may -- well, you can probably understand it, and make somebody else understand what you're trying to do, or what you have done,

are doing, you know. Because when you get down to a 17 bar chorus, oh, my God! You know. Dah dah, dah, dah, dah dah -- and then, now we're going back to so and so, you don't mean it. He says oh, what's happening?
Well when does the meter run out? Or when -- how they going to get back in there?
In other words, it's hard to keep your place. You lose where you are.
You don't, because -- and you couldn't dance it, you couldn't sing it, you couldn't -- you don't plan nothing, you know. You know.
Was Fats doing his mocking style of singing before he was given all these lousy tunes, or --
Yeah.
-- was it the lousy tunes that brought it on?
That helps.
(Laughter.)
That helped. He'd say oh, mercy. am I doing What, what have I done? what have I done? Help me, send somebody. Some ways of different singing he brought out, and oh, oh --
But he was singing like that before he got the dog tunes.
Uh-huh. Uh-huh. And he jumped in the

middle of the piano, and stop, go take a drink, go to the john, somewhere, anywhere, come back, you know. And -- you just couldn't help it. I mean you'd say what am I doing? I mean why? He'd say forget it, take it out. I don't need it. And then they'd have to talk him back into the idea of staying there, because as I told you, the business office of the publishers, and the recording studios, have gotten together, and they made an idea. They sold talent, time, and whatnot, and they weren't going -- they weren't going to give that money back.
(Laughter.)
Did Fats ever succeed in not doing something that he was asked to do?

I don't think so. I really don't, and now that you mention it, I've heard him say it a few times, and they would -- now Tom! Now, Tom! And he's raving. Now, Tom! I -- so and so. Don't Tom me. Blah, blah, blah. Here you come with love@ I (Unintelligible), and he'd be screaming and walking up and down the room, and they'd be trying to quieten him down. Now Tom. Tom. Just a minute.
(Laughter.)
What were the rest of you fellows doing while all this was going on?
Sitting quietly, damned quiet, I'd say, you're right Fats. We don't blame you, you know. Maybe
you hear that.
A little encouragement.

Yeah, because you don't dare say too much. Who asked you? He may say, but maybe, I mean that's the feeling you would get, but that mean you don't want to put your two cents in too, I mean you can tell, I mean you know better, you know?
Were these long sessions, then, I mean with all this arguing and everything going on?
Oh my God, yeah.
You din't get through them easy.
NO, of course you start, what, supposed to be four hour, four to five hours, and we did more than that quite often, you know. And --
Most of it spent arguing?
No, I wouldn't say that. No, because you got to rehearse the tune, keep going over it to make a record before we're happy.
Oh, I see.

See, and before he's happy, and he say let's try it like that, and bang (snaps fingers) the guys would jump up like -- the engineers, and record! Record! Beautiful. Beautiful! Don't touch it. Don't touch it! And sometimes Fats would say -- he would look at me, you know (laughs). I hate like hell to take this credit, but I mean I

bugged him. Well, maybe I did, and I -- if I didn't like something, and I thought it was going to endanger him, or us, down the line somewhere, I'd get his eye and say, you know, kind of shake my head a little.
I see.
You know? Because I -- maybe I saw something he didn't see, or maybe I thought he didn't hear, and he thought the same.
When you speak of endangering Fats, what do you mean? What kind of thing -- I mean session would endanger him?

Well, oh I mean should you record something, you record something, and it didn't turn out to be so right, and I'd tell you later, and you'd say well why didn't you tell me? Why didn't you call it to my attention? That's why I hired you, because I liked the way you think, and the way you hear, and the way you play, and you may tell me then, I kind of depend on you when we do something, if it isn't right I figure you will help -- you will tell me, or call it to my attention. You know?

Because nobody's perfect, after all, you know. I mean I'm not telling you, I just said it. And now looking -- then he'd -- okay, take five, and wander down there, and we'd take a walk and go to the john, which was way down around the hall somewhere. I wouldn't dare say anything to him about
this situation, in front of the guys, you know, I wouldn't dare, you know.
I see, so this was when you took your walk.

Yeah, he and I, nobody but he went, you know, just he and I would know what expired, what went on, you know? After we get out he say what's the matter? I say I don't think you want that. Why? You know. I says such and such. He say yeah? No wonder. Thanks. You know. A lot of times he's told me that.

I've had a lot of times he's told me, say Hermie, come-here I'd say what? "Get in there with the plunger." But I didn't think much of the idea, maybe, anyway. Or I would use it to the best of my ability. I thought. And so -- and I would ask him to take it out. I didn't want to tell him right in front of the guys, I don't like that. You should take it out. And he'd say damn, this guy ain't going to run the session, you know what happens in those --

So I'd take him aside, and I'd explain to him what I thought, and we would compare notes, he said you-see, well all right, now that you mention it, I think you're right. Or I don't think you're right. Keep it in. Or whatever. You know. And then I would say well if I were you I wouldn't do this here. I would have done it earlier, or not at all, or something, you know, and then we'd go back. He'd say cut another one.
And he'd say okay, instead of coming in such a place, you do this, and you do that, and so and so.

Ah, that is better, Fats, maybe they would say, or we'll keep both of them, see. Now they would do this, and they would do -- maybe they'd sell both of them, but you still had two we had left, see? Uh-huh?
Did Fats have a serious side to him? When he was --

Very. Very. Oh, oh heck yeah, I mean when it came to business, and music, oh man, you -- you never met a man more serious in your life. Never. And, with all our drinking, and bottles he used to buy, and all that business, he'd tell you, said 'now don't get drunk. If you get drunk you fire yourself. You're fired.' He said 'I'm supposed to be the drunken Fats Waller.' He said 'if I can drink whiskey on my job and play, you'll have to.' So if you got drunk and couldn't play, couldn't do your work (smack) you got fired yourself, that's it. He wanted no parts of you.

And if he said 'now I'm not supposed to tell you when to drink, what to drink. That's for you to know, and for you to do. If you don't have the money and I buy you a bottle, I'll sit it there, and I'll use it. You have to take it from there.' And he could drink all night and all day and come to work, come to work, like a clock, and never waver.
Now Buddy, you've got to do the same. And if he

figured you were drunk, and he give you a chorus, he'd say take another one, see? Now see, if you were laboring, and you just get through that first one, there ain't no way in the hell you're going to take it for another one (laughs) and not show it. So you fire yourself.
Well, are you saying that in order to work with Fats you had to be able to drink the way he drank?
No.
Or just don't get drunk.
Drink the way you want to drink, not the way he drank.
I see.

But he drank, and he suggested, he expected you to drink, and didn't think ill of you or mean of you if you did drink. But be able to do your work! That's all he wanted. Just -- just be able to play when your time comes. Do your work.
How did Fats work out on the sleeping? Did he need much sleep? Or could he get along with --

Yeah, he did, he did. He got good -- when he wanted it. I want to say he slept, you didn't see him every night for -- for instance, I've known several times where we're going to record, or we're going to record tomorrow, 8:00 o'clock, be at the studio. He'd stay up all night,

partying all over, oh, Harlem, here, there, downtown, whatever, and get up from wherever he is and walk in the studio. Never late. And Good morning! How are you? Where is -- oh, and his hands are steady, just like that. Where another guy, if he didn't drink, he'd be waving at people he didn't even know.
(Laughter.)
You know what I mean?
Yeah, right.

And he'd say go get me a quart, and he'd come in with a quart of Scotch, and probably send out and get a couple more later on. And he wouldn't eat then. I guess maybe that he'd already eaten before he came in. But whatever he want he'd send his valet out and get it, and get what you wanted for you.

And he just -- stripped down to our waists. I usually, most of the time, because I perspire so doggone much, and then most of the guys would take off their shirt and get down to their undershirts, and we'd go to work. And I mean work!
For a solid what, three or four hours?
Yeah, four hours. That was a session at that time. Four hours, and we ran -- it -- should we run into overtime, we, you know, ran into other things.
When the group was on the road, were you the one who was closest to Fats?
Yes, uh-huh.
How --

On the road, or in New York. He and I, we were great pals. We hung out together, and why I answered you so quick, I mean we've been accused of that for so many years, of being -- I was accused of being Fats' right-hand man, and one of those things. I think he liked me a lot too because I reminded him of his brother, Lawrence. Lawrence Waller, yeah, because he used to tell me that. Quite a lot. You sure remind me of my brother Lawrence. I don't see it.
You mean in appearance? Or personality?
Maybe appearance, personality maybe.
What did Lawrence -- was Lawrence a musician?
No. No, he was a --
An older brother?

Older brother, yeah, very nice. Very nice man. He's the one -- he and Fats, and two or three other guys, were making the rounds in Harlem, a hundred and what? 47th Street, and they went in a bar, and they were sitting down having some drinks and whatnot, and some guy came over and butted in and started to start something, so they got up, all left, went out and got -- Fats got in a taxi, and so forth. All of them was getting in the taxi. And this guy ran out,

and they saw him pull a pistol.
So Lawrence moved in to protect Fats, and got shot
in the hip.
My gosh!

So he -- and -- but he -- Fats loved him very, very
much, too much, before that. This was in later years, I mean
after Fats -- after I joined Fats, you know, and I know he
thought so much of Lawrence, and I'm sure he thought more of
him then, because if it hadn't been for Lawrence Fats would
have been a dead man. Be killed, maybe, you know, with that
shot. And for no reason. They didn't know the man. And the
man didn't know them.
He -- I don't know, this thing just happened.
You were very close to Fats then --
Very!
-- all the way through.
Very, yeah. Yeah.

Well then how -- in view of that,
when, for example, Fats went off to Europe and left the band
behind, goes off to California and leaves the band behind,
how did this affect your relationship with Fats? Did you feel
bad about it? Or say anything? (inaudible)?
Well I felt bad about it, but I didn't -- still didn't blame Fats, because I knew why, and Fats didn't do it. And Kirkoby did it. That's what I mean.
Did FATS ever say anything to you about it? About --

Afterwards, no, he said fellows, I'm sorry, but -- I left it up to Ed. He said, I don't know. I, you know, what Ed -- he used to sell this, don't you worry about the business, you worry about your music. Leave the business to us, to the office. You know, because we don't want to have you concerned about this, or worrying about that. It's like so many people walk up to you in the theater, or here or there, oh, Mr. Autrey, Mr. Waller, Mr. so and so, I wrote some tunes. I wrote a tune. I know it's going to be a hit. Will you please listen to -- you know, everything. You hear that every day. Thousands of times a day, if you let yourself, you know. And after you hear so doggone many tunes, you will hear it, and you will rewrite that damn tune. You're not -- you're not aware of it. I mean it's embedded into your brain, your subconscious, or whatever you want to call it. I mean the guy -- if there was somebody that was more intelligent he could say -- he'd know exactly where it comes from. So when you put it on paper, then they call you a thief. The man stole my tune.
There have been loads of suits based on that. Kind of hard to prove, though, sometimes.

Yes, it's so. What happens, a good smart manager tell his client, tell his agent, don't listen to nobody's tune. Don't do it. Write your own, and let them have theirs, and keep it -- one of those things. See.
Herman, was life with Fats on the road any different from life when you were all in New York together? You all lived in New York, didn't you?
Yes. Uh-huh.
When you got on the road, did life change any?
I would think it maybe -- if it did, it was better, more of a tight together family, like, thing.
You support each other more.

Oh, sure. Certainly. Yes. I mean you're concerned, where are you living, did you find someplace to live, is it nice? Or did you eat? Or do you feel well? And such and such a guys would get sick through the night, whatnot.

Well I'm trying to think of one case, Johnny "Buggs" Johnny Hamilton, for instance, he had ulcers, and he had this and he had the other, and quite often he got very sick and would have to leave and call the doctor, and we'd have to leave
him a few towns -- times, here, there, you know? Well, I never went through that. I was lucky, maybe, whatever you want to call it.

But all of us were concerned for his welfare. I mean, so we'd leave him, and Fats would say well, if you need anything, whatever he needs, give it to him, send me the bill, or call me, or one of those things. You know.
In a case like that, were you sometimes in the group along with Johnny Buggs?
Yes, he came in, but I mean I was the main one.
You were carrying two trumpets then, right then.
Yes, I mean he would come in, but not in the six-piece group. Not in that. This was the big band.
Oh, the big band.
Yeah. When they -- one night here, one night there.
Well, when something like that happened, when somebody gets sick, and you had to leave them, what would you do? Pick up a local musician wherever you went? Or --
No, no, we would -- no, because there's usually a few days or a week, and the two trumpets, with the rest of the guys, they could carry them.
How about the six-piece group. Did you have to -- if something happened to somebody there, would you --
No, that had to be replaced. I mean Johnny 'Bugs' replaced me. I had what, flu, or a cold, or something, and Johnny 'Bugs' and what's his name? He's in Europe now, still in Paris. Coleman.
Bill Coleman, yeah. Uh-huh.
Yeah, hm, and for a few days -- and have a date, or a recording date or something, he would replace me, and everything.
And if you're on the road, did you send to New York for somebody? Or did you pick up a local --
Well that didn't happen to me on the road. No.
Why was he called Johnny 'Bugs'?
Johnny told me that story himself. When he was a little baby crawling around on the floor he say he used to eat every bug he could catch.
(Laughter.)
Now whether he was lying or not, and I think -- [he had a nasty mouth] you know?
(Laughter.)
That's a wonderful --
And -- so he was a damned good trumpet
player, you know. Oh, I thought the world, people, Fats and all of them thought a heck of a lot of Bugs, and he was a very nice guy. Uh-huh.
In the late thirties -- when did you join Fats, in '34?
When I did?
Yeah.
Who, me?
Yeah, you. '34?
Uh, yeah, we started -- let me see --
I think that's when he started --

'33, it was '33 or '34, the latter part of the two. It was so close together there, and I do know we started moving together in '34. Right? It was 30 -- maybe the latter -- a few days in '33, maybe, because I was in New York, I had just come to New York. I had quit Doc Hyder's band, you know, and I was -- had come into New York, you know?
But then there was -- then there was that period when you were with Fletcher Henderson.
Yes. Yeah.
Yeah, now when were you with Claudet Hopkins? How did that come about?
Fats went to Europe, and one of those times he went to Europe, two or three times --
First time, or what?
Uh, no, couldn't have been the first time, because --
What did you do the first time when he went?

Same thing, hang around and, you know, work wherever I could. Grab club dates, or whatnot, you know, and there wasn't a hell of a lot then, for me, as a colored guy, I'll put it that way. They -- well, there weren't too many colored club dates, anyway.

So Claud needed somebody. Claud was going to -- where? -- West Virginia. He had some dates in West Virginia, here and there. And he asked me to make them with him. So I asked Fats. Fats gone, so I said Fats, is it all right for me to make these dates? He say yeah, go ahead.
Had Fats gone to Europe, or is it -- was he still in the States?
Yeah, he had gone and come back.
Oh come back, I see.
Yeah, he was here then.
So you were working with Fats again.

Yeah, but I mean we're in town and nothing happening, we were sitting around and I don't know for what reason. I don't know if he didn't feel like going out, or what, because he could always -- well I want to go here, go there, and point, and that's where they sent us. You know?
And he said go ahead, I'll let you know. I said just let me know when you're ready, and wherever I am, I'll come in. He said oh, don't worry about it.
So, I went with Claud to do a few dates, and while we were out the singer, Claud Hopkins' singer, hm, hm, hm, hm hm, hm, thin man.
Orlando --

Orlando Robertson. Came back and as the people heard, he was back with Claud (snap, snap, snap) Claud's offers start -- got swamped with -- we want Claud. We want Claud and Orlando, mainly, since he was back.
Oh, I see.

So some more dates come in, and instead of us coming back to New York, and Claud say I got two or three more dates, can you make them? I said well, yes, I guess so, you know. And since I hadn't heard anything, I said two or three more dates are not going to hurt. And one -- this particular date took us to West Virginia, and Fats' booking came in, because the thing in Chicago, the hotel in Chicago had the room. He didn't mention it to me, and that -- now that's where Fats was like a kid. He would get very mad, should he say well, call Wilson and tell him I want -- he'd say why? What do you mean, he's not here? Get him!
You'd say well, he left town. He left town.
(Smack)
he'd hit the ceiling, you know? And he's mad. He's
like a kid when you steal his favorite toy, or something. You know, he'd pout like a bastard. See?
(Laughter.)
When they -- all the same time, say go ahead, you know, so he don't appreciate me, see? You go away (smack) leave me all by myself. I need him. He's not here.
(Laughter.)

See? Now, we were playing and a certain guy says go out and get me a pint. No! No, I didn't. Some fellow came in and said (and) it was raining like hell in West Virginia, and man, if you've ever been to West Virginia, that's the wrong place to be when the sun is shining, but then when it's raining, Jesus Christ! I mean, you know. said I just heard and I thought [---] So, so this is the way Fats operates on recordings. I said recordings? No, live. I say oh, no. He say oh yes. Like I say. See. I say where is it coming from? Panther Room Bathroom in Chicago. I said what? And he told me what happened. I say -- give him some money. I say go out and get me a pint of liquor. I took the stuff, I didn't -- gullah, gullah, gullah, gullah, gullah, man, I almost went out, because I knew about what was happening. And he told them, he told Kirkaby, call Hermie, get Hermie, I want Hermie.
Now Tom, uh, it's no use you worrying about that now. You -- we can get along. We can -- we don't have to,
because it would do this, and -- he say okay, well you're the manager. You take care of it. He says okay, and he closes up and drink some more whiskey.

So Kirkeby kept me out of the band for how many months? For Quite a while, because of that. And each day I was off, it went farther, and farther, it looked like -- so I was saying to hell with you. I'm happy where I am. You know, and nobody could tell -- it was too damn late. That's one of the things that I held against him. And he did it on purpose, because he wanted me out because I knew too much about Fats's business, and money, and things would happen I had warned Fats. I say man, you being taken! Such and such and such and such. I say we call -- being that -- being a carnival man I saw so much going on.

Oh man, I saw a man with 11 hundred dollar bills. He just sold his cotton. And he stood there trying to win an Indian blanket in the carnival. He lost all that money trying -- he wanted it, and the damned blanket only cost $5.00, four or five dollars. He could have bought one at the store. He wanted to take that blanket home to his family, to his wife, an Indian blanket. He lost eleven one hundred dollar bills. I was on the show. See what I mean?
And I've seen, I know how those things can go, and I saw it happening, and I said well I can't stand by and see it happening to him, when I know what's going on, so I said
they want to get me out of the way. And I say Kirkaby, the bass player, Charlie Turner, yeah, who was a contractor. That's the word I was trying to --
Contractor, right. Back earlier.

Yeah, yeah. And see Charlie knew what was happening, so Charlie said well cut me in too. Which I don't blame him. You know. What the hell. I knew he was stealing, you look at him, just like a politician. Throw a few bucks my way, and go ahead. What the hell.
And that's what went on. And they kept me -- or tried to keep me as long as -- until he put his foot down, and say I've got to get Hermie. I've got to have Hermie. And matt --
And how did he get you?
Well, they called me there, and they told me to get back to the band.
How long were you gone?
Oh --
How long were you with Claude? Let's put it that way.

Well I wasn't very happy. Let's see, how many months did that run into? Because after Robertson came back we did a few things, quite a few things, got to go, and have another job, I had to stay with him. Until I got -- you know -- got a chance to get back with Fats.
Exactly how many months, or weeks, or this -- I rightly -- I don't --
Who was in the band then? Was Ed Hall in that band?
Ed Hall?
Yeah.

No. No, no. I didn't work in that band with Ed. Ed had left before I ever joined him. And I joined -- I joined them -- that was quite a while after he left. I stayed with the group because I did a recording date with Claude Hopkins. He did my tune, for one thing, 'Yacht Club Swing.'
Oh, he did 'Yacht Club Swing.'

Yeah, and I went in there and I played first trumpet for him, because -- I'm trying to think, who was his first trumpet? Who left? When I came in. Well, on some of the recording dates I played, it was that way, I played first because I was a soloist, and sang a couple of things with them, and played -- you know.
Anybody that you remember particularly from the band? From the Claude Hopkins Band?

Claude Hopkins group? Yeah. Howard Johnson on the -- tenor piano, then, he was playing. Let's see, the banjo player, guitar player, who he had had -- been with him for years, hm, hm, hm, well let me move on. What the heck,
I know everybody that was in the band. Why can't I think of them? I cannot think.

Naturally Ovie Alston had gone, you know. He used to be there years ago, because he was the band. Bobby -- Bobby Johnson, Tenor saxophone player, yeah. I'll put it that way, and I'm trying to think who was playing the alto then, but Rudy -- we weren't together, but he had to have been in that band.
Tenor man, who used to be with Charlie --
(End of Tape Six.)
-- here we're talking about Johnny Haughton Horton, Shorty?
Yeah, Shorty Horton, uh-huh.
Shorty Horton is the trombonist.
Now was -- he was -- was he with Claude, or not?
Naw -- yes, he went with Claude. He was with Claude too.
Not when you were there.

I don't think so. I'm trying to -- I'm trying to -- I'm trying to remember. I want to be honest, because he and I worked with Fats, as I told you, and I'm telling you now, with Fats Waller, and he recorded 'In The Gloaming' with Fats on a big dance record, 12 inch thing, and 'Rump Steak Serenade,' you know, and what all, they was in the same session.
And he was a very good -- very fine trombonist, and a very fine (laughs) fellow. And we -- yes, we worked with Claude Hopkins.
You mentioned one of the saxophonists who was with Claude when you were with him was Benny Waters.
Benny Waters, yeah. Hmm, oh, Johnson.
Howard Johnson?
Howard Johnson.
One of the saxophonists. Who was the drummer? Do you remember?

Yes. Yes. Hm, hm, hm, by golly, oh, wait just a minute, who would have been playing drums then? Oh! Yeah, another Johnson, uh, uh, oh, he's working at a bank now. He's a bank messenger, guard, or something there. Walter Johnson.
Oh, Walter Johnson.
Walter Johnson, the most handsome -- (laughs) -- and what a nice man, what a nice drummer.
Had he been with Fletcher too?

Yes, Yes. He was with some of everybody, and they were proud to have him, proud to think about him, because every second that I've known him, every year that I've known him, I've never heard anybody say anything about Walter but a perfect gentleman, and I think it's kind of nice, you know?
This period that you were with Claud Hopkins, was that all just one tour? You went out to West Virginia, back, and --

Naw, it wasn't -- naw, heck no. I mean we went -- we went -- oh, we did -- later on we went farther than that. I'm trying to think how far south did we go, or when or where. We had a girl singer. Yeah, because we -- I remember Birmingham, Alabama.
What was it like traveling --
With Claud@?
-- with Claude in the south, and in places like Alabama?
Well --
How did you live?

It seemed rough, because at that time we had to go knock on doors, and say pardon me, Madam, would you, or do you happen to have a room that you would like to or care to rent? I'm here with the band, such and such a band, we're going to be here two nights, three nights, and need a place to stay. Yes, or no?

No, but -- I say well do you know of some place, and they say well go down the street by the old oak tree and make a left and turn, and don't go in there, because that's a -- they, you know, that -- how you get those directions, and you finally -- you hope -- find some place, you know.
But you have to go all over town yourself looking for them?
You have to, yes.

Weren't there -- after -- if you're playing some place in Birmingham, let's say, there had been other bands that had come through and played, and after that had gone on for a while, well weren't there certain places that became established to live --
Yes, if you knew where to start asking.
But didn't the people who ran the ballroom, or wherever you were going to play --

Well there were -- they would -- you'd run into anybody in the street, and say know where I can get a room, fellow? Yes. Why don't you go down to Mrs. So-and-so's, or they'd figure you know. Yeah, but where is that? Which direction? Oh, well you go down here, then turn, and turn, and -- they'd direct you that way.
Oh, I see.

And in Birmingham they had a little shanty there, little thing they called a hotel, and it's -- oh, well we're having a convention, in town, church convention, or something, and we're all filled up, you know, maybe, you know. I mean that -- well you had -- you ran into that even in the biggest hotels, sometimes. You get into town and there's some kind of convention, and it's full. I mean, so
that's different. And maybe you get -- well, if you keep looking, had plenty of time to spend, you -- usually you would find something, here, there, and with --
Did you -- after you had left the South and come north, and then when you went back with bands, with any group such as Claude's, did you ever have any real trouble? In the South.

Uh, I'm trying to think. Yeah, I have -- I'm trying to pin it down, because you would run into -- I'm glad you asked me that, because being born in the South I knew what to expect, and I knew what one could do, should do, or shouldn't do.
I've always heard this.

See, because well, when I was born, from a little baby up, I wondered about these things, and -- you know, I saw, and I learned. It's one thing that puzzles me, and I've never been able to shake it. My father had me out one day, and he was going to buy me an ice cream cone, and he said we're going down -- now come on. I said well why can't we stop here? At this little ice cream -- he said no, we're going down to the other. I said what? They sell ice cream here. And he didn't want to tell me, explain to me that we could not go in there and buy it. He was going to take me where he would have

less trouble. I mean I realized that later, many years later. But I couldn't understand, why did he go -- what do you want to go way the hell, way down there, around the -- you know, when we could get it here. You know?

Okay, as I told you, I learned. Now, in the -- after I joined these bands, and we went down south, all the way down to the bottom, and back here, then we got up, you know, not exactly a chip on the shoulder, because you don't do that, I mean you say well, you walk into a place with your head down, because you expect -- you're expecting -- generally expected that there was going -- something is going to happen to you.

So anyway, and you go in, and you don't get it. And you're treated damn nice, and with a smile, well when are you fellows coming back through here? Be sure and stop now. We will be looking for you, and stop in and eat with us, and just different restaurants. We said well thank you, we will. You know. Well that makes your food --
these were white restaurants? Really?

Yes! And they -- and it makes your food digest better, and you say well, that's -- you know. Instead of the guys looking at you, say don't come in here, that way, what you come in here for? What do you want? You know, and that -- well, if they're going to give you the meal you still don't -- you don't enjoy it.

So that happened a lot of times, and we came in, hi fellows, hey, they remembered two or three names. Come on over! Sit down! And the waitresses would be running, grabbing this, and grabbing that, and the managers, and the bosses and what not, everybody, you know. Sit down, be there. Be happy. what did you see? What do you like? Is the meat this and that? You know?
And you say well confound, these people have changed, or something, or they think we're human after all. Anyway, it becomes delightful.
Was this in the thirties that you're talking about, about the time when you went down with Claude?
Yeah, yeah, uh-huh.
It was -- even that far back.
Oh sure, because the thirties, yes. Even the forties, later than that, the fifties even, are you kidding? Sure.
No, but I mean that you were greeted pleasantly in white restaurants. (inaudible).

Yeah, that's what I mean. So now we came back to Ohio, I mean Illinois, Michigan. We played Canada now. We come out of Canada, going into Detroit, we stopped at the border, and we get some -- we saw a joint -- hot dogs, and crap, so we got out and ordered for the -- I did, several of us, and ordered some hot dogs and hamburgers,

or whatever it was, go to them and say We don't serve your kind here! I say what? And she was very indignant, very mad. I say -- well I called -- I don't know what I didn't call her, and went under my breath, and my -- then I started to think. I said we've been all down Alabama, Georgia, and all that stuff, and been treated swell. While there, where I expected to run into this, and didn't -- and here I am back in the north, you know, mid-west, where I expect to be treated like a human being, and I run into this.
It really knocked me on my feet, you know? So you ask yourself why, how does it get turned around that way? You know what I mean?
Did that happen very often to you in the north, as opposed to the south?
Yes, it -- yes it did. Yes it did.
More so than the south?
No, not more so, but I mean --
But more than you expected.

More than I expected, and when I didn't expect it, because I said well I'm out of that part of the country where this has been going on for hundreds of years, and now I'm here where it's supposed to be human, where it's supposed to be nice, shoot! Man, I -- well, what are you going to do with a thing like that when you -- you say well I wouldn't care -- what do you think? This is the way
it is here, and get out, and which we run into a hell of a lot of that. You know.
Get out.
Yeah. I mean like us, we don't serve your kind, we don't serve you in here. And you're not going to Anything like that, be served.
When you went down south with bands were you playing primarily to black audiences, or white audiences?
Well, that depends. If we went down south, you played to a black audience, or a white audience.
You weren't --
You didn't -- nah, you didn't mix it.
Right.

They did not mix it. And that's another thing, we played Florida with Fats, first time Fats went to Florida they offered him, oh, man, they offered him a mint to come. For he wouldn't take it. Fats had never been south in his life, and all he heard was stories that he didn't want any parts of it. So I said well it's okay, now, with such and such and such and such. He said 'Forget it! I don't need it! Let them keep it!' You know.
He said I'm not going! And finally, anyway, there was talk -- talked him into it, so we got to Miami. Now Miami, Florida, and we had to play outside of Miami, 30 something --
34 miles, Fort Lauderdale.
Right, uh-huh.

So we went there to play, and pulled the bus up there, and Kirkaby was there. Took out the stuff, so Kirkaby sat up the band himself because he was -- he didn't want to pay a valet. He put the few -- valet money in his pocket. He made that himself.
(Laughter.)
And see, I always want to get back to poor Kirkaby, I mean, you know.
(Laughter.)
He's got every nickle he ever stole, and he stole plenty, believe me. He is -- he's doing all right.
You know who he's been owning for the last 40 years, the outfit that -- the singers that -- he owned them then, right before he had Fats. I mean before he came out --
Oh, the --
"Deep River" --
The Delta Rhythm Boys.
Delta Rhythm Boys.
Delta Rhythm Boys.
He still does, uh-huh. And he's had them ever -- anyway.
We were in going to Florida.
They're in Africa. (Unintelligible.)
No, I mean when you were --
In Florida, yeah.
Getting back to the story.

Oh, yeah, yeah. (Laughs.) So we were sitting there, and getting ready to go on and play, and some friend of ours, somebody from New York, came in, Hello! Blah, blah, blah, blah. I say come on back, and so and so, and sit here with us and have a taste. He said all right, all right. I say --
Black friend?
No, no. White.
White, uh-huh.

So I kept petting him down, and he said I mean, after all, don't -- you know where you are. I said come on, man, you're not like that too! He said no, that's the law here. I said what?! State law, he say, no white man can be under the same roof with a black person, none, no where, in Florida. I said I didn't know that. I thought maybe he was -- and he said look, man, I'm white and you're black, I can't come see you --

It wasn't he and -- I -- the thing, you know, I said the hell, oh gee, I'm sorry. I kept pinning him down, now come on with me, because I knew him when we had been stationed together here, in the states, and around places, so
it's almost time to hit. Long, tall policeman come up, and said all right, break it up. Said get out of here. You know, get out of here, he said.

Said well I'm the manager. Said I wouldn't care who you, you're going to get out of here. He said what?! He said look, I'm Fats Waller's manager, and so and so and so and so. Nobody's allowed in here, or can stay when the door's open, they start, so he say well I'm the manager, and I have to take the tickets. He say not in here, you won't.
So in other words, he had to drive -- turn the car, the bus around, and face it to the door, and sit where he could see, and had a stop watch.
(Laughter.)
Stop clock, no kidding --
: To count them, right?

To count them as they went in, and whatnot. That's the way he had to do it. That's the way the night went down, and of course the manager he cannot come in here and collect tickets, money, or nothing. And they didn't let him in.
: How long did you stay in Florida?
One night, two nights, except, you know, because we were moving.
: And out. (Laughs.) That's --
I -- that's the way we did.
Getting back to Claude Hopkins, you were with him for what, several months, I guess.
Yes, I'd say -- well I had -- it turned out to be so unpleasant thing, and now -- I -- I would like to have forgotten, forget about it, just so --
Why was it unpleasant?

Well, when I worked with Claud's band, it was bad enough. I mean we played theaters, like Howard Theater, and Washington, D. C., and different -- I'm trying to think of where else, Washington, Baltimore -- anyhow, Baltimore, and we did -- I'm trying to think did I do that. Yes, I did do the Apollo with him. Oh, did I do the Apollo!
With Claude?
Ye-e-e-s.
What happened?

Well I mean, as I was -- I get -- I could see the curtain going up, and it got -- we were in the Apollo Palmer Theater, yeah, and we'd just gotten -- it was on payday, and I'd just gotten my pay slip, and I counted my money, and I was $5.00 short. So I started thinking, and I counted the rest, and said maybe I made a mistake. So I walked on and said 'Hey, Claud, I think there's a little mistake here. I'm $5.00 short in my money.' He said, 'no, you're not short.' He say 'that's what it is.' I say well why? I say you didn't talk to me. You

didn't ask -- he said well I don't have to say, because I cut you and everybody $5.00. I said you don't just cut me $5.00, and don't talk -- ask me about it. If I'm -- if it's agreeable, or not, or what -- why? What's happening? (Unintelligible.)

Well that's the way it is, man. What you going to do about it? And all along the curtain's going up. So I reached with the other hand and grabbed him, and lifted him up out of the seat, and get -- and hollered Herman, don't do it! Don't do it! Don't do it! at me. I was getting ready to -- you know.
Give him a punch.
Oh, man! I was going to lower the boom.
(Laughter.)

Said, Don't do it! I said man, give me my money. Don't talk to -- you know, curtain's going up, and I mean -- I don't know. I lost my -- well, I came to my mind, I lost my mind, because had he called me aside and said well Herman, it's necessary for me to ask you to take a cut, five bucks, or something, I may have taken it, and maybe yes, maybe no, but you just don't take my money, and say well that's it.
Yeah.
What are you going to do? What do you want to do? You know. Well I was going to show him what I
anyway going to do, this him!
(Laughter.)
Anyway, so we went on through and played the show, and --
You dropped him before the curtain got all the way up.

Yeah, so I said okay, now, I don't know how long I stayed with him after that. I don't think it could have been very long, because knowing Herman, I was saying nobody will mess with my money, you know, so later on in years, after I left Pats, and after I'd finished a lot of things, I got somebody -- oh, a friend of mine told me about this job in the mountains.
In the Catskills?

In the Catskills, yeah, and at the Club Neverly, Kenny Davenport, to be positive, exact, his -- part of his -- some parts of his family, I think his mother, worked there, and secretary to this main man, the big boss, and he knew about this job, and asked me if I wanted it, and sent me up to take it.
So when I got in touch, and they -- everything went fine. So the man told me, this manager, told me, McClosky's manager, I never talked to him then --
McClosky owned the hotel?
He owned it, yeah, and the guy told me,

said we have a room here, it's the Safari Room, African room, said we've never had a -- said it's a million dollar room, it's never been packed. He said if you come in here and can pack this room, say you can write your own ticket.

Now they had 12 or 13 piece band down onstage who played for the acts, chorus girls acts, or whatever they were, you know, when we came in, and you look up where it would be the spotlight up there, that's where the Safari Room could sit there and look down on the people, and it was a beautiful room with all kind of African gadgets, and things, and hanging all on the wall, you know, this stuff.
Shields, and --
Yeah, all that stuff, that you would find -- would find in Africa, and skins, and stuff, you know. Statues.
Anyway, I said well okay, so we started working, and we were playing in that room, and we started packing them in, and in a few days everybody was coming in to hear us, and about four pieces.
Who was in the band?

Piano, well, when I get ready to come up I'd ask him would he come up with me, and I told him, I said well who have you got on the group? I said well I've got so and so and so and so. I had Claude Hopkins. Claude Hopkins would go on piano. I said yes, and I had drummer,
Marquis
Marcus Foster on Drums, hmmmmm, ah, trying to think of who did we have on -- Herman Autrey on trumpet. And so the four would finally get down, three pieces, and who the hell did we have on bass?
It may come.
Yeah.
SO what happened?

So we started playing, and the people liked it, and we made the people like it, and we played, and entertained them, and they were very, very happy, and this particular time I started -- I got ill. I had to rush -- be rushed to the hospital. I got a -- I could not pass my water. So the doctor said come in the hospital, you need an operation, so into the hospital I went, and I asked Claude, I said well take over for me until I come out, and so and so and so. I said I'm paying him this and that, and he knew what he was getting. I said collect the money. The money is such and so. And oh, I told the manager, I said well, this was on my day off, and I say you know what your promise was. If we did -- he say yes, you did it. You've done it. He said, so the raise, and things, and you will get it. He said but the boss is out now, and -- in the Mediterranean, and when I get in touch with him, or when he comes in, I'll tell him, and tell -- quote your price to me and I'll tell him, and I'm sure he'll be agreeable. You know?
And we shook hands on it, he said well I'm sure that will be all right. so I passed the thing on to Claude, and I went into the hospital, and --
Did Claude get a trumpet player to replace you?

Yeah, I told him to get somebody to replace me, because -- because of what was happening, so when the boss, the big man did come, he had somebody to call. He had his secretary to call me, and call -- I had a phone in my room in the hospital, and then, Mr. Autrey, Mr. McClosky, the boss wanted to know, do you need anything? Whatever, you may have it. All you have to do is mention. So and so and so and so.

So I said well, thank you. And I started thinking and I said well, so many guys have been in my position and they start bugging and begging the boss for this and this, and he -- I said to myself, I won't do it. I'll show him that I'm a man, I mean, you know. And I said oh, well thank you very much, but should I need anything I will let you know, and we'll leave it like that (unintelligible).

And she said well just let us know. And I stayed there, what, thirty days? Almost, or something that way, about. Anyway, so the doctor told me, said that okay, you can go back to work next week, if you want to. I called. I said well I'm calling it, you know. I'm -- the doctor said
I could come back to work. Oh yeah? Well you -- I called the union, and they called, well you -- did you talk to Claude Hopkins? I said no, why should I? Should I? I said well I will call him then.

Well, well you talk to him. Whatever Claude says is -- so the manager says all right with me, and I got the manager, I got the union man, and finally, he said while you (unintelligible). And I said look, man, I've been in the union 40 years, and I'm supposed to call you, and I don't care where you -- what you're doing, you're supposed to take care of my business for me, you know, I know that.

And well, I said what I want to know from you is, is my contract still good? Is there another contract? Well, uh, well uh, well yes. I said well why? Who's -- I said well tell me this, is it in Claude's name? Well, yes, I think so. So okay.
: In Claude's name.

So I called Claude. I said man, I don't know what's happening. You'll have to talk to them. They won't tell you. Everybody started passing the buck. So I got him around, so sorted what was going on, and I had been had, so I turned it over to them, and (unintelligible) and this and that and that and that and that, and just and that was, and this and this and the other, so when the thing went down, Herman was still left waiting, wanting.
So okay, so the whole union, everybody heard about it thought it was the dirtiest thing they ever heard of, you know? And --
Have you seen Claude since?
Oh, yeah, I've worked with him since then.
You've worked with him?!
Yes, on a couple of jobs. Somebody booked him, and we got on the job, I was there and he was there, so he started looking me -- ducking, you know.
(Laughter.)
But I didn't say much to him. I had I wasn't going to- made up my mind (unintelligible). Why? You know, I mean why should I? I mean --
Just let bygones be bygones.
Well yeah, but I thought like hell, I mean you know.
I remember a record that Claude made, I don't think you were on it, called 'Safari Blues.' Does that come out of that room? The Safari Room?
It could have been. 'Safari Blues,' yeah.
It's a nice little riff, too.
I haven't heard of it.
Catchy little riff, very nice.
I bet you -- no, no. I don't know. So
he must have (unintelligible).

So what -- well, this -- we're getting ahead of our story, up -- to get up the Neverly, but when you came all -- finished with Claud Hopkins band, this was back in the thirties again, and Fats had been --
No, oh you mean the big band. Claud's band.
Claud's big band, yeah, and Fats -- you would have been hearing Fats from the Panther Room, while you were with --
Oh, yeah, yeah. Uh-huh.
And -- well, did Fats finally get you back? What happened?

Yes, I had to -- he couldn't stand it any longer, and he made Kirkaby, and everybody else, call me to get Herman back, you know. And I was glad and he was glad, and we were happy. We united, and -- Oh Hymie! Hymie, it's so good to see you! Like that.
Why did he call you Hymie?
Well Fats started calling me that.
Why?

Well, I don't know that -- let me see, what happened? We were in Philadelphia, and some girl I knew came into the hotel somewhere and asked for me, or called me, Is Hymie -- Hymie! You know. Because Herman -- Hymie, in

Jewish, you know, think it's Herman, and Hymie, and Jewish name, Chaim, and all that, the same. So they started calling me Hymie! And Fats picked it up. He started calling me Hymie and on a lot of the recording dates, Hymie! I said what do you want?
So I used to get a lot of mail, Hymie.
Hymie?
Yeah, uh-huh. And still do, here and there, once in a while, get a letter, card, or something. Hymie, you know?
Well when you went back, when you got together again with Fats, did you just stay with him for there still breaks quite a while then, or were you (inaudible)
Let me see, what are we talking about now, '42, until --
-- you know.
This was steady then, from there on then.
Um, more or less. He left -- he left again to go do 'Stormy Weather', and whatnot, and --
Well was that when you -- when you joined Stuff Smith?
Uh, yes. I -- no, I joined Stuff Smith in '39, because we went from here to Chicago, and did so many
months there, and from there we went to Hollywood, and in '40, or in certainly in '40, or '40, I was in California, in '42, we came back from California.
This was all with Stuff?
Yeah.
Oh. So there was what, period of three years when you were with Stuff?
No, it wasn't -- oh, because I'm trying to think now, must have been late thirties then, because '40 we were at the Freyvilla Frugal Club in Hollywood.
You and Stuff.
Yeah.
Had you replaced Jonah Jones?
No, No I didn't replace -- well, Jonah wasn't there. Let me see, I'm trying to think who -- who had been there? Okay, I guess it was Jonah. I can't think of another -- another --
But you came in more or less at the time that he left. He must have -- he joined Cab about '39, I think, '39, '40.
Well I think Jonah was the last -- maybe Jonah was the last trumpet player he had before me, could be, like that, you know?
When -- when you moved -- when you started playing with Stuff did you sort of take over Jonah's
Did you
role with the derby hat and the comedy and everything? He played (inaudible)?
No, no. That's the way I played myself. I mean truthfully I never saw -- I never -- I'm trying to think now, how many times, or when have I seen Jonah perform? And I've --
Under any circumstances.
Yeah. And I've known him for years, and we've been friends and admirers of each other. I still admire Jonah, but I don't remember seeing Jonah --
Well isn't this -- isn't this normal, Herman, that musicians, if they're working, don't have a chance to see another musician working.

That's it, that's it. That's it. I mean I can hear you on a recording date, and judge pretty well by what you're doing, or hear somebody mention what you're doing, maybe. You know, and that -- I can do that. But -- and then too, more -- more or less, guys my age, Jonah, enjoying another guy; we've played practically the same. We would have done the same thing. We were always looking for ideas, sounds, with buckets, cuspidois, and any damn thing you could find you use them, you know, and trying to make it -- once you run across a sound that was different, or that you liked, well, you latch onto it, that's all.
And you -- by then you had your own
sound pretty definitely down.

Pretty definitely down, yeah, because people like what you were doing, and that was a cue that okay, you're catching on, and they like what you're doing. Don't change it. Stick with it. In other words, that's -- you know.
How did you happen to join Stuff? Where -- did you go from Fats to Stuff, or did Fats go out of town, or what?
Yeah, I went from Fats to Stuff, to Stuff, yeah.
What happened to (Unaudible) with Fats at that point?
Wait, I'm trying to think. Oh, Fats -- the Panther Room, because we followed him, we went into Chicago, and he was coming out of the Panther Room, and we went in to --
Who's "we" at this -- this is Stuff?
Stuff.
But you'd already joined Stuff by then.
Yes, was with Stuff.
Well how did you happen -- well my question is how did you happen to join Stuff?
Join Stuff. I'm trying to think now.
Did you go from Claudeto Stuff, or
from Fats to Stuff?

Uh, trying to think, oh, gosh. I -- because I know -- I knew Stuff -- I'm trying to figure -- because I met Stuffy years ago, in Washington, D. C., when I was living in Washington, I was working at the Howard Theater. 'Cause he sold me a recording, a -- an apparatus there, machine.
Disk recorder, it must have been back then.
Yeah, yeah, one of them things, and some records, and things. And it was a snow job. He laughs like hell about it. He --
(Laughter.)
