I say you're rotten. You're dirty. He says, what's the matter, man?! Blah, blah, blah, blah, he used to tell me about the times he was with Trent, Alphonso Trent.
Alphonso Trent.
Trent in Texas, and he told me some stories about that that were terrific.
What, he was doing a con job?
Yeah, he was -- he was -- no, he was in there, and this wasn't when I was with the carnival.
Yes, I mean you were talking about the stories with Alphonso Trent, but they --
Yeah, but this very one in particular,

they said they were doing one nighters, going from here to there, and sitting in the car, and they'd be working at night, and they were riding along, going through the desert somewhere in Texas, and they ran over a rattlesnake, or a snake, or some kind of snake, and as the wheels turned, somehow, the snake came around and they brought him up, or threw him in the car. (Laughs.)

And all the guys was laying there asleep, snoring, you know, trying to wake up, and day was just breaking, slightly (laughs) had some guy feel this thing moving in his lap, and he reached down there and he said aaaah! He grabbed the thing and handed it to Stuff. He said Aaah! what is this? And threw it out the car, you know.
(Laughter.)
The same snake that they ran over, you know. They got -- but nobody got bitten by the damned thing, but everybody was excited and going nuts.
The snake must have been in bad shape.
Yeah, and so was the man.
(Laughter.)

And things like that, so he came to my house and I had -- I needed a record player, and he talked me into it, and he said man, this and that, so I said okay, I think I give him five or six dollars for it. And some
records, and I didn't see Stuff no more, and the next time I saw him I had to catch him. I said man, that was nothing. He laughed! He knew. You know.
(Laughter.)
That wasn't why he gave you a job, though, was it?
No, no, no. No. I'm trying to think, this -- had we worked together, or where? Had we worked together, why did he give me this job?
I'm trying -- what I'm trying to figure is why had -- why were you not with Fats at this point?
Well, this is all going back to the Panther Room. That's why --
Oh, I see, that's why --
Yeah, because I -- working with Stuff, I had to go with Stuff --
Didn't you go with Fats to the Panther Room too, or was that --
No, I didn't go in the Panther Room at all.
Oh, I see. You missed that compeltely.

I missed that completely, because of Kirkaby, let him talk me out of it, because I had been back with Stuff -- I mean with Claude Hopkins. Now, I went with -- I'm trying to think of her name again, that went with Stuff,

aaah, where we rehearsed, Slick Jones, drummer; Jobertug, Joe Beeters, Al tenor saxophone player; Hal Hall, bass player; Herman Autrey, trumpet, and we were getting ready to go to Chicago. (unintelligible).
Well this sounds like he's putting a whole new group together.

Yes. And now I see. That's the way it looks to me, now, because he went in, and Joe Sherman, at the -- uh, uh, on -- down the Loop there, Randolph Street, 68 Randolph Street. Yeah. Joe Sherman. I'm trying to think of the name of the damn club. Uh, uh, uh, (smack, smack) (unintelligible) at the [meantime] and Jimmy Noone was there with his band at the same time.
Well this was much earlier, was the Apex.
No, no, no. Wasn't the Apex. No, no. No, 68 Randolph Street. Yeah, that's the address, see, I know the Apex, I know what you mean by the Apex.
But you didn't go -- I thought you went in the Panther Room.
No. No, we didn't follow Fats there. Fats was in the Panther Room --
Oh, Fats was coming out of the Panther Room, and you went to the other club. I see.
Yeah, we went into town as he was leav-
ing. See? That's what I mean. And 68 Randolph Street, for Joe Sherman, and because Jimmy Noone and I wrote the 'Apex Blues' before or after, which I don't know anything about the Apex Room.
I was -- that was probably about ten years before. This was back in the late twenties when he was playing there.
Oh, well.
The Apex Room.
All right. But I mean Jimmy Noone was working at -- working upstairs, and we were downstairs.
I see. In this club.
68 Randolph Street.
Right.
Uh-huh.
Well then -- so you started with Stuff there in Chicago.

Yeah, and we finished playing, and went to -- went from there to Hollywood, and to Billy Berg -- Troyville Billy Berg's Troyville Club, and we were in Hollywood, and we stayed there for -- hm, how many months? And -- because -- this drummer was there. I've got a picture of him, where we did a jam session, Buddy Rich and all that gang was -- came in there, and all the movie stars, everybody, anybody you could name. Benefit.
Working with Stuff, was the show mostly Stuff, or did the rest of you get a chance to do --
Oh, plenty. Oh sure, you play, and blow your brains -- you did blow your brains out, but believe me.
(Laughter.)
Why?

Well, that's the way he worked. You know, he got things going, you know (snap, snap, snap) and you stay right there (snaps) for about 40 choruses, because he'd take about 18 or 20 himself. All depends.
What was the difference between working for Stuff and working for Fats? They're both rather extroverted leaders, I think.

Well, this -- in a way, it wasn't too much different, because both were -- I was -- and my idea of a genius, both were, because were hard workers, they loved music, they knew what they were doing. And I used to get such a kick out of Stuff, because Stuff would be playing -- one, two, one two three four, dah, dum, dumdle, dum, deedle dee, baddle doodle deedle doodah, deedle deedle, you said it Stuff, go up to out there minor, and he would -- then on the next big -- next bar, bahdle, doodle deedle doodle dah, and come right out. I mean he was just a capable and able to do it, where a lot of guys would have to stop and think, now where
am I? He wanted me to go into a minor, now which minor? Where? I got -- now maybe this is a good place. No, this isn't too good.

I mean it takes you ten or twenty bars to go from here, to get in the minor, but Stuff would go in the minor key next best, see? I mean that's the capable -- capability. That's how capable he was, and how much he knew about music, and keys meant nothing. You know? He was just that doggone good.

And Fats could have done the same thing, but I never asked Fats to do that, but with Stuff, and he's blowing and patting his feet and playing, and I don't care what the tune is, it didn't mean nothing to him.
I see. What sort of person, aside from being a musician, what sort of person was Stuff?

Stuff -- well, like -- more like Fats Waller, and in the nature of being a square fellow, a good fellow. Man, he -- money meant nothing to Stuff. Meant nothing -- nothing to Fats. In other words, so they'd give it away. I mean you need it, take it. Go ahead, forget it. I mean you know. And he'd -- would forget that he had given it to you, as far as that goes.
In other words, I -- I liked that because I've seen quite a few people who give a blind man a nickle and go to the next corner and stand there and talk two hours about it.
I just mentioned -- I was just down the next street and I gave a man a whole nickle, to buy a steak dinner with. You know what -- you understand what I'm trying to say?
Right.
And it meant nothing, but Stuff -- would okay, take it. Go ahead. Meant nothing. And give it away. And you could have it, and when he say you got it, it's yours. He meant just that.

That's one thing I never could -- never could or did get straight about Stuff. Una Mae Carlisle, I think they were sweethearts once, and maybe they liked each other, or knew each other, and he told me that he wrote the tune 'Walking By the River' for her. And bah, bah, bah, bee -- remember that tune?
I remember that tune. Yeah.

And maybe he did, and maybe he didn't. And he told me, about -- hmmmmm, we played -- I played, -- I don't play, but all the bands I've played played it, he said he wrote that, which he could have, as far as that goes. I mean you know, he was capable of writing anything, because Stuff was a heck of a musician.
And back years ago when the snake was in the car he was playing banjo and guitar.
Oh, really?
Yeah.
: In addition to the violin?
Yeah, he was a banjoist before that.
: I see.
And then all this jazz --
: But he's -- my recollection is that he started out in carnivals too, just like you did.
Could be, yeah. Yeah, I heard him saying so. And by the way, he used to tell me that I looked like his father.
: Oh, really? (Laughs.) Well, you remind Fats of his brother, and you look like Stuff's father. Did you have a close relationship with Stuff? As you did with --
Very, very, very, when -- Moline, Illinois, you know where that is?
: Right.

You've heard of it. Well I was with -- there with Stuff, and we come out California and Chicago, and that business, and Stuff took ill. He was -- well, I would say that he was -- he lost his mind, or he was losing his mind, or -- I'm trying to think of a nicer way -- you know, I'm trying to think of a nice way to put it. Anyway, --
: Well I mean technically, do you know what was wrong with him at the time? Whether it's nice or
not.

No, no. What I mean is -- I don't like to be -- I had to call the authorities, and they came in the -- picked him up, put handcuffs on him, took him out, because it was about ten below zero, and he had stripped down to his trousers, and he's walking through the --
(Telephone.) [PAUSE ]
: Let's pick it up.

Yeah, we were in Moline, Illinois. I'm trying to think of the club we were working. And it was a very nice club, too. And I was there -- at that particular time Joe Glaser had booked us in there, and for business reasons Joe had turned everything over to me, and asked me to take charge of the business of collecting the money, paying the band off, including Stuff, and whatnot, because Stuff was such a generous (Laughs) -- he would give the money, my money, anybody else's money, because he was every night, give me a hundred, give me a hundred-fifty, give me two hundred, anyway.

We knew he'd keep that up, you know, and the next night he may say give me three hundred, two hundred, well when payday comes there's nothing left. You know. And he didn't realize it was accounted -- anyway, I had charge of the monies, and so Stuff -- I think that helped to make him feel worse, so -- and he -- one of the night -- that time he was drinking rum and Coke, and he would have quite, quite,
quite a few a night of rum and Cokes, you know?
Could he hold his liquor the way Fats could?

No, never know -- no, he couldn't, but he drank a heck of a lot. But, I had to give it to him, he didn't stagger and fall out and get sick. He just went out of his mind, I guess. I'm going to put it that way. You know? And sweets too, sweet stuff, rum and Coke, I couldn't drink it anyway, the thoughts of it made me sick.

Anyway, so he got -- he was walk -- coming down the street, popping his fingers (snap, snap) like he was listening to a jazz band, stripped down to his trousers, about ten below zero. Well you know that's the wrong way to be. (Laughs.) I think, and a girl was walking up the street, or down the street, whichever, and they ran into him, and he looked at her and said Hello, Baby, and kind of reached his arm out, his hand out to grab her, like he was going to brush her hair, or shoulder, something, and boy, she looked at him and saw him and she started screaming and running.

You may not like it, after you hear it, but he gives his all. I give a man that, you know.
Do you remember the recording date you did with Sam? How you got involved in it?
Hmm, well, no, yes and no. I've done several with him, and he's always called me for a date. You know.
Uh-huh. I see.
So I don't remember any particular
date, but he's called me, any time, you know?

Well, anyhow, now to get back to the period after World War II, and after Philadelphia, you gigged around, and what's the next thing that, as you recall, happened? Did you stay in New York for quite a long time, gigging? Was that the way it worked?

Yes. I mean you had to, because well one job, and I'd be out looking, and trying to find something else, and hoping it was soon, and something good. Because you've got bills to pay. You've got to make a living. You've got to earn a living, somehow, the best way you can.
I'm trying to -- I can't tie in any more dates. I wish --
I was wondering, did any of these jobs last very long? Were they all just --
No.
-- short things that you'd leave a few weeks, something like that, and go on to something else?

Short, yes, something, yes, something would happen, and then when you took a lot of those jobs, you would take, well you knew it wasn't going to last only a few days, and you hoped it wouldn't, because you already maybe you'd promised something -- had been promised something that's going to happen weeks, or month later, and you can't bet on it. You hope. You know, because if you could bet on it, the
guy would lay some money on you. Don't worry. Here's some money, and date -- on such and such a date we do this or we do that.
Well, that's -- how many people who's able to do that, any agents, I mean. How many booking -- booking agents, land leaders, land -- whatever -- band leaders, or whatever they are. You know?
Well were these financially hard times for you, Herman, compared to what you'd had, let's say, in the Fats days, and the days --
Oh heck yeah. Oh --
-- with -- so this -- after the war was a rough period for you, then.

Oh, yeah. It was a -- because you still have a family to protect, and they're going -- if they're nice enough to go along with you, you look back -- you've got them to thank, because they could have been gone. With somebody else. With -- they say well look, this guy can't pay the rent, he can't do the other. Come over home with me, Baby, and other women do it well, now (unintelligible) in all walks of life. You know. Whether it's a profession connected, or what. You know.
Still goes one. Movie stars, you know? This cat can't hold on, so he can't make it for what reason, any reason, split.
Did you feel pretty depressed at this
Yes. Yes, uh-huh. Uh-huh.
How did you come out?

Well, at intervals, at times, I'd come back and -- to my wife, and I'd look at her, and I'd tell her, I'd say well, thanks for what you're doing. Well what do you mean? I said well hanging on. She said well I'm supposed to hanging on. I married you, and that -- encouragement. That little bit is what's needed, right there. Something would come up, something would happen, where you could say well, okay, I'm still in there pitching, and she would -- (unintelligible). And the world, it will get better.

A good woman, a smart woman will -- has been known to do that. But on the other hand (laughs) it takes a -- look, mate, if you don't get straightened out, let's face it, forget it, you know. I mean and you've had it. I mean you know, and in a way you can't blame her. I can't. I mean let's face facts as they are.
But you've got -- you had this support.
I had that support, and I appreciate it very, very much.
Was part of your problem, in the years right after World War II, when be-bop was big, was it the style of jazz was changing to something that you hadn't
Yes. Yeah, that's right.
Did this affect you?

Yes it did. It did. It affected everybody, because when you play jazz, jazz like I am, and like I have been for many years on that, and you bring your records home, and your music, and your own family, your children, say (Bronx cheer) pop, that's old. You know. That way -- they don't play that anymore. I mean let's get the so and so and so and so.

And you'd look, and say well, this is it. I've had it. Because you can't tell them that they're wrong. You try, and they're not wrong, because that's what they think and think they like, like. That's what they're like. And then (unintelligible).
But they're also wrong too, aren't they?

Yeah, wrong, yes. So one day you keep hoping maybe a little longer and they will see, say man, this is it! Too many times, oh, well that's one, and in Europe with Red Richards. We were in -- ah, Amsterdam. Amsterdam? Germany? Yeah -- huh?
Amsterdam, Holland.
No, not Holland. No, Germany. Uh, (taps) damn -- dam, it's --
Let's see, Amsterdam, Rotterdam --

No, no. No, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no. We had a heck of a thing there, though. It's a big thing. It was jumping, and had two bands in there, and it's a big place, and they're doing -- yeah, yang, yang, yang-yang-yang, yang -- oh man! You know. God doggy!
This was some place in Germany.
Oh, big city. Uh -- my wife's -- the band -- one of the boss's -- his wife, she worked there, so that's where he was from. Anyway, I was -- it'll come to me in a minute.

We were playing there, and where the waitresses had cleared the place, it was so dark you couldn't see what in the heck you were doing. Man! That was the God damndest joint! On the way back I was going back to the dressing room, put my horn down, hang my coat up, or put it down, or something. I passed couples in the corners, in booths, and whatnot, and they were making it! I mean everything was happening! Nobody -- shoot, they paid me no mind.

And when the curtain -- when the lights would go on I never saw so many pretty looking gals and nice looking boys in all my life. They were beautiful. So the other band started, and we started playing, and the kids come up and they say who are you? Where did they come from? This is something new. They'd never -- they had never heard of anything like what -- Oh, and they came up, and they put their arms around
us on the bandstand, they kiss us, and holding, and dancing with us.
So the manager came up. He said will you sign a contract right now? He said I'd like to bring you back in six weeks, so many weeks. And we signed a contract, and the money was fabulous.
That's great.

Well then, we never heard anything -- you're new! What do you call this? What is this called? And they'd say you know, I played, bang! bang-a-bang! So loud you couldn't hear your ear lobes, and falling out and everything, and we start playing tunes, and -- enh (snap), buts (snap), buts (snap), bits (snap) bah, oh beeble deeble deeble, doo, you know. And they were out there dancing, and they -- you know, best they could, because they didn't know about any what you call it, way you used to dance here.
Lindy hop?

Lindy Hop. They didn't know nothing about that. I mean once in a while -- once, you'd look, you see a person who has seen or heard of a little of it, and they were -- well watch and see what this guy's doing, and they began to feel it, and they wanted to get with it, and they have to, they find out they have to. And that was it!
Tell me this, Herman, when, how old were your children when they began to enjoy what you were
doing, when they didn't feel it was old-fashioned, or something?

Well, one of my grandsons told me, he's what, twelve, thirteen, now, and I'm not sure but what he still has found a -- and I gave him a trumpet, and I haven't seen Tony to talk to him in so doggone long, other than the telephone, because I've been in and out of the hospital, and they're down in Maryland, and he's a karate expert. He has a -- he has a -- what do you call it? --
Chop?
Yeah, I mean when you get the --
Black belt.
-- belt, yeah. He's -- twelve or thirteen, he has it, heck yeah, one of those belts. He's got it.
(Laughter.)
He's damned good, as a kid. So -- but --
How about your own -- how many children do you have?
Well, I've got -- let's see --
You have a daughter.
-- I've got two from this daughter, and three from another daughter, and I've got six from another daughter.
You've got three daughters of your own.
Yeah.
Now, you're -- your own children, not your grandchildren, but your own children, did they think what you played was old-fashioned?
Uh -- well --
What -- I'm getting back to that be-bop period.
Well I -- well I mean -- well, well, '30, early thirties, my daughter went to -- they -- this was nice, but I mean, you know.
(Laughter.)
You know. You know.
They're being nice to you.

Yeah, I think so. They didn't -- they wasn't too bowled over. Well Dad, I mean after all, you know. It's nice. But none of them have really -- they use the word [crossed out], they thought that I was terrific. Going along with the magazines. Oh, any jazz magazine they say I'm terrific. But not my kids, and I'm sure they've seen the magazine, they're around the house, other places, for them to see, if they wanted to have. You know?

But in any event, so after -- after you came back to New York from Philadelphia you were faced with this prospect that there was another kind of jazz that was getting a lot more attention than what you had been play-
ing, and was -- Yeah, yeah.
How long did -- how long did that go on affecting you, and affecting --
Affecting me?
Yeah.
Well, oh --
As far as jobs were concerned, and where you -- how much you could work?
Well up until now it still does.
It still does.
But a lot of the people have been able to shake it.
Yeah. Because I think, as you are talking about these kids over in Germany that the attitudes are changing, they're rediscovering the kind of thing that you've been doing all you-life.
Yes. Yeah, yeah. I've got it there, why can't I think what it is? So and so ham --
Hamburg?
Hamburg, Germany.
Hamburg, Germany. That was the town?
That's just where it was, because I brought -- I've got a good friend of mine, I brought him some cigars to his home. I brought him cigars, some cigars back,

you know, from Hamburg. And that's a big place, and man, it was jumping, oh! It was jumping. It was terrific. And the meantime, my daughters -- my daughter was there with her husband, who's general -- not general, uh, uh, he was a major, and then what's the next after major? Colonel.
Colonel. Right.
He's a colonel now. He's over in the -- where all that mess is going on now, got -- God I hope he gets back safely.
Vietnam. That's theoretically over now. Is that what you mean?
Yeah, but I hope he gets back here.
Well, they're supposed to be all out by now.

Yeah, well I hope so. And he was there, in Hamburg, with my daughter, and two children. And we had a ball. We met, I was doing (unintelligible) a concert over there, and they came over, and we got together, saw each other, and whatnot.
But as I was telling you, that too is -- well it wasn't -- it was a little on the -- between, you know, on both sides. The guys with all that hair and stuff on their face, and they were playing --
It's a whole new world.
Yeah, you know.
I have a note here, Herman. It says in the late 1940's you spent a lot of time in Canada, and had your own group in Canada. Is that right?
No.
No?
No, not in Canada. No. I was there with the Saints and Sinners in Canada.

Well this is -- no, we're talking about the forties. Not the sixties. Right after World War II. I'm trying to get that part sort of straightened out. You came back from Philadelphia. You gigged around New York for a while. This was the be-bop period. Things were kind of tough, as you say. And what happened -- let's get into the 1950's. Do you relate anything to the 1950's?
Well, yes, that's when I got hurt, got the automobile accident.
That was --
I had a trio.
Ah, that was the year 1950, wasn't it?
Aaahhh! Oh Canada! You're right.
Right. Right. Okay --
You are right.
Now.
You're right.
Now, relate to that, now, had you been in Canada when you had the accident?
It happened on my -- on my way back. I had been there before.
Okay, well now let's talk about how you got to Canada that time, before you came back.
Right. Well --
What were you doing in Canada before the accident?
Well we hadn't been before '49, or [PltHsburg]? something like that, we'd been up to Phillipsburg. That's about 55 or 60 miles, on this side of -- uh, Montreal.
South of Montreal.
South of Montreal, near -- near -- uh, uh, uh, state of -- near Vermont.
Vermont, toward the -- oh yes. Down toward Vermont.
Yeah.
When you say we, who's we? In this case.
Well I had a trio. I had a piano player. He was driving when I got hurt, broke my hip.
How did you happen to have a job in Phillipsburg, Canada?
Well, it was one of those things when --
that's -- other depression had person would start there, there's no jobs, and nothing for a guy to do, so you had to go out and grab anything you could grab to try to survive!
So -- excuse me.
I was going to say, were you gigging around Canada with this trio, or did you have --
No, no. We worked in a hotel, hotel.
Oh.
And they were paying you -- oh, a lousy 50 or $60.00 a week, and with room and board. So --
How long did you stay at the hotel?
Oh, a year and something, maybe a little more, in there.
A long -- a long --
Yeah, uh-huh. Yeah. So I would stay there and play, and what money -- cash money I got I sent it back here for my wife. To pay bills, with
Who did you have in the trio?
Wilkins was his first name.
Was he the drummer, or --
The piano. He was -- it was his car that we was riding in when we left the highway, turned over and over and over, and when we finished I was wrapped around the steering wheel, and broke my hip.
I'm sure this is not something you
want to relive too much, Herman, but how did the whole thing happen? Why were you coming back to the States at this point?
No, we had left the States, and going back to the job.
Oh, oh. You had --
Yeah, we were going back. Yeah, I didn't want to go --
You had left the job, and you were going back to it.
Yeah.
I see.

I didn't want to go. We were on -- had been home on leave, and -- and (unintelligible) just to take the -- we'd been off of the job, and I told them I wasn't sure -- I didn't want to go back, and it's a matter of running out on the guys. He said well, come on back until we can get somebody, and so we can -- the drummer, and I, want to make it. I mean the drummer and the piano player say we'll make it, and you know, come on back until I grab -- get somebody.

I said well, okay. I don't want to leave them hanging, you know. You don't walk away and leave a guy when he needs you. So we'd been riding all day, and a big Lincoln car, and we got about 30 miles of our destination. That's when it happened. The lights went out on the car, and we

left the highway, and went over, and then back, and then missed a hole about 20 feet deep with water in it. Turned over and over and over. I don't know how many times, and [ ] came and said he was only doing 35 miles an hour, and I was in the hospital seven months with a broken hip, and I'm still suffering with it, and I've got to go back in the hospital maybe next week and let them take the pin out that they put in there, which has -- was broke about a year ago.
And I've got to go back in the hospital now and let them take it --
Do you know why he went off the road?
Uh -- because the lights went out on the dash.
Just the lights went out? I mean he just went right out, huh?
Yeah, when the lights -- it was about 6:00 o'clock in the evening, and snow had just started falling.
Oh, snow, too.
Yeah, and --
Oh, I see.
Yeah, and the lights went out on the dashboard, and you can't see where you're driving, and they had very thin -- not -- rather narrow highway with the saddleback, what you call the saddleback road?
Oh yeah, the hump, and --

Yeah, and one car go this way, and another one car comes out, and you know. And we knew, hadn't been traveling the highway, what I say, two or three years, that we knew it. But when it's dark, it's dark, and who knows? The man -- now, the man wasn't drinking -- we'll we'd stopped for about 15 minutes, maybe, and I knew the people who owned the club, and we had a drink. I had one drink -- that's -- and he had one. And we were rushing because we only had 30 miles to go, and it was about dinner time.

We wanted to get in and have a dinner before going to bed, so my friend in this club says stay here, Herman. I'll -- we'll have dinner here, and I'll drive you over there. I said Naah, I'm just going -- you know, riding all day, you know.
Oh boy. Yeah.

Been riding all day, I might as well go on in, so had I stayed there with him I'd have been better off, you know. And on the way out the lights went off again, because I was sitting there. Had my leg folded just like that, kind of crossed, and and then I'd doze off, maybe, you know. I had a couple of drinks, or one drink. I'd been riding all day.
And I heard him say 'look out. This is it. I can't
hold -- his eyes -- well I said to him 'you can do it. You can hold it. Hold it! Hold it!' And we went into this thing.
Now, I was knocked out, because something hit my chin, and the steering wheel was all bent because the gear shift, I think, I think I hit that with my hip.
You were sitting in the front.

Sitting in the front, beside the driver. I hit that, broke my femur, and he was thrown out, or got out. I don't know which. But when I knew anything I heard voices saying Is he dead? Is he dead? And I came to, and I said please help me, or something. They reached down, and I said Don't touch that hip! Don't touch my leg!
Were you on the ground when you came --
No, no, no, no. No. This left leg was wrapped around the steering post, with the left foot, toe of the foot, looking back at me.
Still in the car.
Still in the car.
When you came to.

And this foot, toe, was looking back at me, wrapped around the steering post. So they reached down there somehow and got me out -- and weighing 240 pounds, that's a lot of weight to lift, dead weight, to lift up with a car laying on the side.
Yeah. Was there an ambulance there?
Not yet.
Not yet.
They got me out, and they laid me down in the field.
Who were these people? Were these just nearby people who --

No, people, nearby farmers, and -- that we knew. And they heard this noise, becuase they were eating supper, they said, and came out, and say oh, my God! How is -- is he dead? And I looked, and I said oh, don't the stars look pretty? I heard somebody saying, gee, what a man! In other words, I was glad to be out of the car. I'll tell you why, because when this thing happened, we'd been riding all day in a big Lincoln. I was afraid this thing would catch fire, and me being pinned in there, I was turned behind -- around the wheel, wedged in the seat and the dashboard. I couldn't move. I was wedged. So I had to be lifted out. I said if this thing catch fire, God forbid, I don't know -- I'm gone. You know. So I said please get me out. Please get me out. That's why. So I didn't know until later the guy had turned the key to turn off the motor. This thing is hotter than hell. It was really hot. And he had turned the key. Turned off the ignition, which I guess helped, because the boom! I can imagine.
: That was a piece of fast thinking.
Yeah, uh-huh. So he's outside --
Huh?
: What happened to him?
He had a bump over his eye. They put some iodine on it, sent him home. Kept me seven months.
: Was the drummer with you?

No, just the two. Piano player and I. The drummer went home to Pittsburgh to see his mother, and visit with her a couple of days, and then he was coming -- he came on alone, caught a train and came on alone.
: What was the drummer's name?
Roscoe Thurston.
: Roscoe Thurston.
Uh-huh.
: And piano was Wilkins.
Yeah.
: And you were in the hospital for seven months.
Seven months.
: And when --
That was Saint, Albans, Vermont.
: Saint.Albans, oh, back in the United States.
Yeah.
Was that the closest hospital? Is that where --
Yeah, that's where it happened, right outside of S[scribble], Albans. But --
You weren't into Canada yet.
No, no. We was on our way. Uh-huh.
I see. Well, when you came out of the hospital, Herman, how long was it before you could work?

Well, when I came out of the hospital I went back to Canada, which is just across the border about seven miles, on route seven, seven miles? More than that. I'm thinking about route seven. But -- okay, 18, 20 miles, maybe from -- maybe, or 30 miles. Anyway, which is nothing in a car. And I went over there and went to work. Now they had to take me --
Went to work where, in Phillipsburg?
Back at the hotel, yeah. That's where I was on my way.

Well -- now this was not like the thing you were telling me before, about the Neverly, where you were in the hospital for a month, and you don't have a job any more, but this -- you were here seven months in the hospital, and you go back, and you've still got a --
Yeh, well the drummer and the piano player were still working there. Who else was -- who was my
replacement? I think it was a tenor saxophone player, I think, as far as horn. It was only a trio.
Uh-huh, but you did get the job back.

Oh yeah, well they kept working, and they would come to see me, and all the people around there, it was like a home thing. Once you meet those people they -- they will love you for life, and they're -- and it was so nice being there, because they would cook pies, and cakes .
Really?
Yeah, different -- little kids come up and say, Mr. Herman? I'd say what? My aunt sent this over. She thought you'd like it. like it! You know, and that --
How did these people know you so well?

Well, because I worked at the hotel, and they came in on weekends, or whatnot, to dance, for different reasons, and they met me, and they liked -- liked my playing, and a lot of them had heard that I'd been with Fats, and whatnot, and this that and the other, and at that time Montreal -- uh, radio, had it, and they would record -- I mean thing every day --
Broadcast?

Yeah, broadcast it every day that Herman Autrey's here, and he did this, and here's some records he made, and this that and the other, and then a lot of people who didn't know me before would know me now.
I see.

You know. And they came down, and that's how they know, and then they started -- and then they heard about me writing a gun, or write this, or write that, blah, blah, blah, they became very much interested, and they would come in with a cake, pie, this, can I do anything for You? Anything, and they'd bring cigarettes. You know. And I would -- I became -- to know you know, I knew a heck of a lot of people.

Had you -- in your career as a musician had you ever run into this kind of friendly neighborliness before? Mostly, when you were working in clubs or hotels or something, I would think a kind of impersonal relationship. They'd come in. They know you there, but they don't know yououtside the club. Is it different here?

Well yes. Well yes and no, because I think that's an individual thing, because you meet people, and once you meet them, and they know you, then they'll come and invite you to their homes. I find you different, or you seem to be nice to know. Would you like to, or would you do us an honor to come to my home and meet my family. I think in -- it makes a gentleman, to meet my wife and daughters, and kids, or whatnot.
Wife, meet my -- you know, one of those things, come out to dinner one day, and then you go and you do that, and
this goes on. This goes on for years.
: I see.

Because once they know you, and you know them, they would introduce you to other very close friends of theirs, and it becomes a natural thing. You know. And it's doggone nice for a person, people come up, which I've met years ago, even before I met Fats, they come up to me and say well look, the next time you come this way remember, this is home. There will be a room waiting for you. And should you offer them pay for that, you would insult them.

You say you're one of us, so drop a card and let us know when you're coming this way, and your room will be ready. Oh, I know so many places where I could have done that, or I mean often has to do that. You know? Throughout years. And I think that's a heck of a thing.
: Did you usually --
Including Switzerland, by golly.
(Laughter.)
Right. I was talking about that. Did you often take up these offers and spend the --
Well, all --
: How did you feel about it?
Well you know, I mean you don't want to do that. I mean you come up, and you drop a card, or something, when they come -- what happened? Why didn't you

write us? Or why didn't you call? I say well, didn't you get my card? You know. You -- use the best bluff you can, oh, I didn't want to do it because I don't want to put you out. So now we're not going to take no for an answer. We will be insulted if you don't come out Sunday, one of those things. And oh, you just have to do it.
You have to drop all other commitments that you made, and you know.
So this was the -- this was the kind of atmosphere that you had in the Canadian-Vermont area.
Well, Canadian-Vermont area, and a lot of American --
Well, but I mean in a specific thing where you go in a hospital and people come to see you.
Oh, they -- oh, they were terrific. Those Canadians, I mean when you're going, and you come up, they say well you promised last time, remember? Remember?
(Laughter.)

Oh, man! And I've had people to get mad at me. Okay, we don't have a new car like such and such, but we doing-- I think we -- I says it's not a matter of that. So you have to trade -- get out of it the best way you can. You know?
Right. Right. When you went back to work at the hotel, Herman, after you'd been in the hospital
Very bad, because they had to take me in a chair. I was sitting in a chair. And they would move me from here in the other room, you know, which was huge.
You couldn't walk.
No. No. And they'd take me, put me up on the stand. Once I was sitting in a chair I could play. Only anybody come up wouldn't know what was happening in this, unless they saw me try to get off.
Now, when I come out (Unintelligible) get me and get me on top of the steps, and my room wasn't too far from there, because it was a hotel room upstairs. And -- and that's the way it went.
I see. With the pin in your leg -- this is -- we're talking about your left leg.
Yes.
Did this leave your left leg shorter than your right leg?
Yes, it's about two inches or more shorter.
What happened to those two inches? Where did they go?
Well, as you can see - see it? see the difference?
Yeah, the knee, the knee comes up
differently.

Yeah, it does that, so I asked my doctor when it happened, was it going to be shorter. He said there was no reason why it should be, because it didn't take out any of the bone. But I found out later from the different people, that usually happens. For some reason the injured leg draws up, and that's why I have to wear a built up shoe, for two inches and something, on that left side. I have my shoes built up. The sole is built up.
Now I'll get up. You see it?
Oh yeah, uh-huh.

So I got to go in there, look, there's a pin there, right in the bridge, in the femur. They got to take it out, and put another one in, or whatever the hell they're going to do, and which I did not want, but I'm in trouble. I'm in pain, most of the time, especially when I'm walking, you know?
So you've gotta do it.
Yeah (inaudible). But this pin, which broke, what, a year ago?
Yeah.
Was -- and that would be 1974, was -- had been in since 1950. So it had been there for 24 years.
Yeah. Uh-huh.
Did you have trouble after you got to the point where you started walking again, was it difficult
learning to walk? With the difference in your leg?
Yes, very, very. With the difference in your leg, and used to moving, you know, being a guy who's act --
You were a fast man.

Oh, yeah. Fact, fast as I am -- I used to try to bos a little bit, and you find out you're not able to do those thing because you can't move like you -- once, like you want to, and fast enough, and what happens, you -- you make yourself almost ill because you get mad at yourself because you can't do what you want to do.

And should be doing. You know what you should be doing, but you can't do it. So now it's a matter of accepting that you've got a -- once you accept it, and people call up, all right, Dad, all right, Pops, all right, Grandy, you know, what they mean, and then you figure -- you say well gee, I'm being honored. They're very nice.
You know, once you accept that, then that begins to you look at the guy who's saying that, and he's old -- your old -- he's older than you. Yeah, you know, I mean well, you say okay. Well.
Did you get adjusted finally? I mean to a point that it didn't bother you, although I would assume that it -- just physically it was a problem moving around, wasn't it?
Well that --
Up and down on stands, and things like that?

That, and you you had to get adjusted to, because a lot of jobs I could get on, even now. They'd say well, would you need a high chair? Would you need a chair? Can we get you anything? Can we get you a -- I say no. Yes.
Don't make any difference --
No favors.

No favors. No. Don't make any difference. Say well, Mr. Autrey, we would pay you this, but after all, you such and such and such and such, I said want you to know I'm selling my horn. In fact, in the last few years a lot of the authorities, guys say well Herman, my playing has been much better, and has been in so many years, and they say that the critics, say I'm still right now, age and whatnot, better than this one or that one, or so and so and so and so.
Because in -- in my lipping of the horn.
And I've been able to play this, and play that, and do a lot of things that so far other guys have not been able to do, which I'm glad that I'm still being accepted, and able to play. You know.

Did you find that because once you were walking, but you walked with a limp, insofar, just as getting jobs were concerned, was there any kind of prejudice against you, do you feel, because of that? Even though, obviously, that has nothing to do with your playing.
Well -- I'm trying to think. Vaguely I want to say -- I want to say yes, because it's all -- my disability there, I mean not being able to do this, or they had a little doubt, maybe.
A doubt. Yes, this is what I'm wondering.
Yeah, yeah, yeah. And they come up, well can we get you this? Don't you need that? Don't you need the other? And I say well no. The hell with it. No, I'm okay.
You want to be accepted as --
Yes. I didn't want -- I don't want people to say oh get him -- put a bed down for Pops, you know. And drink this, and because he's -- after all, he has a bad
leg. I say man, never mind the damn leg. Just blow. And I've been able to blow out -- blow out many, God damn it, I play --
(Laughter.)
How long after you got out of the hospital, Herman, were you able to walk around again?

Well, when I got out of the hospital. Well, I go back -- to put it this way, while I was in the hospital I had my horn, and I used to lay, and sit up in bed and play, play my horn. And thank -- why I'm laughing, I used to play loud enough for the lady down in the kitchen, what do you call her? Huh?
Dietician?
I used to play so she -- yeah. She liked 'Mockingbird', so I used to rah dah doo dee dah, and she send me some icecream.
(Laughter.)
That was a signal,

So that was -- yeahhhh. So every time I wanted something I'd play where she could hear, and she'd come up, thank you for playing that tune, and then she'd send me up a big plate of icecream. Anything else you want? I say no, everything's fine. Thank you very much.
So I did -- (laughs) -- you know. These tricks you learn, now, through the years, you know?
Yes, but also we -- you were keeping your chops in shape.
Keeping my chops in shape. And then I knew the things she liked. I knew what the hell -- I knew what I was doing. (Laughs.)

Oh, no. I've been very lucky all my life, with chops. I mean problem, chops problem. I mean while other guys can't do this, or can't do that, I've been able to well, in a few minutes, or a couple of days, to get myself together. In other words, chopwise. And do some very good playing. I mean what they call being -- I've heard natural chops?
Have you?

Embouchure? Perfect embouchure, or this that and the other. And I've been very lucky that way. Very. But I don't rely on it, because after the guys say Herman, come on down old play. Naw, man. I haven't touched my horn in days. Aaah, you know you, you don't need that. I say ah, I'm not going to bank on it, you know.
So far I haven't had to bank on it, so I'm going there, you know, scared to death, and the thing just went beautiful, went well, you know?
Great. When you went back to Phillipsburg, after the hospital, you played in the wheelchair, how
much longer did you stay in Phillipsburg?
Ah, hah, hah, hah, how many months?
Quite a while, then.
Yeah. I'm trying to think now. And I got -- I'm trying to think when I come home what was happening.
Well, let's work it this way. Why did you leave Phillipsburg?

That's what I'm -- that's what I'm trying to get to now. Had things closed? Or what did I get out of there and come home? Because of what? Eh, I can remember, I mean I can't seem to think too interesting. You know, it wasn't simply because -- I don't know if it was business, or --
Things just weren't working out.
Yeah, and --
So then you came back to New York.
Yeah, came back home, uh-huh.

Came back here. Now, you're back in New York, and we're into what? We're into the 1950's, and we're back in sort of the same situation you were into several years before, the potential of gigging around, but also the kind of jazz you were playing was no longer just the only kind of jazz around. There were very --
No, I start going to -- yeah, you're
right. Because they started going into rock stuff, and that kind of --
That -- you're now into almost the rock period. Did you -- did -- having been away for so long, from New York, did you have trouble getting gigs?
Yes, because once you lose contact, you know --
Yeah, it's rough.

Because a guy'd come up to you and say Hey, Herman, what are you doing tonight? You know, when they get so they can't do that. You call up one, say oh, he's out of town. You (smack) -- next time something comes up he says well this guy's -- somebody told me he's out of town. I'll call somebody I know's in town, because I don't have time to waste, you know, checking on -- I'd like to have him, but I don't have the time to be -- you know.

So now was this -- was this period, then, a worse period for you than right after the war when you came back from Philadelphia? That you said was a bad period. But now you've been away, and the situation has changed a bit.

I would say -- well I would say it was worse. I'll tell you why, why I say that. Because the trends -- the changing trend from jazz to rock, and you don't have as many jobs of jazz as we had before, becuase people
are doing one thing or the other, and if you don't have a banjo and some [Tin Pan] (unintelligible) Bang-a-ding-a-ding-a-bang -- you don't work, and you don't eat. You know.

And I was doing it, so you don't go into that, so you don't -- those guys, you turn around and read a paper, and hear where this guy's making thousands, and you're not make $15.00 a week. You know what I mean? There's your answer, you know?
How did you survive during those years?

I don't know. I don't know. It depends on your wife, and pick up a few dollars here, a few dollars there, and maybe you're lucky to get a one night here, a one night there, and we do get it, and put it to good use. You know, trying to fill up all the holes you possibly can. Because -- and then should your wife get laid off from her job, well -- which did happen, it all depends on the type work one has.
What was she doing?
Well, she's been an operator on the same job for twenty -- around 27 years.
An operator on what?
Pocketbooks and change purses.
Pocketbooks and change purses?
Yeah, about 27 years. Same company.
And she hasn't been laid off, or has she --
Oh, she -- no, oh, she's been laid off.
But she goes back.
Been just like now, she has to take off because of an automobile accident.
Yes, but I mean --
But in the meantime, lots of time they lay her off, and they -- according to -- what do you call it?
Seniority.
Yes. Seniority. Yeah.
Were there periods during the 1950's when you weren't working and she wasn't working?
Plenty of times. Plenty of times. Sure.
How do you -- how did you come through those times?

Well, you just have to hold on while you're at it. Especially when you live in -- where I lived -- and I told you, I lived in the for my other job for 34 years. Well, that was lower rent, because we moved in there so long ago you didn't have to pay a hell of a lot of money. But --
Rent control?

Yeah, it was 34 years, I mean that's still more -- that's a hell of a lot when you don't have it. Ten dollars is a hell of a lot if you don't have it. You see, by the time you're going to find it, and get it up, so I was thinking -- the thing that makes you stay where you don't want to stay, rats, roaches, water running in on you, ceiling falling, all the worst that a person, a human being could go through, you're stuck with it, and you're ashamed of it. You're ashamed of yourself. You're ashamed of being a man, because you can't do better for your family.
And oh man, it's the worst, you know. When you get a chance to get out and around you say well, thank God, and there you go. You know?
When did things begin to get better?
What year? Let me see --
Yeah, or what incident happened to --
I don't know. I'm trying to think, truthfully. Well, --
There was a kind of a revival of interest in the earlier forms of jazz. It began to happen -- certainly in the sixties. And I don't know if there was any in the fifties or not, that picked you up.
I don't know. I would say maybe my trip to Europe, my two trips, my --
With Red.
-- two trips with Red Richards, yeah.
: That sort of --

And we came back, and things began to move, began to work, and Red seemed to -- we got a lot of work here, Jersey, and New York, upstate New York. Here and there and around. You know. And I think -- I think that helps.

Yeah, uh-huh.
: Well we're coming -- we're coming, Herman, to the end of this reel.
Okay.

All right.

Uh-huh. Okay.

Okay, thanks a lot.
: Uh, now, let's see. I've got to go now. But for the next time -- now where are we now? Thursday. How is Monday of next week?
All right.
Is that okay with you?
Yeah, so far.--

Yeah, so far I don't know anything --
Okay. You know, one thing I've got to give you is my phone number --
Oh, please! Thank you.

Well all right, I'll write it -- thank you. I'll write it down here. I have plenty of junk I can write it on, (unintelligible).
Tear this off and give it to you. I'll give you my home phone, because that's where I normally am.
All right.

Oh, all right. I'm glad we -- I've been trying every day -- my wife say did you ask? Did you ask? Would you like to stay for dinner?
Herman, thank you very much, I appreciate it, but the reason I have to go --

The reason I have to go is because I've got to get downtown and do a couple of things that are trying to tape a radio show, and meet a guy for dinner, so -- (laughs.) But thank you very much. Some time I hope we'll be able to do it.
Well, we got to -- we've got to -- even if it's after we start on the book, or something. We've got -- we'll get together, okay?
Okay.
And you -- I want you to know you're welcome.
Well thank you. (Laughs.)
You're a cagy sort of guy, and you can ask me. Ask me, or tell me, well I'm staying for dinner. (Laughs.)
Thank you very much.
You know me, so I want you to know just how much you're welcome.

Oh, you did it before Jonah.
I think so. I've been accused of it. Before -- I told you about the mute with Fats, remember? (Waller?)
Yeah, uh-huh.
And with Dyer Jones.
Uh-huh, right, yeah, yeah.
And with the show, in fact before Fats I was using the mute, you know, when I first met Dolly, and Dyer Jones, and all that business with the shows, and the carnivals, and all that stuff.

Well, before that -- I'm kind of proud of that idea, of that guy saying Herman Autrey, used a mute like Herman? Well, a few things happened in my life, concerning the mute. When I was working with Charlie Johnson's band at the -- 53rd and Broadway there, the Arcadia Ballroom.

That was -- well, I started to say, a hard place to play in -- excuse me. It was hard to play in because they did not want you to blast and hurt the people's ears, but you know, that was -- with all these mirrors turning around the ballroom there, you know, the notes would bounce off, and then kill you. So I was one of the new guys that Charlie hired, and I went in to -- in the -- tried to do -- said well come up, we'll give you a try out, and see how you sound, so I'll never forget it. Yeah, open horn off and on, you know. And (unintelligible) and in those days the arrangements called for straight -- well, the parts were marked, straight mute, harmony mute, cupped mute, they had to have -- and derby hat, you know. No I had my mutes (Inaudible) because I was -- this is after -- well, this is much after Fats. I mean I had been established, because I'm noted for my mute, you know? And I like it. I like the mute. I like the -- I like that crisp and stinging sound, you know, effect that the mute can give with me a mute.

About two years?
Yeah, two, and two anyway, I would say.
Did the groups that you took into the Embers play with you anyplace else? Or was it just a one-shot thing with whoever you took in?

Well, possibly sometimes you would run -- you would have -- you'd get tied into something else, but just in for the Embers, or should, you have a few other dates, a couple of other dates, to hang on there, you told the guys well, when we finish here we're going into such and such a place. Can you, or will you, go in there with me? One of those things, you know?

With the group? No, No, I didn't take a group into Toronto, of my own. I did not.

No, I played -- no, I didn't take any
groups into Cleveland, but I went in there with Red, oh my God, dozens of times, I guess.

Piano?

Oh, oh.

Naw, I did a couple -- (laughs). Only did a couple of things with Lester Lanin, but man, this will kill you. I told him to bite me all over. I told him -- I don't know what the hell I didn't tell him, you know what I mean. I said you note playing son of a bitch, I called -- you know. Red Allen? Red Richards?

Yeah, yeah.

Well he called that Red Garter, I think
