Yeah, uh-huh.
Well let's get to -- how did you start working with Red? You were working with him, you said, with Frank Carey.
Yeah, that was one night here, doing other different -- one night, you know, what we call club dates.
How did the Saints and Sinners get started?

Well he had the Saints and Sinners. He was -- they were working out in Ohio, Columbus, Ohio, by the way. Lou [Pozey], I don't know if you've heard of him. He was -- he founded the -- Red and his group, and got them together, gave them and the name. He was booking them.
Who? Oh, he was a booker? Lou [Pozey]?
Yeah, uh-huh. And he was very much liked by the people who knew him, and -- well I met him slightly on the very end, and he passed later.
Oh, I see.

And they worked Columbus, Ohio, Cleveland, Detroit, and I'm trying -- I think yes, they worked Chicago. And they had a good band. Vic Dickenson, and Red, and _____ was on drum. They -- I wasn't there then.
Who was on trumpet before you were there?
Hm, hm-hm-hm, white fellow (Snaps fingers.)
Wild Bill was in the group for a --
Wild Bill, yeah.
Was that before, or after, you?

No, that's before, because -- but Wild -- he worked with Wild Bill -- Red Richards worked with Wild Bill's band a hell of a long time. Yeah. And Muggsy. Yeah. He worked with that band for a heck of a long time. And also -- I'm trying to think, who was this guy? He went to California, and I never did -- I heard of him. I never met him. And --
This is the white trumpet player?
Yeah. Joe Barifaldi was playing tenor with him. Because I met Joe, and Joe's a very good man, tenor
2nd clarinet.
Was the trumpet player Dick Carey?
I know Dick. I think Dick might have worked with them on a few things, maybe. I know -- I knew Dick very well. Dick played piano and trumpet.
Yeah, I know.
Yeah, uh-huh.
And played peckhorn, too, didn't he?
Yeah.
Everything.
And I tell you, he and I worked together with Eddie -- Eddie Condon.--
Eddie Condon.
-- on quite a few things. And I'm fun with fond of Eddie. I worked with him for years, in and out there.
Well then when you joined the Saints and Sinners it had been going for quite a while.

Yeah, they had been going, and they'd been to the coast, and back, because I heard Red talking -- had Red Vic Dick talking about it, you know. And oh, they were in -- he -- well he sounded -- he asked me to come with them about a year -- almost a year, maybe it was a year, doggone close, asked me to go with them, and I couldn't make it, because I had pneumonia. See what I mean?
Oh, when was this, Herman, that he
Um, thirty what? Thirty -- thirty --
Sixty.
Well did you actually join him in '64? Is that right?
Mary, when did I go with the Saints?

Uh-huh, and he called me. He had Joe -- Joe Thomas, Joe Thomas was on -- was there with him, and had been -- Joe -- well Joe is Joe, you know. He's a hell of a trumpet player. He -- you've got to give it to him. He's -- well, when he has too many tastes, you know, he's another guy, and I think that's what had happened.
And he called me and asked me, are you coming to make it. And -- well I -- at that time I had -- since I'd been home, I hadn't been on the road since I had this broken hip.
I see, and that was in 1950.

Yeah, I -- so I hadn't been back on the road. I did a few jobs around the city here, you know. A few things. And I was afraid -- truthfully, I was afraid to accept anything, and going on the road, I figured I
wouldn't be able to do it.
Tell me, at that point, Herman, did you have trouble getting around?
Well --
How -- were you walking with a cane?
Oh yeah! Man, I was walking as good just like as right now.
You had the built-up shoe?
Yeah.
And a cane?

Uh-huh. So he said come on -- can you get out? I said well, it's too late to get a plane. I said to heck with the plane, man. So I took a bus that morning, here, and I got there around 5:00 o'clock, about 5:00 o'clock. And they didn't hit til 8:00, so they gave me plenty of time.
Where is this, in Columbus?
No, no. Pittsburgh.
Oh, Pittsburgh. I see.

And the station's right down the street from the hotel, you know. It was nothing. So I got in and I went on the stand, and I really did feel nervous, though, because I said I haven't played, really, had -- where -- a place where I had to really cook, in a long time. I said well what the hell. And the money was nice.
(Laughter.)
So I just -- I got to do it. So we got on the stand, and everything went down, first night, second night. The third night I was boss.
(Laughter.)

Yeah! I called the wife, she said how is it? I said fine! Don't worry about it. So I stayed with them then, damn near ten years. And he took me out, and by God, have it here, got a lot of magazines and pictures and stuff here with the band.
When you -- before you go ahead, Herman, with your leg, and everything, how was it when you -- if you had to stand up all night? Were you standing up, or sitting?
Yes, we used to stand.
Did it get tiring?

Yes it did. It did. And now, the fellows in the band, and a lot of the bosses, managers, would say Would you like to have a chair? Would you -- or a stool? I said no. No, thank you very much. Because I didn't want to -- back in my mind, I didn't want to say well, Herman, we have to let you go because you can't stand it, and take care of you -- you know what I mean. I didn't want them to do me any favors. I don't want it, because at the end of the week, I put my hand out, say give me -- I don't want to hear that it rained. I don't want to hear anything, you know, because
I went through that so and so. Well, you know what happened? We -- I didn't want to hear that.
(Laughter.)
So I stood up, and I toughened myself. I got tough, and after a while it got so it didn't bother me.
The muscles got built up?

Yeah! At first it did. Then I got where I said oh, what the heck. I don't need it, because I'd be walking around the place without the cane, a lot of times, and forget where in the hell I'd left the cane. I'd try to find it.
(Laughter.)
Looking for the cane and -- (laughs.) I mean, you know, hippity hoppity. I'd be gone, you know. Specially after I'd had a few of these.
Right. But anyhow, you stayed with the band for ten years.
Yeah, I went to Europe twice with them.
Well, I was going to get to where all you went to. At first, in the United States, were you playing mostly in the mid-west?
Yes.
In Pittsburgh, Chicago area?
Well we'd go to -- as I told you, Pittsburgh three or four weeks. And we'd go to Cleveland, for two,

three, sometimes more. And Columbus, Ohio, the same thing, three or four weeks, Columbus. I'm trying to think of -- oh, Toronto, Canada. We used to go for four, three and four, twice, and three times a year. So I mean it -- the time that we had -- what 30? 33 or 34 weeks a year?
Right there.
Doggone right. And that wasn't bad, you know.
And what happened the rest of the year? Did you pick up other dates, or did you lay off?
Well sometimes we would, and truthfully, you'd rather be home. Because you were out so doggone much, you could enjoy being home. You know?
Well if you went back to Toronto two or three times a year, does that mean you played more in Toronto than anywhere else?

Well, maybe yes. Maybe yes, because Toronto, it would be -- it was the greatest jazz town in North America (unintelligible). The people there really go for jazz, and they really enjoy it, and the people -- and they know their jazz. And I met so many jazz collectors there, record collectors, and the people would come up and ask for a tune, and they knew -- we would know what you were playing, and when you were playing it correctly. Had it right.
By the way, they gave me this horn there.
: Oh, really?
Yeah.
: Herman has just taken a trumpet out of the case, showing me. Hey, that's great.
And they gave me that.
: What was the occasion of giving you the horn?

Well, that's an interesting story. I was there with Red, and meantime, Vic Dickenson had an old -- he'd been playing, been using for years, and the darn thing was about gone, you know. And what, 30, what, 30 something years, I think he'd had this.
: Yeah, let me hold the mike here. And then you have two hands for that. I've got it. Okay.
Thank you. And --
: You're talking about Vic and his --
Yeah, so --
-- horn that was falling apart.

-- a friend of ours wrote in to the company, the head of the company and asked them, told them that Vic Dickenson needed a horn, and could they do something about it. So the big manager wrote -- that's it. Let's turn it around. Notice the name of that?
: Right. Uh-huh. This is your European trip, now. In 1968.
Right.
With Red Richards, Vic Dickenson, Herman Autrey, Woodie Powell, Dan Mastry, and George Reed.
Keep that.
Okay.

And that -- so when the man comes in to -- into Toronto he give him a horn. So he -- the manager came in to this club where we were playing, and they asked for Vic, and Vic went down and started with him, said -- he said well, said Herman, come over and join us. I said thank you. And they would talk, and Vic showed them the horn that he had, and the man said that's awful. Wow! Said Herman, what kind of horn do you use? I told him, and he said well I have a [ ]. I said, in fact, Fats Waller gave it to me in 1936.
And he said well let me see it? And he looked at it (laughs). It was just hanging together, you know. Believe me.
(Laughter.)
So he said okay, Vic, come on out to the factory and -- they had a factory there in Toronto -- come out to the factory Monday. And Herman, you come along with him. I said okay.
Now he didn't promise me a horn. He said come on out.
He hasn't said anything, so far.

So when we get out, and I go around with Vic, and Vic try out, oh half a dozens of horns were in this there, and beautiful factory, and all over these beautiful horns, all that stuff. And Vic would play this one. How would you like to have this ? So, finally, we decided on -- I said I like the sound of that one better.
This is the trombone, right?

So, Vic said I think so too. Anyway, now we went and -- (Laughs) -- went in there so the gentleman who worked there, he said okay, now I want to show you some. I said well, I'm visiting. You didn't tell me -- he said aw, well take a look at it. I said well all right (Laughs).

So I took a look at the horns, and here he went in the office and went through the business, and he kept -- the manager kept looking at me. He says Herman, what am I going to do with you? I said I don't know. I said well, should he make me an offer, save me a few bucks, I will buy me a horn, maybe. You know.
So -- so he pulled out two or three long papers there, and he says sign here, sign that one, and sign here and sign this, says go out and pick out a horn.
(Laughter.)
Just like that.
So I went there, and Vic was with me,
and I pick, pick, pick, pick, and I got -- I picked this one. So --
: This is an Olds, Herman?
Yeah. So he wanted me to take a much better horn, a Mendez model. You know Mendez's?
: Rafael Mendez?
Uh-huh. Ohhhh! It was beautiful. I have a recording of his. But I -- I didn't like it. The bell was more like a hammered brass, or -- and it cost much more money than this.
: Uh-huh. What model is this?
This is the -- in the bell. It's in the bell.
: I'm trying to -- trying to --
Here.
: I see, I see it right here, but I'm trying to decipher it. R-e-c-o-r-d -- Recording.
Yeah, Recording. Uh-huh.
: Recording, made -- yeah, made by Olds.
Uh-huh. And I don't know, I seem to like this. I like it much better, and it looked like a sort of a damn fool, but I -- that's what I liked, and what I wanted. So --
: Well, I --
So I got it. And later on I tried to change my mind, I think, but I was too late.
Oh, you decided you would have liked something else better?
Uh-huh.
What, the Mendez?
Yes, mainly because it's a better horn. I mean it's got the -- could have gotten the better horn.
Oh, I see, so you get it -- you endorse the --
Yeah. Uh-huh. That's the (inaudible).
letter from the
Well what's -- yeah, this is -- well, this says Turner Musical Instruments, Limited. That's the Canadian thing for Olds?
Uh-huh.
I see.
Uh-huh.
And so you --
In other words --
-- endorsed -- you endorsed the Olds.
-- you know, so in case I --
What Herman has given me is a letter from Turner Musical Instruments, Limited addressed to Whom it May Concern, U. S. Customs.
yeah.

Saying that this will confirm that Turner Musical Instruments, Limited has presented Mr. Herman Autrey with a new instrument, Olds R-10 Recording Trumpet 579992 in return for his artist's endorsement of our product. Mr. Autrey has provided us with a signed publicity and promotional release which allows us to use his picture and endorsement in our advertising. And it's signed by A. A. Betts, vice-president.
That's him.
(Unintelligible).
Where -- where did you usually play in Toronto?
At the Rialto, and the last place we were playing was at the Ben Get -- naw, that's Washington, D.C. It's the darndest thing.
I'm trying to think of places in Toronto. Did you play the Townhouse?
No.
No?
That wasn't big enough. I mean for --
Was their a Colonial --
Colonial. Colonial.
Colonial Tavern.
Colonial Tavern. And the -- I still say the Ben -- I got to have something in my hand here, but with the name on it, the -- we lived there so damn long, made
records from there, and everything.
You --
Right on Young Street.
ON Young Street.
Yeah.
Want me to open that up, or what?
Yeah, you --
I'll hold that, and then you can open things up. The place you're trying to remember was on Young Street, in Toronto?
Yeah, what was --
The Colonial Tavern also?
Also, yeah. Cava Caber Bob, God damn it!
Cava Caber Bob, right, and that was the record that -- right? The record label.
Yeah, uh-huh. Uh-huh. Yeah, we was there, we played Cava Caber Bob very much. I don't know what that is. (Unintelligible.)
This is a lyric.
Oh? Oh, well.
That's what that is.
Yeah, that's it. Oh, that's all right.
Okay, but anyhow, so you played the Colonial Tavern, and you played the Cava Caber Bob.
Cava Caber Bob. Uh-huh.
And you recorded for the Cava-Bob label, did you?
Uh-huh.
How did that come about? Was the label in existence at the time, or did they start it for you? Or what?

Yes, they start -- I think we were the first, because we were the first jazz band to play there. You know. Saying they started, started this thing, and they made a recording of ours, and got us kind of moving there. It did pretty good. But not as well as the one we did in Germany.
Okay, now tell me about the first time you went to Europe. When was that?
Um, sixty what? Here it is, right here.
In this one? This is '68. That must be a later one.
Yeah, yeah, this is my passport.
Okay. I saw you had something there a little while ago. Yeah.
Don't tell me I've lost that.
Oh, there it is. There it is. Right down here, this is the pass -- Herman's passport, and let's see, when did you start? Ohhhh, let's see, you went --
Sixty --
'69, (inaudible).
Wasn't it?
: Yeah, was '68 the first time?
I think so.
: Oh.
Whatever it's stamped, whatever it is anyway.
: Yeah, everything else and -- they're all stamped '68 and '69.
Yeah, well '68 was --
'68 was your first time there. How did that trip in '68 happen to come up?
Well, Red had, as you know, been to Europe, oh, my God, eight or ten times, about five or six times. Everybody had been over more than Herman had. And --
You hadn't been over at all at that time (laughs). Couldn't be less.
So they had been over several times with different groups, you know. Red went over with -- oh, my God. How many, because different groups, Rudy Powell had been over with different groups. And --
: Vic had been over?
Oh, Vic had been with -- Vic lived over there.
(Laughter.)
So this thing came about after the recording came out, and -- Hugues Panassie --
Oh, uh-huh.
And I knew -- I'd met Hugues back in '38.
When he came over here?
Yeah.
Yeah, uh-huh.

That's when I met him, and he wrote us up, and whatnot. So Hugues was the greatest cause of me coming over, because he told get Herman me different with Autrey, and Herman hadn't never been over, and a lot of people there wait- ing to see me, and whatnot, and so it helped me quite a bit to make the trip.
Was the main reason the whole band was booked was because of you, then?

No, I wouldn't say that. I wouldn't -- no, no. But -- I may have had something to -- you know, because I mean -- well not to do with it, but I think it might have carried a little weight, since they said they were going to bring Herman Autrey. I'll put it that way.
I see.
Maybe. You know? And when we got over, and where we went the place was capacity.
Where did you start, when you first went?
That's why I gave you this.
Oh. Oh.
See, you've got the first place right there, and everything.
This was in -- let's see, European tour.
First date should be there.

Oh, here it is. Here it is. In Antwerp, March, right. Started in March 19th, 1968 in Antwerp. March 20th in Paris. March 21st in [Eiserlom?] What's that? [Eiserlom.] I don't recognize it. March 22nd in Lubeck. March 23rd in Frankfurt and the German Jazz Festival. March 24th in Hamburg at the Star Club. March 25th at Limoges Lemose. Boy, you're playing one-nighters, aren't you?

March 27th in Stuttgart. March 28th in Dijons. March 29th in Montreux. March 30th in Baden. And March 31st in Schafthausen. That's -- one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten, eleven, twelve straight days of one-nighters.
That's right, and we were moving. Oh, man! And when we got to Switzerland, and the Alps, one night
we were very lucky. I thought that was it.
Why?
Well the poor man driving the bus, you know, it was his -- he owned the bus. And he was tired, and he didn't have any relief, nobody to help him.
Did you have one bus that drove you all over -- all these dates?
Yeah.
I see.

So now we're wa-a-a-y-y in the hell up in the mountains, clear up in the Alps, I mean, snowing and ice, and everything, and the wind was blowing, and it almost blew us off the damn thing, and the man went to sleep. Went to sleep, and George Reed, the drummer, and Dan Mastry, bass player, they said Watch it! Look out! And started screaming, and he came to himself, and the guys said man, pull over. Pull over there.

Well, there's too many miles in between here and some of those places you named then, and 200 and 300 miles, all that kind of stuff. That's -- a man can't do all that and he worked last night, and I mean naturally, we're in the bus. We're sleeping, we can -- or nod, trying to, but when you're driving you don't close an eye. You don't bat an eye. You've got to keep awake.
So we almost all of us could have, several times,
gotten killed there, with this thing, you know? What sort of places did you play in? What were they like?
Well, some of them were very nice, and big. And I think --
Like you started in Antwerp. Do you remember -- that was your -- did you just get off the boat and -- or did you fly, or take a boat?
No, we fly.
And you get off the plane in Antwerp and just go right in --

Yeah, we got in -- yeah, because went down to friends and had dinner, had -- they knew some people there, and we went to their homes, and had dinner, fooled around with dinner. We came to the place to play, the concert, and there was -- as I remember -- it was quite spacious, quite a nice place, and they ran a good crowd. And then we left there and went through an alley, or someplace, and came out this street there to a nice place to eat, nice restaurant, and you know.
And from there you're going to go to bed, because you had to -- shoot! Just like in the Army.
You've got to keep moving?
Keep moving, because you had to be up, get up a couple hours or so of sleep, and get up and get a
taxi, and you get to the airport. See? Because -- Oh, this all wasn't done just by bus, then.
Not all.
Some of it was --
You'd get to the airport, or get up and get into the bus, and he had to leave early, [the second] time. You know. And that's what -- that's the way it was happening.
Were these all concerts, Herman, or did you do some in clubs?
Most of them were concerts. Hamburg, Germany, I remember.
The Star Club.
Yeah, that was -- well when we went in they hd two jazz bands there. Jazz -- I mean jazz -- uh, uh, rock.
Rock, oh yeah.
Nuh, nuh, nuh, nuh, nuh -- man you couldn't hear, oh, you couldn't hear -- and so dark, huh?
You went on in between two rock bands?
No, they were -- when we got there they were in -- (laughs). They were playing, you know. And began, and as we went down the side trying to get figure how
in the heck to get in there, it was so dark, and everything was happening. And those different booths, we would play, man, they didn't see us. They didn't give a damn. You know?
(Laughter.)

So went on in the back and ordered us a couple of bottles of Scotch, and you know, sit back there and get our nerves together. And when they finished they said okay, get on the stand, and the lights came up, put the lights up. And they'd never seen nobody looked like us. They'd never heard anything like us. And we opened up the set, and oh, they had some of the most beautiful gals in there I'd ever seen. They looked like they was -- who are they? What is this? What are they doing? I never heard any music like that, and they'd never heard music like ours.
And they went -- oh! And the girls came on the stand while we were playing. They were all around our necks, and what not, sort of thing.
(Laughter.)

And the manager ran out with a contract, he said sign a contract, and I want you to know he said six weeks. And the money was fabulous. You know? He said sign a contract right now, and we just got started. And --
Did you sign it?
Yeah. So Red got together and sat talking business there, and they -- so many weeks for him some of them reached for
him and wanted us to come back, because we were -- we weren't going to be in Germany, weren't going to be there much longer. We was getting ready to come back to the States.

And he wanted us to come back, and had another tour all set. And the money! Oh man, it would have been very nice. But the guy who was booking us, he had a little trouble. He and his wife separated, divorced, and hanky panky, you know. And I think his wife and his business partner were making it. I mean they were in love, and they wanted to change horses in the middle of the stream. One of those things. You know?
So it just loused up the whole damn thing. All the money was gone.
You couldn't take this six-week deal on your own? You had to go through this --
No, because --
-- booker?
This guy who was booking us over there, he was there, tour. He was handling the tour, and --
What had Hugues Panassie done? Had he arranged for the man to do it?
No, he was away down in Paris, but I mean he -- he tells you what to do, or those guys what to do, and he books -- helped to book, and sees that you get this, and sees that you get that. You know.
: I know, yeah.
its pretty bad.
If he says no, well
: Well now this -- in this one place in Hamburg, I assume that they really didn't know who you were. That they'd never had this -- heard this kind of music before.

No, {unintelligible} especially the kids, you know, people dancing, and everything, because it's so dark and you didn't know what the hell you -- you'd really have to know everybody in there to be bumping into somebody and saying hello Joe, what the hell. They didn't have no lights in there, and they'd never heard music like ours.
: But in the other places you played, they knew --
Oh, yeah, they --
-- they knew you from your Fats Waller days, didn't they?

Oh sure. And they knew the tunes that we announced and played, and they knew -- they didn't know when you played it right, too, because different guys would say man I got -- one guy says I've got 52 records of this particular tune. By different bands. You know. And they would know the tune that you played, and they would appreciate -- they wanted to see how you would treat this.
: Yeah, I see.
And how this guy would treat it, and then they'd compare, in their minds, I guess they would comparenotes. But which band, or not, did the better job on -- you know?
How did you do from a point of view of publicity, Herman? Did you get more publicity over there than you normally got over here when you were traveling around?

Yes, I think so, because as we -- as we came into towns, got off the planes, you'd look, you'd see a big, life-size pictures, you know. The guys in the band. Buddy Tate, for one, had a huge -- they'd have a huge thing of him, you know. Because Buddy had been over there so much, and he was known -- and well liked. You know. So --
Were there a lot of newspaper and magazine interviews, radio and television?

Yeah, they had some television, they -- well in Spain, I don't know why it came to my mind. Well, the first time we'd been in Spain, and oh, it was so pretty. The flying in, the skies looked like buttermilk. I mean they said buttermilk skies, and that's -- maybe that's what they meant, because we were so damn high up, and flying and everything was so quiet, and sun, everywhere you looked was sunshine. Everywhere! Everywhere!

Now as the plane starts to settling down, we're coming down over the sea there, and the water was so pretty and blue! And here and there you could see a ripple -- what you call them? The -- as the water would --
Waves?
Yeah, you know, just enough white -- just enough --
Oh, whitecaps.
Yeah.
Whitecaps.

And when they sat down, the airport is right on the side, and the whole thing looked like a beautiful pool table, and you set the plane down, and here's the airfield, and here's the water. It was so damn close I thought they were going to sit in the water there for a minute, you know?
You were worried.
Yeah -- no! It was so quiet, and so peaceful, and beautiful. I mean I was -- I'd never seen anything like that in my life. So --

Now, we hit the ground, okay, come on fellows, you've got to run like hell. I used to get me a wheelchair, had me a wheelchair standing by, you know, 'cause so that I couldn't move like the other guys, by the time you grab your coat here, and grab your luggage, and get this and do the other, and the guy

walk along like me, I would take up too much time, you know? So they have a wheelchair waiting for me, and they rushed -- now you have to get the heck out of there and get to the studio, because we had a TV show. And we got in there to me, it was damp and the people were so damn -- I mean in the studio was cold, like they needed -- I don't know.
Colder than it was outside? In the air?

Yes. Yes it was! It was the damnedest damp. thing. So we got in there and rehearsed like mad, because we had to do a show, and were some singers -- did we have a singer? We had some special things to do, and each one of us had to do a couple of tunes. I had to sing something, and someone -- and now, when we finished that, they'd get out of there and go to -- to a concert, another place.

Oh man! And from that you had to rush because you've got to get back on the plane, and was it -- no, we took the train out of there and came back to France, and that was moving the next morning, and this thing was -- oh, man. And we came through the -- the fields, the vinyards, of grape -- the grapes everywhere you look, to see, you know.
In France?
Yeah. And farms, farms, after work -- woods after so many hours you'll see a little town, maybe, you know (laughs).
Finally we got -- where the heck were we now? Well, finally got back to Paris, and got -- ah, this place in France, this man's a doctor. He --
Let's see, Limoges?

I think it -- I think it is, doggone it. He's a doctor has this whole -- he own -- has his own, well, we couldn't call it a hospital, it was -- I think it was -- but it was too big to be called a hospital. He was -- then he owned, he owned the -- a thing there where they had grapes, and they made their own wine, they gave me a couple of bottles to bring back. And it really was nice. Nice people. Yeah, I got the address here somewhere, written down here somewhere.
Were you moving so fast, Herman, that you never had time to stop in town and get to see much of it?
No -- yes -- I mean -- in Paris I liked to went out of my mind.
(Laughter.)
How long did you stay there?
Let me see, we were there a couple of days. Was it two, or three days? But what happened, coming through the city there, man, whew! I never saw so much traffic.
(Laughter.)

But what do you -- how do you spend your time now? How do the days go by?

Well, truthfully, when I get up in the morning I have to help my wife get out of her, help with breakfast, get breakfast for here. I mean see her off. Maybe I have to see about the car, because she has to drive to work. If there wasn't a car, she couldn't get to work and back.
And she takes me to this clinic or that clinic. I couldn't get there and back. One of those things. And because I haven't been on a bus or subway in years, and I don't intend to go.
(Laughter.)
Because man, you know, I could -- I
don't know what it is. Hitting me in the head, or -- Well, it's not only that. You've got to fight your way on, fight your way off.
That's right, and there's nothing I can do. I mean I say here's - I a guy can't run, they could get at me --
(Laughter.)

And then -- well, I ran into trouble a couple of times coming home from work, you know, carrying my trumpet in one hand, and my walking cane in the other. So I felt this guy in back of me. I knew I was being followed. And I'd stop to take a look. He was stopped, standing behind a post. I see, yes. I've got company!

I said now, if I got real nervous -- I was shaky, real shaky. I said if I could get -- I've got my subway fare. If I could get down under my window, here in the Bronx, if I can get up to my wife, get somebody, I will. So I was -- I kept stopping, looking back, stopping, looking back, so the last time I stopped I looked down the street and I saw one of my wife's cousins.

And he was double trouble any time, drunk or sober, and was pretty well drunk. So he said Hello, Hermie, how're you doing? Well, we were setting there talking a while. He say, You all right? I say yeah. You all right? I say -- you sure you all right? This guy was coming toward, he could
evidently see -- why I was watching him, or something. The guy passed. He say You sure you're all right? I said oh, yeah, everything's fine.
Because I didn't -- I didn't want him to --
(Telephone.)
I didn't want him to get into trouble, you know? [PAUSE]
That's one of my wife's good girl friends.
What were we talking -- oh, we were talking about getting around the street.

Yeah, and I didn't -- I wouldn't tell him, this man that was bothering me, he was trying to rob me or something, because I know -- I could imagine what would have happened, you know, because he -- he told me before, he had done -- had done 15 years for some guy, you know. Some guy had handled him wrong, so they had a fight.

Anyway, I finally got upstairs, but it really hurt me. I was so mad! Because I said if a guy sees me, I'm a cripple. I've got a walking stick. Now here's what he's going to do, grab my horn. If he grabs my horn and run I can't catch him. I can't -- if I sit my horn down to fight him, he can pick it up and run. You know, they hit him with the cane, you can pick it up and run. I say that's the worst. It really hurt me. I was really hurt. I'm -- you know. Well.
Do you see -- or do you see many of

Yes. Quite often, I mean, you know, especially when I go to -- well, I sit there -- go down to Ryan's. A couple of -- excuse me. A couple of those from Ryan's have another place now that they call it the --
Where abouts?
-- Red Balaban band.
Oh, the Condon's. Eddie Condon's. Called Eddie Condon's.

Yeah, I was down there once since they opened. And a few places around town. And usually, when you're in those places, there's always somebody coming in, or walking in, and you haven't seen them in a heck of a long time. He comes -- I heard you were here! And blah, blah, blah. Come on, have a taste, or you know, the whole thing, which is very nice, sometimes very nice indeed.
Herman, looking back -- we've been going over your life now for several days. Looking back over it, how do you feel about it? Do you feel that you did what you wanted to do?
I'd do -- and If I had things to do all over again, by golly I would. I wouldn't change a day of it.
What are you proudest of, of the things you've done?

Well, I'm trying to think. What am I proudest of? They asked me, when I was a very small kid, three or four years old, four years old, not three. I do remember, four years old. I knew I wanted to be a musician, because I had heard the music, and I saw my brother and my dad playing, and they tried to stop me, and they saw they couldn't. And my dad say, are you sure that's what you want to do? I'd say yes. They'd say okay.
And I'm proud that I was able to make it. That's what I'm trying to say. I'm proud of that.
Is there any part of it -- of your life -- that you would have changed?

Only to be a better musician. I would say. You know. Because I had a chance -- well, scholarship to Tuskegee, under Captain Dryer. He was the leader of the band at Tuskegee then, and something happened. I couldn't make it. I didn't get a chance to get in there, and later on in years I was in Boston, Massachusetts, there, and I had a chance to get in the conservatory there. That --

Well, I had many chances. I had a chance in Washington, D. C., in the Howard theater there, you know. I could have gone and studied music, and a few places I did have a teacher here, or a teacher there, but you know. I picked up what I could here from this one, and from that one, and like Prince Robinson, tenor saxaphone player, he was quite a musi-

cian, and he taught harmony, you know. And he -- I have some of his books. He -- you -- he left the books and things, his harmony books and things, to me. And he was supposed to take me on as student, and he passed before we could get together. You know?
And I'm sorry I missed that, from him. He said don't worry about it. I've got the books right here now. They were very expensive books, too.
But you never did actually do any studying, take any --
Yes, I did studying, but I mean I didn't do the studying that I --
That you would like to do.
Would have What I'd like to. Hell yes, I --
Who -- what people were the most important people in your life, that you met, that had the greatest effect on you?
Aww, that's quite -- professional, professional --
Either way, professional, or personal or whatever.
I'm trying to -- I'm just trying to think. I don't --
Would Fats be one of them, or --
Oh heck yes. Definitely. I mean -- I

mean -- well, okay, now I'll start with Fats. Fats, Stuff Smith, the violinist. I think they -- those guys -- well they didn't come any greater. Eddie South was a very fine man. I worked with him too, you know.
Oh, you did? I don't think we ever mentioned Eddie. When did you work with Eddie?

I worked with Eddie here -- what year I was in the Apollo Theater. Every time he came in the Apollo theater he had to augment the band. I would work with him, and he asked me to come on the road with him, which I didn't do, but several times here in New York, in the Apollo I worked with him, and (snaps fingers) Milt Hinton was in the band. I worked with Milt, and Eddie, and the guy they called Chops.
(Laughter.)
Porkchops.
I don't know.
Yeah, he was in the group, and when Eddie first came, and I liked -- but Eddie -- Eddie kind of drove me up the wall there.
Why?

Well, Eddie was a hell of a musician. He would bring an arrangement, say okay fellows, after this show we can go downstairs because I've got a couple of things to go wrote over, you know? And you'd meet him down there, and he'd pull out this -- well, three or four pages, might be one
page, but if it was down there, that's what he wanted.

Now you take the -- rehearse this and play it down, and he say okay, we -- I guess we'll stick it in the show. Now, as you know -- and you come out of the Apollo, you want to run around the corner there, there's a bar, and you say okay, rack them back, throw them back, you know, give us a few, you know. You're with some friends. Either they're buying, or you're buying, but you've got -- and the time is going.
So -- but there you've got to take it easy, because you don't want to take too much and get back to the theater and can't play. You can't remember. You can't get no chops. I mean you blow the gig.

So man, I was in there one week there, I was in there with him every night. You'd have to have -- rehearse this thing, and I was setting there waiting, and they didn't -- he didn't allow, you know, he didn't allow any music stands on the stage.
So you had to memorize?
Memorize it, or put it on the floor, and you'd stand up, you'd look down, you know, and like that, you'd be playing. Looking down on the floor, and you see it, you keep going, you keep playing.
(Laughter.)
Lay it on the stage. And I said oh,
boy, if he's going to play it -- so come in, have to rehearse it. It's hot. You could do it. This show he doesn't do it. Next show he doesn't do it. Whoof!
Tomorrow you say I know he's going to do it first show tomorrow. He don't do it.
(Laughter.)

So now you start going out of your mind. You don't know how to drink. You don't know how to do anything. You know, because he's going to play the damn thing. And they made -- the whole week may pass and you still don't do it.

So, but it was good, the music was good, and he could play, you know. But Stuff, it didn't matter, because Stuff was -- Blap! He'd call the key, so and so. Uh-one, two, one-two-three-four, daddle doodle daddle doodle dah -- he's going to hang in there, you know, for about 20 choruses. Of course he's going to do 25 or 30 (or 40) choruses, so you go and stick in there best you could, and long as you could, and make it sound as good as you could.
So that was the difference between Stuff and -- him when he handed out you know, (unintelligible) the music.
I see, they're very different.
Oh, heck yeah.
What -- overall, what effect do you think that Fats had on you? What did he do to you?

On me? Well, well he -- well, let me see. Character, he was such a gentleman, and a hell of a musician. I don't know if I've ever met a better -- any better musician than he. And he's such a -- every day -- every day he's such a nice guy. I mean every day was sunshine, I mean. He could have a thunderstorm, and he'd say what's the matter? Come on, let's go! Wake up (snap) smile! Let's go. And he'd drink? Come on, that's what you need.

What's the matter here, you've got troubles at home? Whatever, he's (snap) he wanted to make you feel good, and think well, tomorrow's going to be a better day, this afternoon, better, one of those things. You know?
He couldn't possibly always have felt good, did he? There must have been times when he felt pretty lousy (laughs).
Well I mean to be a human, human being, I can't see how he -- but he said he did. And he acted like --
He did? And you were very close to him, too.
Oh, yeah, you know, he and I --
But you never saw him when he was --
No. No.
-- depressed?
I never saw him say Go away, Hymie, I've got troubles! I've got something to think about. Don't
bother me! Never! Never.
That's amazing.
Never, nobody every heard him say that. Now he may have had those times, but --
Musically, how did he affect your career? What did he do for you?

Well, he made me -- well I learned a lot from him, playing with him, in front of him, well, for instance feeling, approach, so much, you know. And that way, and I thought about somebody else. I'm still trying to think of him.

Well I mentioned Caroline Thornton. I mean I wish lots of times I could have been the musician she was. It was like being with Fats, because she was capable. She knew what she was doing. She did it, and did it damn well. The man who taught me and my dad, Mr. Longmyer, I admire him tremendously. Oh, he was such a man, and a musician.
I don't know, I like anyone who seemed to -- uh, master their -- you know, if they know -- if that's what you do, be good at it. Don't be -- if you don't, forget it. You know.
Do you think that the -- the kind of music that you played all your life is sort of disappearing? Do you think things are changing to that extent?
Well, it did. I would say it did. I
mean with rock, and all that stuff, and well, it didn't exactly disappear, but I mean --
You were still here, and there were a lot of other guys who played.

Yes, but I mean you ran into so many so many people say youngsters. I mean -- aw, that old antique, tired music, and so and so and so -- but it's coming right back! Here it comes! It comes right back, and people -- you can't -- look at my man there, with -- the -- uh, doodle deedle deedle da-dee, dee deedle deedle deedle deedle dee -- it was -- the ragtime. Joplin.
Joplin. Oh, Scott Joplin.
A lot of people had never heard of him, and never heard of this, but by golly, look, the whole -- it came back. His tunes came back and upset the whole country.
Right. Eubie Blake came back too.
He was supposed to be retired and all.

I know Eubie -- I know Eubie very well. I worked under Eubie in pit bands, lots of times. Yeah, he was directing the band, directing the orchestra, and oh, Eubie used to say -- we used to -- man, in Philadelphia, particularly, and Standard Theater. We had about oh, ten or twelve piece band. I guess. And Eubie was conducting. And they used to rehearse us. And he says Watch me! Never mind
the -- look at me! I -- anything you want is right here in this stick. Watch my hand. He say I'm going to give it to you. See it? There it is. That's the important thing. (laughs.)

He said Look at me! And it was there. He wasn't kidding. Eubie knows. He knew. And during the intermission the guys would say let's chip in and get a bottle, you know. Eubie would dig somewhere down there and find that dime. Okay, here's my -- hnh, hnh, hnh, and the dime, and when the whiskey comes back he'd say okay, don't forget, I'm the leader. I'm the leader. He'd grab the bottle and take the cork off, and say google, google, google. [Say] his dime.
(Laughter.)
Leader's privilege.
And a dime into a pint, you know how much, huh? You can imagine the thing. God dog!
(Laughter.)
Oh, man!
Did you belong to any of the musical Clef groups in Harlem, the Eat Club, or --
Yes. I was there. I was out there.
What was the other one?
They took me around, and to go in the club -- club, Bass Hill, remember Bass Hill?
Oh, yes. Uh-huh.
Hill --
: Ernest.
Ernest Hill, yeah.
: Ernest Hill, right.
Took me around there. Ohhh! That's been so many years ago.
: You were pretty young then.

Yeah, and (snaps) -- I'm trying to think what else. That other club. (The Clef Unintelligible) club was then, and what else? Was going. And he -- because he told me how important it was that I join, and the fruits that was in this, and -- you know.
: Did you join?

I went around to join, but I -- no. I don't think -- what happened, it didn't go through, or something didn't happen. I didn't go back, or I was supposed to go back, or something. But anyway, that was -- I don't remember signing up.
Were there any other musical organizations around Harlem that you were associated with? Or were you too busy working?
I don't remember (doggone it inaudible). I don't think so. I don't remember.
I know there's a -- I'm trying to think of the name of the group that started out with guys from

Louisville, Kentucky, I think. You know the group I mean? I think Dickie Wells was in it, and a lot of pretty well-known musicians who came from Louisville at the start of it, andc then a lot of other people since have joined it. It's a sort of social club.
Yeah.
But it's -- and I can't think of the name of it off-hand, but you weren't in anything like that.
No, I don't think so. Not right off, no.
You're not a social club type, are you?
(Laughter.)
I went in the Elks, and I come out of there. Yes.

Well Herman, I think we've covered everything pretty much that I can think of. Is there anything you want to say? Any person that we haven't mentioned that you'd like to say something about? How about your brother? What's -- you're fairly close to --
Von?
Yeah, you're pretty close to your brother?
Oh, yes, he's my baby brother, and that's all I got now. And he was supposed to have been here.
He told me he was coming earlier. You know. I guess because of the bridges and the tolls and things --
Oh yes, everything is messed up, right?
Yeah, could be. Gee, I would love to play that record for you before --
Okay, fine.
-- before we go.
I just want to ask you one thing about Von and your relationship to Von. You've been very close to him. How much younger is he than you?
Ah, about six years --
Six years younger than you.
-- six or seven years younger. Uh-huh.
And you were the musician in the family. Did he want to be a musician?

Yes, guitar. He played guitar for a while around New York here, but it -- it was during the Depression, and it was hard to find jobs, and you know, the guys who could play couldn't eat, you know what I mean.
Right. Was he disappointed that he didn't make it as a musician?
Very much so, very much, because he was -- he had a good teacher, and he was playing pretty good, you know. I mean he wasn't outstanding. He was no star. He was
It was just too bad it didn't develop.
Yeah, so he put it down and he got himself a job and did -- did pretty doggone good, because he owns his own home, and I don't.
(Laughter.)
Whereabouts does he live there?
East Elmhurst.
East Elmhurst on Long Island?
Uh-huh. Uh-huh.

Uh, I found a thing that was in an issue of Coda magazine, the Canadian jazz magazine? That had a big Fats Waller issue, had a picture of you in it, and the thing of Von's, about Fats, and he said that Fats always called your mother Mom? Was Fats -- what was Fats like? With your mother?

Oh man, this would be good. You'll like this. We played, what, Birmingham, Montgomery, Alabama, Birmingham, Alabama, and we were on our way south, going down into Florida, and Mobile, and all that business, and New Orleans, and whatnot. So naturally route one goes right through Evergreen, my home town.
So we get -- we got in the bus and rode down. We got there. Mom -- they were expecting us, and Mama and all of
her church friends, and all the people, and they had a table long as from here to my front door, man, you know?
(Laughter.)

With all the trimmings, you know? And all the neighbors had cooked this, and brought this over, and brought that over, and all they had to do was sit down and eat until you go crazy, you know. So [crossed out], the bus pulled up, everybody says so this is -- this is Fats Waller! People hadn't seen me since I was a little boy. And Fats was weighing three -- well, two or three hundred, and a few pounds over.

So -- and he grabbed Mom, and Mom grabbed him. So we had a plum tree, oh, it must have been about seven, eight feet tall, the plum tree? And it was -- oh, six to eight, ten feet wide, you know, what a plum tree looks like. And the plums were just hanging. They were ripe and nice. So I said Fats, what the -- he say Plums! He says, oh my, he just grabs them, he say look at this. Mom says Help yourself, See. But don't get sick, because he had [crossed out].
He said hold this. I've got to get up in the tree. She says No! No! Don't get up in my tree!
(Laughter.)
Mom was laying into him. He said these are so good I'm going to climb the tree and get some more. And that big 300 pound man climbing up in the plum
tree, wouldn't be nothing left. (Laughter.) : Of him, or the plum tree.
So she thought he meant it. Oh no! No sir! Don't do that! Don't do that! And I had to laugh.
: Did you -- if you hadn't been home in that long had you seen your mother very much while you were off?
Well, I took a run home once in a while. Yes. And you know, now and -- not too often. Just long enough to know that they were well, and --
: Has she passed now?
Yes.
: How long ago did that happen?
: '53. Oh. Uh-huh, 22 years --
And my father, '46.
: How old were they when they died?

Let me see, well, my mother and my dad were 73, 70, you know, 73, 74 years old. And my mother was real old when she passed. And she passed in California, and I had just come out of the hospital with this busted hip.
: Oh, that's right. You had --
And I couldn't go to the funeral, and oh, that tore me up. Oh, man, you know. And uh, well.
What was she doing in California?
She was living with my brother. I have a brother living out there. She was out there with him. And in (snap) San Diego.
Nice country out there. Real comfortable.

He owned several pieces of property out there, and had her with him, and family, and she was enjoying it pretty good, but after they lost the old man she, you know, you know, after they'd been together all those many years and --
Did Fats's death break you up? Or --
Oh, yes.
As much as your mother's death, or alike that, or --

Yes it did, it did, because I came home from Philadelphia that day, I came home -- I used to come home every weekend, and I was on my way back, and it came on the radio, and the people started calling up, and saying Fats just passed. I said oh man. Now, I've got to get -- catch a train. I've got to get to the station. I didn't have a car then. I wasn't a driver. I had to get to the station to catch a train and get back to Philadelphia to my job. And I just wasn't up to it.
Oh really?
No.
You just didn't go?

Oh, I finally got back there, but you could imagine the -- you know. I wasn't much of a trumpet player, and you run into people, and that's the way it affected most people, I found out. And I heard people say, people just -- wherever -- in the street, down Broadway, anywheres, wherever they heard it, looked like everything -- a lot of things just stopped standing -- stood still.
Well, it was such a surprise, such a startling thing that happened.

And that's the way he affected people, because he was such a lovable guy. He loved everybody, and how many people came up with a he helped everybody. He was, (unintelligible). The sad story. He'd say just a minute! Wait a minute! Okay. Don't worry about it. You know, and he'd meet you or me on the street, or somebody he would know. How are you? Well, I haven't seen you in a long time. Well how is the Madam? And how are the kids? And he'd judge by your conversation what you're saying, he would know how well you were doing.

And during the conversation, if he felt like it, you wouldn't see it, or know a word about what he's done. He'd put his hand in his pocket and peel off a bill. He'd say well, say hello to the Madam for me, the family, and he'd shake hands with you. And he'd push you away, and he's gone. You close
your hand, and when you look at that thing, he's gone, you've got a bill in your hand.
He's a great guy.

He's done that. I've known so many people, and they'd be standing in the street with tears in their eyes. Or come back stage to see him and probably they wanted to beg him for some -- ask for something, and just couldn't do it, but he would know. He could tell that you needed a buck.
How was his own home life? Was it happy, or not?

Yes -- yes -- (Laughs). I tell -- he was living in the Bronx, and when he'd come home, every so often, he stayed away from home a week, two weeks, three days, five days, four days here at this party, that party, at swank clubs on the east side, and what not. I tell you -- I think I told you about it. And he, and his wife would be waiting for him, his first wife. And they would fight, and she raised hell, and so people, the neighbors, got so they would say -- Here he comes! be -- their heads out the window, and they'd say Hey cops! You know, they'd holler it out the window. Pretty soon you'd hear ZZZooop! Windows opening. Yeah? Did he come in yet? Yeah, he's here. And they would sit there and wait, wait and hear and see the argument. You know? And he'd come in. She'd say

Don't you dare come in here! Blah, blah-blah-blah, Blah, blah blah, blah blah, and she would say I'll shoot you! And -- (Laughs.) Fats said he got tired of running. She told him this so many times he said ah, she ain't going to do nothing.
So this time, this particular time, he didn't run. She ran to a drawer and got the gun and said BLOOEY! Shot him right in the butt!
(Laughter.)
Of all the times he didn't run, that's when he got it.
Could he sit down for a while?
Oh, man. A bullet in the butt, you know. He say she'd been telling him that so many times he didn't figure it was going to happen.
(Laughter.)
That -- well you know about his 'Ain't Misbehavin'' and all that stuff. Did you hear the story about that?
No, what's the story on that?
He wrote that in jail!
He did?

Yeah, she had him locked up for alimony, you know, and he wrote 'Ain't misbehavin', blah-dah doo doo. All by myself, deedle doodle doo, I used to sing the damn thing, Ain't misbehavin' saving my love for you. Hear me
talking to you. I know for certain, you're the one I love. I'm through with flirting, baby, it's you that I'm thinking of. Ain't misbehavin' saving all my love for you.
He was in the hospital -- hospital, -- he was in jail when he wrote this --
Didn't Andy Razof write the words?
Yeah, right, Andy wrote that.
Fats wrote the tune.

Andy Razof and J. C. Johnson. They collaborated. They did a lot of those things. So he was trying to make it lighter on himself for -- you know, give him a break. And then he wrote -- another thing he wrote while he was in there, 'My Fate's in Your Hands.'
Wasn't 'Keeping Out of Mischief' one of the --
'Keeping Out of -- yeah. Keeping (sings) Out of Mischief, dah --
These were all while he was in jail?
Huh?
This was all while --
In jail, yeah. Man, he wrote these tunes in jail, The love that cannot be. all of them came out to be hits.
How long was he in jail?
He told me. How the hell long was he
in there? How many months? I don't remember.
Oh, months? It wasn't just a few days, or --

Well, I mean it was -- you know for alimony, you know how those things can go. He told me. I've forgotten now. I'm trying to think of some of the other things he wrote while he was in jail. Hmmm, hmmm, hmmm, You're my judge and jury, dah dah dah dah doo dah.
'My Fate is In Your Hands.' That's the one, yeah.

Oh, all those things. I mean you've heard of them. You will have anyway. And (when) he came out of jail, let me see, what did he do then? Well, naturally they separated, and he married his second wife, Anita. And then he had these -- Maurice and Ronald, two sons.
No children by the first wife?
Yes. Yes, Junior.
Oh, Junior.
Yeah, he played piano too. He's in there, he's in the Bronx. Uh, uh --
I thought that-- well Maurice does.
Maurice plays piano. I did a thing with him not too long ago.
And is it Thomas, Junior, who also plays?
Yeah. Yeah. And doesn't play badly, either.
But not as good as the father.

Oh, none of them did. Well, I would say that Maurice could have at one time, but -- and it gets back to the same question you asked me, why don't the young people take up jazz, and why didn't jazz -- because they didn't like it. They figured -- brrzzppt -- that's old antique stuff. Get with the new thing.

Now Maurice supposedly made (unintelligible) my old man, that's his bag, and he went for the modern thing. And starved to death. He couldn't get arrested! Now he's going -- last time I saw him he's trying to do like the old man.
Oh, he is?
Yeah. And I did a thing with him he wasn't -- back of the thing, was -- um, downtown here, concert, and --
Oh, is that the Theater De Lys that he was -- where Maurice played with --
No, this was a hotel.
Oh, hotel.

Where he did a concert, and sold a lot of tickets, and whatnot. Trying to think who the hell else it was. Who all were there. They had quite a band. And after that he was going to Florida, or somewhere, to do something in the -- and a lot of -- what a heck of a booking! But I
haven't read anything about what he's supposed to be doing now, you know? But he's -- I hope he's doing good. I hope he's doing all right.
I hope so. Well Herman, thanks very much. I think we've got it all down now.
I think we've got it all down. I think so.
Yeah, and do you want to play that -- you've got a tape of that other thing?
Yeah, yeah. Yes, I've got to Find that thing.
(Music up.) "Do You Know What it Means to Miss New Orleans" by Saints and Sinners.
(End of proceedings as recorded.)
